THE ORCHARD AND THE HEATH. I chanced upon an ,-arly walk to spy A troop of children through an orchard gate; The boughs hung low, the grass was high; They had but to lift hands and wait For fruits to fill them; fruits were all their sky. They shouted, running on from tree to tree, And played the game the wind plays, on and round. 'Twas visible invisible glee Pursuing; and a fountain's sound Of laughter spouted, pattering fresh on me. I could have watched them till the daylight fled, Their pretty bower made such a light of day. A small one tumbling sang, " Oh ! head !" The rest to comfort her straightway Seized on a branch and thumped down apples red. The tiny creature flashlng through green grass, And laughing with her feet and eyes anyng Fresh apples, while a little lass Over as o'er breeze-ripples hung: That sight I saw, and passed as aliens pass.: My footpath left the pleasant farms and lanes, Soft cottage-smoke, straight cocks a-crow, gay flowers; Beyond the wheel-ruts of the wains, Across a heath I walked for hours, And met its rival tenants, rays and rains. Still in my view mile-distant firs appeared, When, under a patched channel-ba.nk enriched With foxglove whose late bells drooped seared, Behold, a family had pitched Their cae.p, and labouring the low tent upreared. Here, too, were ula.ny children, quick to'scan A new thing coming; swarthy cheeks, white teeth: In many-coloured rags they ran, Like iron runlets of the heath. Dispersed lay broth-pot, sticks, and drinking-can. Three girls, with shoulders like a boat at sea Tipp'd sideways by the wave (their clothing slid From either ridge unequally), Lean, swift, and voluble bestrid A starting-point, unfrocked to the bent knee. They raced; their brothers yelled them on, and broke In act to follow, but as one they snuffed Wood-fumes, and by the fire that spoke Of provender, its pale flame puffed, And rolled athwart dwarf fuzzes grey-blue smoke. Soon on the dark edge of a ruddier gleam, The mother-pot perusing, all, stretched flat, Paused for its bubbling-up supreme: A deg upright in circle sat, And oft his nose went with the flying steam. I turned and looked on heaven awhile, where now The moor-faced sunset broaden'd with red light; 'Threw high aloft a golden bough, And seemed the desert of the night Far down with mellow orchards to endow. GEORGH MEREDITH. "Poems and Lyrics of the Joy of Earth."

Silence is the safest response for all contradiction that arises from impertinence, vulgarity, or envy. He who is sympathetic has his enterance into all hearts, and is the solver of all human problems. To him is given dominion where he thinks to serve; and the love which he gives without stint, as without calcubtion, he receives back without measure, as without conditions. A CASE FOR A LAWYER.—Here is a cutting from an old number of an Essex paper :—" A correspondent furnishes us with the following slip from a genealogical tree which, according to his statement, appears to have flourished in this country. A widow married a young man, and her daughter-in-law married his father. By the widow's mar- riage with the son she became her husband's grandmother, consequently great grandmother to a son, the fruit of this marriage. Now, as the SON of a great grandmother must be a grandfather or great uncle, this boy must be his own grandfather." THE TIME FOR MARIIICT:Some curiouss speculation might be raised as to se causes of the preference which prevails for parti'-diar seasons as the time for marrying. In the Sprine:,* the poet says, a young man's fancy lightly turns tol'ce.As a fact, however, the first three months of .the ;ear are the period when the fewest weddings are cele- Prated In England, the favourite quarter being the months of October, November, and December. This is true not only of the country as a whole, but of the indtvidual counties. Lincolnshire is the only county where the Spring weddings ;exceed the autumnal ones. In two other counties on the uppsite side of the island, Hereford and. Salop, the maximum 'of marria¢,•es is found in the second onarter of the year. But these three counties are the sole exceptions to the rule. It is tolerably well known that May Is not a favourite month for mirrriages, and it appears that both in town and country the fewest marriages occur in that month. The rule does not hold good in all countries. On the contrary, in Den- mark, Germany, and Switzerland,. May seems to be a favourite month for matrimony In France, too, May mar- riages are slightly in excess of those in other months. Whether, as has been imagined, the English repugnance to May weddings, which is even exceeded by that felt in Scot- land, is dus to the association of that month with the coitus of the Blessed Virgin is a moot point which will probably never be settled. In ancient Rome it was deemed unlucky to marry in May, because the festk-al of departed souls was held in that month. ABOUT THE EVES.—" The eyes," Emerson says, "speak all languages. They wait for no introduction, ask no leave of age or rank; they respect neither poverty nor riches, neither learning nor power, nor virtue, nor sex, but intrude and come again, and go through and through you in a moment of time. The eyes of men converse as much as their tongues, with the advantage that the ocular dialect needs no dictionary, but it is understood all the world over. When the eyes say one thing and the tongue another, a prac- tised man relies on the language of the first. If a man be off his centre, his eyes show it. You can read in the eyes of your companion whether your argument hits him, though his tongue will not confess it. There is a look by which a man shows he is going to say a good thing, and a look when he bas said it. Vain and forgotten are all the fine offers and offices of hospitality if there be no holiday in the eye. Some are aggressive and devouring. There are asking eyes, asserting eyes, prowling eyes, and eyes full of fate—some of good and some of sinister omen. The alleged power to charm down insanity, or ferocity in beasts, is a power behind the eye. It must be a victory achieved in the will before it can be signified in the eye. It is certain that each man car- ries in his eye the exact indication of his rank in the im- mense scale of men." All this is very fine, and most of it very true; but how much more pointed and effective might the philosophic dreamer of Concord have made his oracular sayings if he had understood the true physiognomy of the eye—known why it languishes with love, glows with passion, gb ams with hate, sparkles with mirth, clashes with anger, melts with pity, and lights up with joy, or is darkened in sorrow; why prayerfulness turns it upward and humility bends it toward the earth; what expression commands, what forbids, what reproves (giving "the chas- tisement of the eye"), what commends with "an approving look," and so on. Rosana ow LONDON LIFF..—The tendency of the entire national energy, writes John Ruskin, is to approximate more and more to the state of a squirrel in a cage, or a turnspit in a wheel, fed by foreign masters with nuts and dog's meat. And, indeed, when we rightly conceive the re- lation of London to the country, the sight of it becomes more fantastic and wonderful than any dream. Hyde Park, in the season, is the great rotatory form of the vast squirrel sage; round and round it go the idle company, in their re- versed streams, urging themselves to their necessary exer- cise. They cannot, with safety, even eat their nuts without so much revolution as shall "comply with the demands of hygiene." Then they retire into their boxes, with due quantity of straw, the Belgravian and Piccadillian streets outside the railings being, when one sees clearly, nothing but the squirrel's box at the side of his wires. And then think of all the rest of the metropolis as the creation and ordinance of these squirrels, that they may squeak and Whirl to their satisfaction, and yet be fed. Measure the 'Pace of its entirely miserable life. Begin with the diagonal struck from Regent-circus to Drury-lane; examine it, house by house; then go up from Drury-lane to St. Giles's Church. look into Church-lane there, and explore your Seven Dials and Warwick-street, and remember this is the very centre of the mother city—precisely between its parks, its great library and museum, its principal theatres, and its bank. Then conceive the East End, and the melancholy Islington and Pentooville districts; then the ghastly spaces of southern suburb—Vauxhall, Lambeth, the Borough, Wapping, and Bermondsey. All this is the nidification of those park squirrels. This is the thing they have produced round themselves; this their work in the world. When they rest from their squirrelli in revolutions, and die.in the Lord, and their works do follow them, these are what will follow them. Lugubrious march of the Waterloo•road, and the Borough, and St. Giles's ; the shadows of all the Seven Dials having fetched their last compass. New Jerusalem prepared as a bride, of course, opening her gates to them; but, pertinaciously attendant, Old Jewry outside. "Their works do follow them." For these streets are, indeed, what they have built; their inhabitants the people they have chosen to educate. They took the bread and milk and meat from the people of their fields they gave it to feed, and retain here in their service this fermenting mass of un- happy human beings —news•mongers, novel-mongers, pic- ture-mongers, poison-drink-mongers, lust and death mon- gers, the whole smoking mass of it one vast dead-marine storeshop--accumulation of wreck of the Dead Sea, with every activity in it a form of putrefaction.

PENSION TO M. PASTEUR.—After Some discussion, the French Chamber of Deputies has voted the proposed in- crease of M. Pasteur's pension to 25,000 frans (£1,000) an- nually, as a national award. TREE PLANTING.—The Mexican Government has con- tracted with Mr. Oscar A. Droege, to plant 2,000,000 trees in the valley of Mexico, within four years from March 15, 1884-500,600 a year, in such places as the Government

shall choose. AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS IN IRELAND.—Reports from all parts of Ireland have been collected and published by the Irish Farmers' Gazette (Dublin) on Saturday. The hay crop is light, but not so deficient as at one time expected to be. The harvest is from one to three weeks later than ordinarily. The wheat crop is below an average. The bar- ley crop is the best cereal crop of the year. Oats vary greatly, but on the whole the crop is thought to be rather above an average. The potato crop is a large and good one, Root crops promise well. Pastures have improved, and stock are thriving except where attacked by foot-and-mouth

disease. TEETOTAL HAUVESTING.—Mr. John Abbey, the total ab- stainer who engaged in the contest with a beer drinker in the harvest field the other day, has published an account of the proceedings, in the course of which he states that he had not done any work in the harvest field for twenty-one years previously. He denies that there was any wager. The loser was to give £5 to the Salisbury Infirmary. His opponent, Mr. Terrill, would not consent to his drinking oatmeal and water, which was very unfair, as it is not pre- tended that pure water is a good harvest drink. He says that, allowing time for refreshments, there were 40a. Or. 33p. of wheat pitched in eleven hours-20a.. 2.r. 7p. by Ter- rill and 19a. 2r. 26p. by himself. He has challenged Mr. Terrill to another contest next harvest, stipulating that he shall be allowed to drink oatmeal water. Acting upon their in- structions, Mr. Jenkins, the secretary, has sent the sub- joined list of questions to a large number of agriculturists who are known to have undertaken private experiments :- 1. What are the dimensions of your silo? E. Is it above or below the level of the soil? 3. How is it conetrueted. especially as to materials? MITrtIATING CATTLE.—A Mold cattle dealer, named Richard Price, was, at Denbigh, fined £7 for having muti- lated three cows. He had cut the animals with a knife for the purpose of identification. He pleaded, in defence, that marks made with scissors did not last long enough. RAILWAY COMPANIES AND FARMERS.—It is pleasing to find county court judges taking a common-sense view of the liability of railway companies in connection with their re- sponsibilities to farmers. At Cockermouth, the other day, John Ferguson, farmer, of Dovenby, sued the Maryport and Carlisle Railway Company for damages laid at £7 to a crop 'of hay. It appeared that a tree belonging to the railway company had fallen, blocked a watercourse, and sent the water, with coal dust from a neighbouring colliery, over the hayfield. The company bad since cleared out the stream. Judge Ingham made the sensible remark that the company's own acts were the strongest against them. They said they I had nothing to do with it, yet they went and cleared out I the stream, clearly showing that they anticipated liability. I He gave a verdict for the full £7, with costs. Antstecrr.TußAL ENTOMOLOGY.—Mies Eleanor A. One- rod, consulting entomologist of the Royal Agricultural Society, writes as follows :—" Will you permit me to men- tion, through the medium of your columns, that, as the time for beginning to prepare my yearly report is drawing near, I should feel greatly obliged to any of your contribu- tors who might be disposed kindly to favour me with any notes of measures found serviceable at paying rates to les- sen effects of insect ravage on the field crops. Daddy long- legs grubs, beet and mangel leaf maggot, and cabbage root fly maggot have been amongst the bad attacks of the year. It would be very desirable to know whether any measures are used (such as are known to be of use against wireworm) to prevent egg-laving of daddy long-legs on pasture or clever ley before breaking up. Similar applications of hot lime, gas lime, sfec., might be expected to be of great service. Mengel leaf maggot attack having only been a serious mat- ter for a few years, we know hardly anything about its pre- vention as yet, excepting the benefit of keeping up growth to support the plant, and special dressings for this purpose do not act in needful time unless there is rain. Cabbage root maggot has been found to vary in amount of attack ac- , cording to the kind of manure (animal or chemical) applied. Any information on these subjects or on hop fly or any other important attack would be gratefully received, and, as before, I hope to be permitted to request acceptance of a copy of the report of those who kindly contribute service- able information." I AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION.—The Institute of Agriculture , for the forthcoming session will open on October 1, when ; Mr. Bernard Dyer, F.O S., F.1.C., will begin a course of forty 'lectures on " Chemistry in Relation to the Soil." The lec- tures will be given each morning during October in the ' theatre of the Museum of Geology, Jermyn-street, London, which will be lent for the purpose by the Lords of the Com- mittee of Council on Education, who have also placed at the disposal of the Institute the lecture theatre of the National History and South Kensington Museums. Concurrently with Mr. Dyer's lectures, a course of practical instruction on the " Use of the Microscope" will be given by Mr. F. I Cheshire, after which Professor G. T. Bettany will deliver a 'course of twenty lectures on "Vegetable Physiology in re- lation to Farm Crops," to be followed by ten lectures on I "Diseases of Farm Crops," by Mr. Worthington G. Smith. I The next course will embrace twenty lectures on "Animal Physiology in relation to Farm Stock," by Professor Wort- ley Axe, and a series will then be given by Miss Eleanor A. Ormerod, on "Farm Insects. Mr. W. Topley, F.G.S., will then give twenty lectures on "Geology and Physical Geo- logy in relation to Agriculture," and, after Christmas, Pro- fessor R. V. Tuson will lecture on the "Chemistry of the I Food of Farm Stock," Professor Buckman on "Farm Seeds," I Professor Tanner on "Agriculture," and Mr. Robert Holland on the "Management of Grass Land." Ten lectures, each on the "Breeding and Management" of "Horses," Cattle," and "Sheep," will be given by Mr. Gilbert Murray, Mr. W. Housman, Mr. Henry Woods, and Mr. J. Algernon Clarke; ten on "Preventible Diseases in Farm Stock," by Professor Wortley Axe; and twenty on "Farm Implements and Ma- chinery," by Messrs. W. R. Bousfield and W. Worby Beau- mont. During the spring months a course of 60 lectures will be given on "Poultry, Dairy, and Bee Management ;" and ten Monday evening lectures on various subjects connected with agricultural science will be given, as in the case of last year. The course of instruction has been arranged in such a manner as to enable students to give their undivided atten- tion to one subject at a time. As soon as each subject, in rotation, has been satisfactorily dealt with, the examination upon that subject will take place, and the attention can then be directed to some other branch of study. It is also de- signed to afford facilities for any persons who may desire to attend any one course, or more, by concentrating that section of work within the shortest time svhiCh is really necessary for a proper study of the subject. As a rule only two lectures will be given daily (generally in the morning), which will allow ample time for a proper record of the lec- ture notes, and for systematic private study. Furthe infor- mation may be obtained from Professor Tanner, Holleran, Secretary, Institute of Agriculture, South Kensington, Lon-- don, S.W.

COTTAGE GARDENING The recent showery weather has given us considerable trouble, for we have not been able to destroy any weeds. Hoeing is useless, and hand weeding is slow work, but in many cases inevitable. Just now we have odd patches of ground unoccupied except by weeds, and, not being partial to this crop, we had the ground dug sufficiently deep to bury them, which confirmed the truth of the old proverb, "Out ,of sight out of mind." Some people dislike burying weeds, but we can answer them that they need not be apprehensive of any mischief from all weeds of the annual class. No one would think of covering the roots of couchgrass, net- tles, and similar perennials, but rather pick up every piece ' and convey it somewhere outside the boundary of the gar- den.

THE FRONT GARDEN.—Any bulbs that may have been grown in pots in the window, more especially the Hyacinth, may now be turned out of their pots and planted in the front garden, where they may be of service, but if left in the pots they will be of no use, and the pots may be wanted for other plants or bulbs. For that reason we plant them out much earlier than this. When grown in pots, part of the bulb is usually above the soil, but when planted in the open ground it should be four inches below the surface of the soil. As we may soon expect slight frost no time should be lost in securing cuttings of any Geraniums of the bedding out class, and if they are firm and kept moderately dry they may form roots enough to keep for the winter. Unless they can have the protection of a cold frame they are best in the window with a south aspect, Geraniums being of such a succulent nature that there is scarcely ever such a thing as killing the cuttings by exposing them to too much sun, and we have seen them form roots when accidentally left on the surface of the soil. Plants of the tricolour section and some of the light variegated should be lifted and put in pots as soon as there is any indication of frost. We must condemn the practice of shortening any of the shoots, as some are wont to do. The vitality of the plant just removed , from the ground is at such a low ebb that too many ampu- tations prove a perilous proceeding. Whilst we thus hesi- tate to remove a shoot at this time, we fearlessly remove all the leaves excepting two or three at the point of each shoot. This may appear anomalous, but it will be observed that I , before many days have elapsed all the foliage will be I withered, and for what benefit it has been to the plant in its present circumstances it might have been as well re- moved at the time of lifting, and indeed preferably, for it could have been done much easier. These decayed leaves frequently communicate decay to the tender shoots, which occasionally rims through the whole plant like gangrene. THE Wilinow.—Some people's notions of what a window plant should be differ greatly from ours. A plant that will only exist for a short period of the year in the window is not a fitting tenant for it. What we regard as a window plant is that which has and may be grown in the window the year round, and those who have the framing of sche- dules for horticultural exhibitions never contemplated any other meaning should be attached to it. It would appear some cottagers take a different view to what we do, seeing that they present at exhibitions such tropical plants as Cocos Weddelliana, a species of palm usually associated with drawing-room decorations and the pocket of their owner more than that of the cottager and his window. The only way to discourage such plants in the cottagers' classes is to state in the schedule that only those plants which can be grown in the window the year round will be eligible to com- pete. The hyacinth season has now come round, and the new bulbs will be offered for sale. They are low in price, easily grown, and are very fragrant. They delight In rich, light soil; loam leaf. mould and some horse-droppings off the road should be got in readiness, as well as some good river sand, CELERY will have arrived at a stage when a few more instructions respecting earthing up may be of use. Assum- ing, that it was planted in trenches, these will have been by how filled up in the process of earthing. Hitherto the work has been very simple, but when the rows come to require banking up the inexperienced becomes thoroughly per- plexed, for it frequently occurs that what he has done one day in the way of banking has collapsed after the first , shower of rain. The truth is he has either undermined his I foundation or he has confounded the structure of a bank or wall of earth with that of stone or bricks and mortar, and has made the former so perpendicular that it could not pos- sibly stand. When we have got our trench filled we pack all the soil required round our celery; the line is then stretched 14in. from the plants im each side, and the soil is chopp the spade being held obliquely, and it is obvious j.. 4; that by so doini; we widen the base of our bank, and as the earth is put to the plants it becomes narrower each time, SO that if a section were made when completed It would repre- fnm 31t. to 3in. Such with all his disin- tegrating bent kc column mm ons ot dPe:;firaasnl'i'd,f atac ir7s t " powers. Many in their first attempt to grow celery are in too much hurry to place the earth to it, think- ing that they hasten its blanching; there may be a slight gain, but it is frequently attained by permanently crippling many of the plants, for we find that if the soil is put too early the centre leaves become disturbed and the progress of the plant is frustrated. The soil is also frequently thrown haphazard towards the plant, as if the mere act of placing it in their vicinity is sufficient. Every head should be grasped by one hand near the surface of the ground, whilst the other is engaged in drawing the most mellow of the sur- face soil and packing it tolerably firm round the plants, for, upon no account should soil be allowed to enter the centre or between the leaves, and the central leaves should always be in advance of the earthing.

He that never changed any of his opinions never corrected any of his mistakes; and he who was never wise enough to find out any mistakes in himself will not De charitable enough to excuse what he reckons mistakes in others. A philosopher and a wit were crossing from Dover to Calais, when a storm arose, and the savant seemed under great apprehensions lest he should go to the bottom. "That," observed the wit, "will suit your genius; as for me, you know I only skim the surface of things." Be reserved, says William Penn, but not sour ; grave, but not formal; bold, but not rash; humble but not servile; patient, but not insensible; constant, but not obstinate; cheerful, but not light; rather be sweet-tempered than familiar; familiar, rather than intimate; and intimate with very few, and on good grounds.

THE LAST GLADIATORIAL FIGHT IN THE COLISEUM.— In 404 Honorius was emperor. At that time in the remote deserts of Lybia, there dwelt an obscure monk named Tele- machus. He had heard of these awful scenes in the far-off Coliseum at Rome. Depend upon it, they lost nothing by their transit across the Mediterranean in the hands of Greek and Roman sailors. In the baths and market:places of Alexandria, in the Jewries of Syrene, in the mouths of every itinerant story-teller, the festive massacres of the Co- liseum would doubtless be clothed in colours truly appal- ling, yet scarcely more appalling than the truth. Tele- machus brooded over these horrors until his mission dawned upon him. He was ordained by heaven to put an end to the slaughter of human beings in the Coliseum. He made his way to Rome He entered the Coliseum with the throng, iat the time the gladiators were paradiug in front of the I Emperor with uplifted swords and the wild mockery of homage—"Morituri te seatant." Elbowing his way to the ibarrier, he leapt over at the]mornent.when the combatants I rushed at each other, threw himself between them, bidding them, in the name of Christ, to desist. To blank astonish. ment succeeded Imperial contempt and popular fury. Tele- machus fell slain by the swords of the gladiators. Legend may adorn the tale and fancy fill out the picture, lout the 'solid fact remains—there never was another gladiatorial fight in the Coliseum. One heroic soul had caught the flow lof popular feeling that had already begun to set in the Idirection of humanity, and turned it. He had embodied by his act and consecrated by his death the sentiment that al- ready lay timidly in the hearts of thousands in that great city of Roml.—"Footprints in Rome," by the Rev. H. R. Haweis, in " Good Words."

ANECDOTES OF TEM COMTE DE CHAMBORD.—Numbers of stories and anecdotes are already being told about the Comte de Chambord, some old, some new, and many prob- ably not altogether reliable. They all, however, illustrate some phase of character or peculiarity of habit. Owing to the life of comparative retirement led for so many years by the deceased Prince, there are no startling and sensational incidents to be recorded of him, but only such simple stories as may be expected of so simple a nature. Many of them refer to his childhood, when his grandfather, Charles X., was still upon the throne, and young Henri was study- ing with his sister, under the care of the Marquise de Gon- taut. Like boys of lower rank, he was rewarded for success at his books by small presents of money, which the young Prince, unlike most other boys, devoted to the poor; indeed, so acute was his sense of charity that it was only necessary to say to him when he seemed inclined to grow indolent, "Take care, monseigneur ; if you are so idle your poor will suffer," for him to set to work with new energy in order to earn his reward. Happening to overhear a distinguished officer ely to the King, "Your Majesty cannot imagine how many poor relations I have discovered now I am a rich man," the simple-hearted boy ran up to him, crying, "Oh, General, if I had known you had so many poor relations I would have worked much harder; but I've still got twenty francs, and yQu must take those." One of his favourite sayings, never to be realised, was, "I should like to be a second Henry IV." His love was for his native country I was always remarkable from his earliest years until he lay, weak and wasted, upon his death-bed, crying, "France! France!" between his moments of pain and unconscious- ness. When he was twelve years old he received his first commission, and on that day was told of the tragical death of his father, the Due de Berri. The boy wept and par- doned, just as his father—lying in the agonies of death in a room of the Opera House—had exclaimed, "Pardon my murderer." After the death of Charles X. young Henri made a European tour, and was put through every sort of athletic exercise. He was taught to swim well at a very early age, and when he could manage to keep afloat with all his clothes he uttered the characteristic remark, "Now I shall be able to save somebody." It was in 1841 that he met with the accident that lamed him for life. He was out riding one day in the environs of Kirchberg, when his horse, a very spirited animal, shied at a cart and refused to pass it. The Comte, a bold rider, persisted; the horse reared, and some bystanders ran to the rescue. "No, no," cried the Prince; "if there be any danger that is my affair." So saying, he dug his spurs into the animal's sides. The fran- tic horse reared again, lost its balance, and fell over, crush- ing its rider beneath it. In its efforts to rise the animal weighed still more heavily upon the Comte's leg, causing him dreanful pain, and, as it proved to be in the end, break- ing his thigh. His only remark was, "What a pity it was not on the battlefield!"

THE EXAMINER, SA TURDAY, SEPTEMBER 229 1883: SOME NOTES ON VICTORIA. No. TH. With the Railways forming an undertaking of the Govern- ment, with the police system a State institution, and with the State school teachers as servants of the central authority, the number of Government employes in Victoria is neces- sarily very large. I have no means of ascertaining the total number of these, and those civil servants engaged in the administering of Government, but I am quite certain that the various services of the Crown are considerably over- .manned. The patronage system under which members and lionstituents alike have had to be placated is responsible for this stuffing of offices and consequent extravagance of ex- penditure of the tax-payers' money. A large quantity of appointments are notorious sinecures, and there is a grand opening for a ministry of courage to effect an immense sav- ing to the State by a sweeping reduction which, though it I would by no means impair the efficiency of the several de- partments, would . greatly ease the labour market of the colony, and, in the end, be the means of developing resources at present dormant. A member of the present Government assured me lately that on his entering office he was astounded at the extent to which officers had multiplied. In his own department he was convinced that the reasonable work of three men was throughout spread among five. It is not that the individual pay is very high as compared with the money that is to be made in other walks of life, but it is that voters appear to have been with remarkable unanimity poesessed of a desire to receive government money for them- selves or to quarter their relatives on the State. The ser- vice will, however, become leas abused in a while. A recent act of the colonial Parliament abolishes retiring pensions to all new civil servants, and a strong coalition Government which has latterly taken the reins of power, is pledged to undertake a root and branch reform, and specially to give the coup to the system of political patronage. In the in- terests of economy and honesty it is to be hoped they will be entirely successful in these purifying labours. Probably the most efficient branch of the public service is that of law and justice. A bench of able superior judges and a body of very capable inferior judges and stipendiary magistrates administer the law in a speedy if not in a cheap form. The County Court jurisdiction is a particularly ad- mirable one, allowing, as it does, of the trial of large as well as small common law and equity causes. In the courts of petty sessions there may be heard trivial claims on sum- mons for goods sold and labour done, and all round I think the appeal to the courts is less cumbrous than in the mother country. There is one feature which could be safely dis- pensed with here, seeing that there is a capable staff of paid magistrates itinerating the districts—a staff that could, of course, be increased, should it be necessary—and it is the class of honorary justices. These gentlemen—they are all styled gentlemen, I suppose, though in some instances they are hardly entitled to it—are in far too many cases neither useful nor ornamental. Through the influence of the mem- bers for the district, the party in office has induced the Governor to sanction their being gazetted J.P.'s. Many— perhaps the majority of them—are in a position both from their standing and general attainments to claim the respect of their fellows, and are relatively as well entitled to a mark of honour as the unpaid magistracy of Great Britain; but there are others who are among the most ignorant and boorish of parvenus, and who commit themselves a vast deal oftener than the law, fortunately, allows them to com- mit other people. A late Government, during an existence of about 18 months, exercised its patronage in this line by making between 400 and 500 honorary justices. Happily the mischief that one of these may do is exceelfilY Hug*, petty session clerks who know the law ate able to check their 6xtravagance and pot theeta straight, when otherwise their worships would drift into gene serious error. The police force of Victoria has lately been having its dirty linen washed before a Royal Commission. This Com- mission has reported that the force is in a highly de- moralised state, and haslOrmulated a long series of recom- mendations for an amendment. This force is a quasi military body, and seems to be animator' by a more than ordinary amount of jealoesy, but, the Royal Commission to the contrary, it fulfils, its functions with as fair a measure of success as can be expected from it as at -present constituted. The knowledge of the sergeants; sub-inspectors, and inspee- tore in charge of atatious and districts, that they are amenable only to the heads of their depArtment of the Go- vernment service, induces what may be described as the "insolence of office," as regards their bearing towards the public they are called on in the respective localities to pro- 'tect. Otherwise the force, which is very largely recruited from the ranks of the Irish colonists, is a decently reputable and effective one. Sir Henry ParkeS, the New South IA elshman, stated during his recent visit to England that the Australian Colonies had Eething to learn from the Old Country. This bombastic remark was much canvassed at the time; for, with every desire to laud and magnify the land of their adoption, the Australians are not so vain as to imagine they have all the excellencies, There are some points in which New South Wales and Victoria are undoubtedly in advance of the parent from which they have sprung. But, on the other hand, there are many points in which these Colonies are terribly below the English standard. In this latter cate- gory the Victorian Railway system, wonder fully extensive as it is, must be included. There are several trunk and branch lines which have opened out the country in every direction. These are capable of further useful and desirable expansion at a reasonable cost. The requirements of trade and the convenience of passengers are on the whole well met as regards both the character of the vehicles and the celerity of the service. Especially is this the ease in the metropolitan district, where the two classes of carriages are all that could be desired, and the frequency of trains in every way up to the needs of a busy centre. In one or two particulars the accommodation for the traveller ie anything, more thoughtful than in Engleed generally—viz., in the provision on evay train of apartments exclusively for ladies, and the insistance that at every refreshment station the contractor shall with the liquors he vends also be ready to supply tea and coffee as desired, and chops aid steaks with potatoes. The refreshment-rooms at these stopping stations may not have the attractive appearance of one of Spiers and Pond's buffets on the Midland Railway in England, but the provender is there, and for a shilling the passenger gets a good square meal. It has to be acknowledged, however, that there is a deplorable want of regular system in much of the policy and management of the railways in Victoria. The system has grown beyond the ability of a single man to manage in the way a conscientious Railway Minister tries to do it. A Board is required for this, and the Minister could then be left to settle with his colleagues of the Cabinet all questions of policy. Some such reform is projected, and there can be no doubt it is needed. Meanwhile, Board or no Board, no time ought to be lost in adopting better ap- pliances for the safe working of the traffic. With the most perfect regulations accidents will unfortunately happen, but the best precautions should be taken to avoid them. lam afraid that in respect of signalling apparatus and brake power the Victorian Railway Department cannot claim to have shown a readiness to follow the best or, indeed, any satisfactory methods. For its omission in this regard it is at the present time paying through the nose_ Two deplor- able collisions on the suburban lines, which would never have happened with such terrible results had the trains been provided with efficient brake machinery, have cost the Department between two and three hundred thousand pounds. Save in the metropolitan district, no trains are run on the Sunday in Victoria, an arrangemert very pleasing and satisfactory, no doubt, to those who want to travel on that day between Melbourne and the suburt s, but hardly so to those whose lot it is to live in the country. The subjsct of Sunday observance generally may be at this point mentioned. There is no delivery of letters any where, and the telegraph offices are also practically closed. A legal fiction also closes the public-houses. As a matter of fact, there are probably not five hotels among a handred which do not on the Sabbath do a thriving trade. Some, in truth, have larger receipts on the Sunday than on any other day except Saturday. Nearly every "public" in Melbourne —and, for aught I know, in Victoria—has a sort of by- entrance, over which is written the word "private." This door is, as a rule, open on the Sunday, and is also con- veniently used at other times. The police have rare periodic fits of proceeding against Sunday trading, but, as all the licensed victuallers do it, fining is not regarded as any dis- ability. The Forbes-Mackenzie Act, as carried out, or rather not carried out, in some parts of Scotland, is a bit of a fraud, but a greater legal farce is that enacted every Sunday in Victoria. The hotel keepers are beginning a rnildish sort of agitation for an alteration of the law 'to that it may sanc- tion selling during certain hours, and their prayer might just as well be granted unless the authorities should resolve to rigidly enforce the existing statute, a proceeding which it is scarcely necessary to say would be more dignified than allowing it to be treated as a dead letter. Parliament has dealt very curiously with the Sunday questioe in Victoria. According to the regulations in operation it is permissible to go to the Botanical or Zoological Gardens on the Sabbath and look at the birds, beasts, and flowers, but wrong to have the public museums and picture galleries open; it is wrong I to travel upon the railway in the country, but right in the capital; and in the same way it is expedient to pass a law shutting up public-homes on the Sunday, but unwise or fu- tile to make an effort to enforce its observance. It is ad- mittedly very difficult to draw the line on the Sabbath ques- tion. In Victoria there would, however, seem to have been a disposition to draw it crooked hitherto. Upon this very subject there is at the time of writing a fierce controversy raging in Melbourne. Parliament has on two or three occa- sions rejected a proposal to open the Public Library and Museum on the Sunday, but the trustees of the building have discovered that they can act independently about the museum and picture gallery, and itiitese they have opened for two or three hours in the afternoon In regard to the library, they are appealing to the legislature, and the agitation pro and con is exciting. A few words respecting the hotels, as all public houses are here styled, and the liquor traffic. Hotels are proportionally quite as thick on the ground as in the old country, and the law allows them to be open to the public on week days lon2;er than at home, viz., till 12 o'clock all round. It fs beat the I commonest justice to say of a greet many of the kotete the% they are supplied with everything, (I am not low speek",n; of the drink but of the food and lodging), t:nat can In Ake —a stay in them thoroughly enjoyable and coe'nfortable. Others there are of the very worst type of dram shop. TT have come to see that these places are far too comn ae people law has been passed which gives them local optic eon, and a n in so Par as it enables them to veto the increase of ze'nses.d Thbe s voting takes place during the municipal conts ts, an t e last figures reported are unmistakably in opr ,osition to any increase. Moreover the House of Assembly resolution in favour of the principal of lo has adopted a ally. It is probably therefore that bef cal option gener- ber. of the hotels will be diminished. W' ore long the num- the imported beer and spirits, colonial le th a high duty on industries have been extensively form& tewing anddistilling prejudice among those who imbibe ins sj,bnt there is a greal .oxicants in favour of

the foreign article. Especially is this the case with spirits of the established "brands." Statistics of the duty paid on each class show most conclusively that there must be a great amount of colonial made spirits drank as imported spirits, and the differential duty goes into the pockets of the dealers. It would pay the colony better one would think to make the home makers contribute the same duty as that which is placed on the liquor imported. Supposing that were to lead to the closing of the local distilleries, then the increased revenue derived from the additional imports would be more than sufficient to amply compensate the colonial makers who have been encouraged by the differential duties to em- bark in the business. This statement of opinion opens up the question of protection, but that is a topic altogether too large for these sketches. I have only noted this matter as bearing on the way in which the public, or to be more correct, the drinking public of the colony are often hoaxed, and the public treasury defrauded. Intimately connected with the liquor traffic is the ques- tion of the extent of crime and poverty, and with some allusion to the latter this letter will end. I may say at once that the evidences of poverty in Victoria are very few as compared with what one sees in crowded old world centres. Still poverty exists here, and it may safely be affirmed that where it does exist it is in nearly every case due to an indulgence in alcohol. Any man that is sober and in the healthy possession of his faculties can get along fairly well in this country. There is not that struggling that there is in the parent land. Yet there is destitution and poverty, and it has to be provided for. It is the boast of the colony that it has no poor law, but for the life of me I cannot see what great difference there is between the home system of looking after the poor and the infirm and that which prevails in these parts. The benevolent asylums in which the destitute and the aged are tended in Victoria are only so many Union houses, with this difference, that they are perhaps a little more comfortable than an English work- house, and instead of being maintained by a poor rate they are liberally subsidised by the Colonial Government out of the colonial purse. This subvention is only one among many by which Victorians willingly tax themselves in ' grants from the public treasury for charitable purposes.

CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. The Cheshire Agricultural Society's annual show was held at Crewe on Saturday. Had it not been for prevalence of cattle disease in the district, which caused the committee to exclude from the exhibition all horned stock, sheep, and pigs, this year's show would have been one of the best the society has ever held, the entries being nearly 200 over those of last year, and 100 in excess of the average for the past 13 years. The offer of additional prizes, however, had the effect of drawing a large competition in the horse classes and those assigned to agricultural produce. Butter and cheese made an excellent show, there being no less than 61 entries in this department. One of the chief features of the show was the exhibition of farm and gar- den produce. Lord Crewe, of Crewe Hall, and Sir Phillip Egerton, of Oulton Park, each sent a large collection; and the merit was so equal that the judges decided to divide the awards. There was a good show of roots and imple- ments

FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE RAIL- WAY AT GOLBORNE. An inquest was held at the Wigan Infirmary, on Thurs. day, before Mr. Rowbottorn, on the body of William Aldred, of 'Crowe, who died in the institution on the 18th inst., in sonsequence of injuries received whilst following his em- ployment on the London and North-Western Railway.— Mr. J. H. Jackson, house surgeon at the Infirmnry, said the deceased was admitted on the 3rd September. He had a com- pound fracture of one foot and the other foot had been re- moved by the accident. The shoulder joint was also in- jured, and he was suffering from a severe shock to the nervous system. His wounds were dressed, and the deceased lingered for fifteen days, expiring from exhaustion on the 18th inst. He attributed death to the injuries he had snrstained.—Philip Lees, of Pipe Ridware, near Rugby, said the deceased was his brother-in-law, and that he lived at Crewe. He was a servant of the London and North- Western Railway Company, and was 32 years of age.— Joseph Hurst, signalman at Bamfurlong siding, and living at Golborne, said the accident happened at 12-30 noon. He was in his cabin at the time. He saw the deceased passing his box and going in the direction of Springs Branch. When about 150 yards from his box be saw a goods train about 10 yards behind the deceased, who was walking in the six foot. He was walking between the main line and a loop line, and he (witness) turned the goods train into the loop lino, and a minute afterwards a man came and told him there was a man lying in the six- foot. Witness wired to Springs Branch for an engine, and he saw some men bandaging the deceased's foot. The de- ceased, being a servant of the company, had a right to be on the line.—William Pearsoil, of 8 laenetone' Staffordshire, said the deceased was his brother-in-law, and he saw him at the Infirmary after the accident. The deceased said he was passing along the line on the day of the accident. He heard an engine behind him, and, thinking it was going straight on, he stepped between the other metals. The engine fol- lowed and knocked him down. He did not blame anyone. —A verdict of " Acc:dental death" was returned. THE COMING K—.—Cammack.—Advt.

THOHAS STONE'S DOGS IN IRELAND.— It is a p:easure to note the capital show made by the dogs of our esteemed townsman Mr. Thomas Stone, Newton Park, at the Kilmotey meeting recently held in Mourne Park, Ireland, His well-known dog Sea Pilot ran second to Markham, after beating such great cracks as Alec Halli- day, Khodora, cLc. Mr. Stone's puppies in the Brownlow Stakes at the same meeting also ran very creditably—both being thrown out by the actual winner. These performances speak well for the assiduity of his under-trainer, Mr. Law- rence, who had the entire charge of the dogs during the re- cent illness of Mr. Mills, head trainer. SUDDEN DEATH AT THE VULCAN.—A painfully sudden death from apoplexy occurred at the Vulcan on Sunday forenoon, the deceased being Mrs. Ackleshaw, a middle-aged woman residing at No. 3, London-row, Vulc in. She was a person well known in the neighbourhood, as she had been in the habit, for a considerable time past, of standing at a stall near the entrance to the iron foundry and selling cups of coffee to the men as they came to their work in the morn- ' ing. She even did this so late as Saturday morning last, but notwithstanding she ha ls suffered from apoplexy, and has been attended by Dr. Patterson. On Sunday forenoon she was standing on the footpath near the door of her house when she was suddenly seized with a 11t, and fell to the ground. Two or three neighbours ran to her assistance, and she was carried into the house. The usual efforts and exer- tions were put forth to restwe consciousness hut they were unavailing, and the poor woman expired in about an hour and a half. Dr. Patterson was sent for, but he was absent from home. He has since given a certificate that the woman died ir.cqn apoplexy. and an inquest has, therefore: not been held. A reilOUS WA.I2-SHIP.—At the now small and rather ob- scure harbour of Newhaven there was built and launched in 1511 the famous war-ship of James IV., the Great Michael, said to have been the largest vessel that, in those days, had ever floated on the sea. Jacques Tarette was the builder or naval architect, and certainly he left nothing undone to gratify the desire of James to possess the greatest and most magnificent ship in the world. "The fame of this ship spread over Europe," says Buchanan, "and emulous of the King of Scotland, Francis I. and Henry VIII. endeavoured to outvie each other in building two enormous arks, which were so unwieldly that they floated on the water useless and immovable, like islands." This extraordinary vessel is said to have been sometimes confounded in history with another huge argosy, built in the preceding reign by Ken- nedy, Bishop of St. Andrews, and known as the Bishop's Barge. But the latter was purely a merchant vessel, and wee wrecked and pillaged on the teeeet ef ,tiitel aoout 1474, whereas the Greet richael was in all respects a for- midable e'illis of war, and she may with some truth be claimed as the first "armour-clad," as amidships her sides were padded with solid oak ten feet thick. She cost £30,000, an enormous sum in those days; but James IV. was lavish in his shipbuilding, and among his many brilliant and romantic schemes actually planned a voyage to the Medi- terranean, with a Scottish fleet, to visit Jerusalem. Linde- say of Pitscottie says that this enormous vessel required for her construction so much timber that, save Falkland, she consumed all the oak wood in Fife and all that came out of Norway. She was 240 ft. long by 36ft. wide, inside measure- ment, and ten feet thick in the walls. She had 300 mari- ners, 120 cannoniers, and i ,000 soldiers' with their captains and quartermasters. At Tullibardine her dimensions were long to be seen, planted in hawthorn, by Jacques Tarette, "the wright that helped to make her," adds Pitscottie. "As for other properties of her, Sir Andrew Wood is my author, who was quartermaster of her, and Robert Barton, who was master skipper. The ship lay still in the Roads of Leith, the King every day taking pleasure to pass her, and to dine and sup in her with his lords, letting them see the order of 1 his ship." The Ambassador of Henry VIII. also gives a description of the Michael, but merely says she had " six- teen pieces of great ordnance on each side," besides many more of smaller calibre. Shortly before the formal declara, tion of war against England, the Governor of Berwick, in writing to Henry VIII. concerning the designs of his brother-in-law, stated that the King of Scotland intended to lead the fleet against England himself, leaving his generals to lead the army t• and, had he done so, the tale of Flodden Field had, perhapl, been a different and less sorrowful one. In 1510 Sir Andrew Wood had been created "Admiral of the Seas" by James IV.; thus, when appointed to the Great Michael in the following year, it must have been in the capacity of commander, and not "quartermaster," as the garrulous Pitscottie has it. Buchanan asserts that the great ship was suffered to rot in the harbour of Brest; it may have done so eventually; but it is now ascertained that in April, 1514, she was sold to Louis XII. by the Duke of Albany, in the name of the Scottish Government, for the sum of forty thousand livres.—" Cassell's Old and New Edinburgh." A MENTAL DELUSION.—A married woman, about 50 years of age, bearing the name of Bridget Hoarty, of Cockhedge- lane, was brought up at Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, as being a person of unsound mind and wander- ing about in the streets.—About five o'clock on the previous afternoon P.C. Corbett found the woman with a large crowd round her in Horsemarket-street. She was persecuting a gentleman named James Ellison, who, she said, was her nephew, and had robbed her of a sum of money. This gentleman told the constable that he had been accosted by her two or three tunes. The women ePPeered le be very I much excited, and under the influence of drink. She was taken to the police station.—The Chief Constable said the woman had frequently been to the police station, and in his 1 opinion she was neither responsible for her words nor actions,' and ought to be kept under restraint.—Dr. Joseph said he had examined the women AO found her suffering from de- Ilusions, and that she was of unsound min.d, As far as he could gather she was in debt, and had had a hard, struggling life, and this seemed to have affected her mind. He thought she ought to be order restraint,—The esoffiens, who had kept up an incoherent chatter, was committed to the care of the relieving officer, eeiclairning that what she wanted was to get her money, and that he was not oat of her mind. Azcortor, or ITS DEPENCE.—I am recording a matter of history—of personal history—on this question, when I say `dust I for one had once no thought of alcohol except as a food. I thought it warmed us. I thought it gave addi- tional strength. I thought it enabled us to endure mental and bodily fatigue. I thought it cheered the heart and lifted up the mind into greater activity. But it so hap- pened that I was asked to study the action of alcohol along with a whole series of chemical bodies, and to investigate their bearing in relation to each other. And so I took alco- hol from the shelf of my laboratory, as I might any other drug or chemical there, and I asked it in the course of experi- ments extending over a lengthened period, "What do you do ?" I asked it, "Do you warn the animal body when you are taken into it?" The reply came invariably, "I do not, except in a mere flush of surface excitement. There is, in fact, no warming, but, on the contrary, an effect of cooling ' and chilling the body." Then I turn round to it in another direction, and ask it, "Do you give muscular strength ?" I ' test it by the most rigid analysis and experiment I can adopt. I test muscular power under the influ- ence of it in various forms and degrees, and its reply is, "I give no muscular strength." I turn ' to its effect upon the organs of the body, and find that ' while it expedites the heart's action it reduces tonicity, and ' turning to the nervous system I find the same reply; that is to say, I find the nervous system more quickly worn out ' under the influence of this agent than if none of it is taken at all. I ask it, "Can you build up any of the tissues of the ' body ?" The answer again is in the negative. "I build P nothing. If Ido anything, I add fatty matter to the body, , but that is a destructive agent, piercing the tissues, destroy- ing their powers, and making them less active for their ' work." Finally, I sum it all up. I find it to be an agent 5 that gives no strength, that reduces the tone of the blood- ; vessels and heart, that reduces the nervous power, that ' builds up no tissues, and can be of no use to me or any 5 other animal as a substance for food. On that side of the ' question my mind is made up—that this agent in the most . moderate quantity is perfectly useless for any of the con- ditions of life to which men are subjected, except under the k most exceptional conditions which none but skilled ob- servers can declare.—Dr. B. TV. Richardson.

Sergeant Stewart and Constable Morton, of the Lanark- !hire Constabulary, were murderously assaulted near Ham- "ten on Sunday while effecting some arrests. On Saturday, at a mass meeting of miners in South Wales, I resolution was passed in favour of maintaining the Uni- versity College at Aherystwith and continuing the Govern- 'tient grant. Mr. John Gray, a member of a local firm of ironworkers, baa intimated his desire to erect and present to the city of Aberdeen a building to be used as a school of art, at a cost ef £5,000. An inmate of the Portsmouth union and three other per- sons in humble positions have come in for a quarter of a Million sterling through the settlement of a long-pending Chancery suit. At Hell, on Tuesday, George Pinder, a master rulleyman, !VI remanded on a charge of attempting to set fire to a ware- 'louse in High-street, the scene of several very destructive fires within recent weeks. The Home Secretary has declined to sanction a bye-law 41013ted by the Luton Town Council for regulating the pro- Cessions of the Salvation Army with bands and drums, Perticularly on Sundays. The funeral of the late Mr. Hugh Birley, MT., took place on Saturday at Didsbury Parish Church, and was attended II a large number of gentleman representing the various Public bodies with which the deceased was connected. CAREY'S ASSASSIN.—At Bow-street Police Court, London, on Tuesday, Michael O'Donnell, aged 48, was brought up 00 the charge of murdering James Carey, the Irish informer, On the 29th of July. He was remanded for a week. ...ALLEGED CONSPIRACY TO DEFRAUD—John Henry rood, printer and stationer, was again charged, on Monday, eefore the -Macclesfield magistrates, with conspiring with G_eorge Brounsen, tailor, to defraud the latter's creditors. bte was committed for trial, bail being refused. Fisie SUPPLY IN MANCHESTER.—A company has been •termed in Manchester with the object of supplying the in- habitants of Manchester, Salford, and the surrounding tistricts with fish, semi-wholesale, and retail, at a price in accordance with the quantity which arrives in the market. A Snip DESTROYED BY FIRE—On Sunday morning, a are which resulted in the scuttling of the steamer Ashleigh Brook broke out whilst that vessel lay in the Birkenhead Cheat Float. The steamer was a new one laden with esparto, and only arrived at Liverpool on the previous Friday from klgiers. AFFRAY ON AN ITALIAN VESSEL.—The Italian vessel Aeresa arrived at Qaeenstown on Monday, and the captain nated to the Consul that an attempt had been made to mar- ler the chief officer in his sleep. The assailant was shot °lead by his intended victim, who had received a severe Wound. CATTLE DISEASE IN LINCASHIRE.—The Lancashire Executive Cattle Plague Committee, on Monday, issued an ctder prohibiting the importation of animals from other ifarisdictions into this county. The order will come into oree on the 20th instant, and continue in operation until the list October. CHARGE OF FORGING DOCUMENTS.—John W. Jays and q!oseph Hebron, two young men of respectable appearance, urre been committed for trial from the LiverpoolPoliceCourt, *barged with forging and uttering documents by which they had obtained £l9O from Mr. Guy, stock and share broker, cf Liverpool, and £9O from a lady residing in Hereford. FRAUDS UPON CRILINTORS..—A- man named Moses Zucker r4d his son Joseph were convicted on Monday at the Old 110:67 of frauds noon their creditors. The prisoner Mosee ;re sent to prison for two years, and Joseph for six Months. Justice Day expressed surprise at the lenient sentences 'cat were generally passed upon fraudulent bankrupts. JiTtel AT A FACTORY.—Damage ta the amount of about ,110,000 was done by fire on Sunday at a factory adjoining Midland railway station, Leicester, and in the occupa- • Gfl of half-a-dozen different firms. The portion in the accupation of three firms of elastic web manufacturers was 4°Mpletely destroyed, but the damage is covered by in. Surance. COLLISION AT SEA.—The ship St. Leonards, of Loudon, *ea sunk early on Monday morning by the steamer Cormo- -44,,_ te belonging to the General Steam- Navigation Corn- "my, about 18 miles east of Star Point. The St. Leonards, Which was bound for New Zealand, had on board 33 pas- 'engera AO a crew pf 29 bands, They were all saved. A 4ente fog prevailed at the time of the collision. 4_BALYATIONISTS STORMING A PUBLIC-ROUSE.—At Worces- w,on Monday, Alfred Osborne, "captain" of the local Sal- letion Army, was summoned for causing an obstruction in .t_it,tle Park-street. He had surrounded an inn, and a woman gone down on her knees before the house to pray, Whilst Osborne preached.liThe defendant was fined 10s, and, 'sliming to pay, was sent to prison with a month's hard labOUr. , A Rlsity DMIONSTILLTION. Captain Trevor, who 'eft Dover for Folkestone in an 18-gallop cask, sup- red by four cross oars, and who was thought to be ko.vfned, was picked up south-west of the Verne Light- -113, by the steamer Bytheville. He had been drifting at Ltal mercy of the waves for 14 hours, and narrowly escaped vOing swamped. He has been landed at Dover. Ills ob- iect was to demonstrate the feasibility of saying life at ship-

AMSTERDAM EIRIBITION, 1883.—The highest award for pianos. The diploma of honour and gold medal has been accorded to Messrs. John BRINSNIEJD and Sotis, of London. By eleven votes to six the Berwick Town Council, on Wednesday, refused an offer made by a Roman Catholic priest to purchase Berwick Gaol for industtial schools and• other purposes. On Saturday, a young man named Daily, a telegraph engineer, was at work at the telegraph on the roof of No. 32, St. Swithia's-lane, E.C., when he slipped on the slates and fell off the roof through a skylight, dashing out his brains. FATAL FIGLIT.—At Leeds, on Wedusdav, Stephen Kelly, a dyer, was reminded, charged with having caused the death of James Gillman in a street fight. It was alleged, that the prisoner bad stabbed Gillman in the head with a knife, after finding that the deceased was too powerful for

wreck. li.kRD TIMES FOR PAUPERS. Dr. Joseph Rogers, the Medical officer at the Westminster Workhouse, has given lintice to the guardians that he will no longer certify for a suPply of stimulants to able-bodied paupers engaged in Wcrk at the workhouse. The number of pauper assistants who have been supplied with stimulants has reached 120. A Member of the Boird of Guardians predicted that there Would be a revolt of the inmates in consequence of the Change. Perhaps they will leave in disgust. ThE DyN/ALITE CONSPIRACY.—It is reported that the authorities of Glasgow have accepted the evidence of one of the prisoners in tne dynamite conspiracy, who has offered t,o turn informer.—The prosecution in the case of the American citizen" M`Dermott, charged with being con- cerned in the dynamite conspiracy, has been dropped. The Tau was once more brought before the Liverpool Stipen- l4lary Magistrate on Tuesday, when the prosecuting solicitor stated that after careful consideration it had been decided Elot to offer any further evidence in the case, and M`Dermott Was discharged. ~.SER J. B. alownetay, M.P., ON SPIRITUAL DESTITUTION.— , zir J. R. Mowbray, M.P., speaking at Newbury on Monday' 11l Connection with the Society for Promoting the Employ- !cent of Additional Curates, referred to the fact that there cad been a growth of the population of England during the last ten years of nearly 350,000 per annum, and pointed out that although the demand upon churches for increased re- ligious instruction, especially in large towns, seaports, and Milting districts, had become very pressing, the two Church societies established to meet those requirements raised only 416,000 per annum between them. Comeenz or DEFRAUDING 13/O.:EELS—At the Liverpool Police Court, on Tuesday, Thomas Livesey, principal of the insolvent film of Livesey, Son, & Co., cotton brokers, was committed for trial, charged with defrauding bankers to U e amount of £lO,OOO. The prisoner is alleged to have fraudulently obtained money by the hypothecatiwi of cotton ti•nd sold the consignment without handing over the Inctley to the bank, and also to have committed frauds c the bankers in respect to "brokers' engagements." Khe prisoner was arrested at Hamburg, and in reply to the charge he said he "never intended to defraud anyone." Secamion IN A Weasrt Comm.—Before commencing his sermon at St. Thomas's, the English Church at Rhyl, ott Sunday morning, the vicar (Rev. T. Richardson) ap- Pealed to the congregation to assist him and churchwardens tc discover the person or persons who had defaced the nameplates of several of the most prominent pewowners in that church. It is supposed that the act was done by some • et-zealous advocate of "Free and Open Churches," St. ahoenas m's being pew-rented almost from end to end, and, being the only English Church in the parish, such whole- • " appropriation" causes much inconvenience during w• e Bummer months. Exousia PATENTS.—The following patents amongst Others published in the Commissioners' of Patents Journal Were sealed during the week ending September 15, 1883:— William Ashton, of Manchester, for improvements in the cc...natruction of braiding machines; Robert Longdon and rsancis Bernard Welch Manchester, improved apparatus for Carrying, protecting, and insulating wires employed for eon- 'reeving electric currents; Benjamin Harlow, Macclesfield, in t2le county of Chester, an improved construction of portable kreproof and other shelving, applicable also to storage and Other racks, to horticultural and other training structures, en; • ; William Henry Brassington, Manchester, improvements :11 Perambulators ; Reginald Heber Silcock, Warrington, traProvementa in or relating to apparatus for sorting and s_creening coal, ores, and other substances; Miles Sowdon, !ilradford, Yorkshire, improvements in looms for weaving; Francis William Crossley, Manchester, improvements in gas figines.—List supplied by Mr. George Davies, CE., • el. Inst. P.A., Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann's-square, Man- :heater. RAILWAY DISASTERS.—Shortly after noon on Saturday, a ollision, said to be due to the inadvertence of a siagalman „tPulling the wrong lever, occurred on the Great Northern nailway at Lofthouse, about seven miles from Leeds. The tir,reat Northern Passenger express, leaving London at nine nck, ran into a goods train, and some 20 passengers were Inlured, several of them severely.—A railway accident neurred at Portsmouth on Monday evening on the joint _ecth Coast and South-Western Railway line. The hind- st carriage of the 3-40 express from Watasloo left the 77.tea15 when about two miles from Portstauth Station 7,_11. dragging for some time its couplings snapped. Some d dale passengers in the carriage were much shaken, httiot not seriously hurt.—A serious accident occurred on f‘ronday evenir.g on the Brighton Railway between New 38 and Brockley stations. A heavy goods train had r'"ed througk New Cross, and was proceedimg up the crrest Hill bank, when severals trucks broke away and ran bc,ck over the incline, colliding with great violence with a 3pn milo.a p nts einideginaen dwhich had been cle9Qatched t Lrai 6-assist the goof the- bank. The trucles arid two brake vans we • their occupants—two railway servants-9, serlotialtee • e.4ll}arece as to render theietremerrarto Guy's • •'PL'a .iPlCpssary, The driver of the -Olia tngiur", was aIA, utecl,7, ••-•,- • - -

him. UUN ACCIDENT.—WhiIe out shooting on Park Lee Farm, Chesterle-street, on Wednesday, the gun of Charles Mars, under keeper to the Earl of Durham, was accidentally dis- charged, injuring four persons, including the head keeper and a man named Charles Rice. The latter sustained very serious injuries. ALLEGED MURDER IN LONDON.—William Scully, aged 17, a bat maker of 13, Anchor-yard, St. Luke's, was charged on remand, at the Clerkenwell Police Court, on Tuesday, with having wilfully murdered George Henry Neal, by stabbing him in the head on Sunday night, the Ist September. The magistrate formally committed him for trial. - TWO HUNDRED COLLIERS FINED.—At the Durham Police Court, on Wednesday, the Carlton Iron and Coal Company claimed 58 each from 205 of their workmen at East Howie Colliery, near Durham' for leaving work with- out giving fourteen days notice. The men pleaded guilty, and the magistrates ordered them to pay the amount claimed. A LIVERPOOL VESSEL ON FIRE —A telegram from Havre, on Wednesday, stated that the English ship Oxford, of Liverpool, which arrived there on Wednesday from New York with a cargo of petroleum, was on fire in that port. The cook had been burned to death' the first mate was seriously hurt, and several others had suffered slight in- juries. Tag BRITISH ASSOCIATION.—The fifty-third annual meet- ing of the British Association commenced at Southport on Wednesday night. Dr. Cayley, professor of pure mathema- tics at Cambridge, succeeded Sir W. Siemens in the presi- dency, and delivered his opening address in the theatre of the Winter Gardens. He discoursed on the progress of ' mathematics from the earliest times. A NoN-Porance.r, OFFICE.—An amusieg incident has occurred in the Wrexham Borough Revision Court. The claim of Thomas Davies was objected to by the Conserva- tives, and the agent of the Liberal party, said that he should nnt press the claim because the claimant wished to ba public hangman, and had sent in an application for the office. The Conservative agent: In fact, you let him drop. SIR HENRY BRAND AT A HARVEST HOME.—Sir Henry Brand, Speaker of the House of Commons, presided on Saturday at the Glynde harvest home. He said the harvest was the occasion for universal rejoicing. The love of home had g,iven England a foremost position among nations. After dwelling upon the mutual dependency of the repre- sentatives of different branches of labour, Sir Henry Brand protested against the extravagant notion of transferring agricultural land to the State. nix DANGER OF DRESS IMPROVERS.—An extraordinary accident has just occurred in Nottingham. Miss Hickling, a young lady, while walking in Waverley-street had her dress set on fire by matches, with which some boys were playing, her dress improver greatly facilitating the spread of the flames, which instantly covered her back clothing. A spectator wrapped her in his coat and rolled her on a neighbouring lawn, but Miss Hickling was severely burnt. A moment's delay would have caused her death. A POLICEMAN FIRED AT.—At one o'clock on Wednesday morning a by was found by a Leeds policeman prowling about the streets, and being asked his business he answered, lad-like, "Nothing." The constable following in his foot- steps, the youth paused and, when they were about twelve , yards apart, fired a pistol, the shot from which just missed the man and lodged in the wall of the Corn Exchange. The • lad, who is the son of a deceased chemist, was taken into , custody, and he has been remanded by the magistrates. TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT A STEEL WORKS. -- A party of members of the Iron and Steel Institute visited the North- Eastern Steel Company's works at Middlesborough, on 1 Wednesday, and daring their inspection a terrible accident occurred. A vessel containing ten tons of molten =Ail , was overturned. and the scalding liquid was scattered among • the company. Mr. S. Davidson, of Horbury, Wakefield, received such injuries that he expired shortly after 11 o'clock on Wednesday night. Several others of the party and a number of workmen were badly bumed. A CURIOUS CHARGE.—On Saturday, at Driffield, Francis Randal, national schoolmaster at Nafferton, was remanded on the charge of endeavouring to persuade John Smith, a sailor, of Hull, to murder a girl, aged 16, and a boy, 13. The prisoner, aged about 50, is a married man, and the two children are natives el Nafferton. The 541 was to have • been murdered on Thursday with a heavy Cudgel, which the prisoner provided, and thrown over the hedge on the high. ' way. Smith, however, informed the police, and Randal was arrested on Saturday morning. Prisoner was refused bail. DISAPPEARANCE OF A CATHOLIC PRIEST.—A rumour to , the effect that a well-known priest in Liverpool had been guilty of fraud and had taken flight;accompanied by a young female, has given rise to a grave scandal on the clergy and laity, of thn Roman Catholic Church. It is alleged that he ontained from Bishop O'Reilly a cheque upon a bank for £9OO, which was subsequently cashed, and that instead of applying the money for church uses he absconded. The missing priest is between 40 alai 50 years of age. whilst his companion is only 18. The matter has already been inves- tigated by the authorities of the Catholic Church, and is be- lieved now to be in the hands 'of the police. THE OFFICE OF PUBLIC EXECUTIONER.—The subjoined notification has been issued from the sheriff's office, Lon- don :—" Upwards of 1,200 applications have already been received for the post of executioner, vacated by the death of Mr. Marwood. These have been forwarded from the Home Office and elsewhere to the sheriffs of London and Middlesex, who are now engaged in so considering and sift- ing them as to have a fitting man at hand to carry out the sentence of the law in case of need. The sheriffs wish it to be particularly known that to reply to so large a number of applicants is impracticable, but that original testimonials, where such have been sent, will in all cases be returned in due course." PERJURY IN WALES.—The Dean of Bangor defends the Welsh people from the charge of addicted-less to perjury ' brought against them by Mr. Homersham Cox, County Court Judge. Dean Edwards very pertinently remarks that when a judge discovers perjurers it is his duty to see that they are prosecuted, and he is equally happy in his argument that "Mr. Cox, being ignorant of Welsh, is not well qualified to sit is judgment upon Welsh truthful- ness."—On Wednesday evening, at a meeting of the Car- narvonshire Liberal Association, at Bangor, a resolution was unanimously adopted condemnatory of Mr. Homersham Cox's language with regard to Welsh witnesses and clients in his courts and calling upon the Lord Chancellor to re- move him and appoint a Welsh-speaking judge to the charge of Welsh circuits. STRANGE ASSAULT CASE.—The Birmingham magistrates, on Tuesday, sentenced to 14 day's imprisonment, without the option of a fine, Mrs. Anne Wigley, nearly 70 years of age, for violently assaulting with an iron rod her husband, a well-known local manufacturer, to whom she had been married 40 yeats. The pair had lived happily during the whole of their married life until a year or two since, when the woman gave way to intoxication, and when in that condition had so assaulted her husband that for the past few months he has slept most nights in his manufactory. The husband begged the magistrates not to send his wife to prison, but this reqaest they declined, stating that it would be a kindness to the woman to keep her from drink for a fortnight. They added that they deeply sympathised with the husband, who was much affected. CHARGE OF BIGAMY AGAINST A CLERGYMAN. At i Birmingham Police Court, on Tuesday, the Rev. Thomas ' M. Hughes, late in charge of the parish of Bickenhill, near Birmingham, was charged with committing bigamy by marrying a woman named Morgan, the cook at the vicarage, his wife being then still alive. Prisoner was arrested on Monday night at Gravelly Bill, near Birmingham, and when the warrant was read, he replied, "It is true; I am guilty of the charge." Prisoner, mho was very neatly attired in clerical garb, is stated to have been drinking 'eery heavily since he left Bickenhill last July. When arrested he was strolling' along a country lane with the young woman, who, upon the unexpected arrest of her supposed husband, burst into tears and almost fainted. Since prisoner left Bickenhill he has been living by means of begging letters and by borrowing money, most of the victims being members of the Order of Freemasons, to which he belonged. The accused Was remanded. RIOT IN BILNCHESTBE.—Two men, named Finnigan and Reynolds, were apprehended in Manchester, on Saturday night, for being drunk and disorderly. Finnigan became very violent, and knocked down and kicked the officer who had arrested him. A crowd collected and threw bricks and stones at the police, some of whom were injured. A man, named Smith, was also arrested for endeavouring to rescue Reynolds. Daring the disturbance a man, named Edward Parkinson, received so severe a blow on the head—from, it is alleged, a policeman's staff—that he died ahortiv after- wards. Smith, Reynolds, and Finnigan were brought up at the City Police Court, on Monday, and remanded.—The coroner's inquiry, on Tuesday, concerning the death of Par- kinson, resulted in a verdict of manslaughter against two constables named Wharton and Farrell. Evidence was given that the deceased WAS struck by a constable, but there was some doubt as to which of the police delivered the fatal, blow. A medical man who made the post-mortem examina- tion said the deceased's ekull was the thinnest he had ever seen, and the blow which killed him would have done little injury to most men, The police constables were, on Wednesday, placed in the dock at the Manchester Police Court, charged with causing the death of Parkinson.—The prisoners were remanded, and allowed bail on their own recognisances.
