PERSONAL.

The Prince of Wales is at Homburg. The death is announced of Mr. John Payne Collier, the eminent Shakespearian critic, at the age of 94 years. Lord and Lady Dutlerin left !England on Wednesday for Constantinople. Earl and Coun'ess Granville left Dover on Wednesday by mid-day boat for Calais on a visit to the Continent. The Duke of Albany has accepted an invitation to open the grounds of Pontefract Castle during the second week of November. By the advice of his physicians, Sir Michael Costa has resolved to leave Brighton, and to spend the winter in his native Italy. Sir Frederick Leighton, president of the Royal Academy, on Wednesday paid a visit to the exhibition in the Man- chester Art Gallery. The Marquis of Carmarthen, eldest son of the Duke of Leeds, attained his majority on Tuesday, and the event was , dely celebrated at flornhy Castle, Bedale. The Earl and Countess of Derby and Lady Margaret Cecil passed through town on Monday afternoon for Knows- ley, from Fairhill, their place near Tonhridge. Lord VVolseley has formed one of a shooting party at Wilt6n House, the residence of the Earl of Pembroke. In two days the party killed over 300 brace, the sport having been remarkably good. Sir Matthew Wilson, the member for the North-West Riding of Yorkshire, was thrown from his carriage while driving from Eshton Hall to Ekipton, on Saturday, arid ! sustained a severe shock. ! Lord Lonsdale was thrown from his horse and seriously ! injured while out cub hunting with the North Pytchley hounds, on Monday morning, and in attempting to clear a five-barred gate. A serious accident has happened to Lord de liesci. While his lordship was deerstalking in the Highlands a few days ago, his rifle burst and shattered two fingers of his left hand. The injured fingers have been amputated, and his lordship is progressing most satisfaczorily. Mr. Gladstone on Tuesday entertained members of the Danish Royal Family, the Emperor of Russia, and a num- ber of other distinguished guests, to a luncheon on board the Pembroke Castle. At three o'clock in the afternoon the I Pembroke Castle left Copenhagen for Lomlon.
PO LIT ECAL. Sir John Swinburne has declined the invitation of the Kist Yorkshire Liberal Association to contest the riding at

the next election. Mr. te. Jones, iron and coal master, of Coed Tref, Meifod, and Wellington, Shropshire, has signified his intention of coming forwarded as an independent candidate for Mont- gomeryshire at the next election. Lord Randolph Churchill, it is reported, will be present at the conference of the National Union of Conservative Associations to be held at Birmingham on the 2ed of next month, but it is not certain that he will be able to-attend the demonstrations on the Ist. The members for West Cornwall addressed the electors at Camborne on Saturday evening. Sir John St. Aubyn said that the Patents and Bankruptcy Acts were both useful measures. Mr. Vivian claimed that, considering the time that had been absorbed by debates on Egyptian affairs, the Transvaal, be.. Parliament had accomplished a satisfactory amount of work. Admiral Sir John Hay, addressing his constituents at Wigtown, on Monday night, declared the British navy to be totally inefficient as compared with the superior fleets of ironclads possessed by other leading nations such as France and Spain. He urged that our naval defences should be increased if England was to retain her maritime supe- riority. Mr. Walter, M.P., speaking at Workingham on Wednes- day night, said he thought that the Corrupt Practices Bill was overstrained in minor points. With regard to the Agricultural Holdings Bill no strong opinion had been ex- pressed by the tenant farmers in that part of England as to its necessity, and no legislation could supply the place of that mutual confidence which was the real basis of the rela- tions between landlord and tenant. He advocated laying down more laud to grass. Mr. Storey, M.P., in communicating his inability to at- tend the Re-form demonstration, at Newcastle to-day (Satur- day) says surely it cannot be long before, in this free country, all law-created distinctions between man and man will be done away with, and the whole citizen of the coun- try be enabled to act on common ground for the common good. One step towards this, he adds, is the assimilation of the county with the borough franchise. He is willing, of course, to support that, but he goes a great deal further than that; so, he hopes, do many of his friends in the North. The Right Hon. J. Lowther, M.P., addressed a large meet- ing of the Conservatives of West Cumberland at Marypert on Wednesday evening. He said the Government had pro- duced a state of things in Ireland which was scarcely con- sistant with civilisation. By ignoring the vote of the House of Commons the Government had seriously imperilled the agricultural interests by relaxing the restrictions on the im- portation of diseased cattle. He strongly condemned the foreign and colonial policy of the Govettement, and declared that a bill merely for the assimilation of the borough and county franchise would never pass into law. A meeting of the Liberal Nine Hundred was held in the Reform Club, Manchester, on Monday night, to determine whether the minority seat should be contested by a Liberal candidate. A resolution proposed in favour of Dr. Pank- hurst's candidature was rejected, and it was decided not to contest the seat in the Liberal interest. Tuesday night's Gazette contains the Speaker's notification that the writ for the election of a member of Parliament for the city of Man- chester will be issued next Monday. Mr. Houldsworth, the Conservative candidate' commenced the campaign on Wed- nesday night with apublic, meeting in Ardwick. Admiral Egerton, M.P., speaking on Tuesday night at the annual meeting of the Midland Agricultural Society at Allerton, said the feeling of the country was against a return to protection, and the requirements of the population would not admit of the total prohibition of cattle importa- tion, even in the face of the existence of cattle disease. At the same time, it was reasonable to demand that the dead meat trade should be more extensively developed. Speaking II on the land nationalisation question, he said he looked forward to an extension of the franchise, when the agricultural labourers would have a voice in the affairs of the nation. On Monday night, Mr. Heneage, M.P. for Grimsby, addressed a crowded meeting of his conetituents in the Town Hall. He congratulated himself on the fact that the Government during past sessions had tealt with several measures which had blocked the way for future legislation. The position of the present Government never was stronger, And it was not true that there was a feeling in the country in favour of a change. He hoped the Government would introduce the County Franchise Bill immediately after Easter. It would then reach the Lords early in July, and if they passead it they would be clear for future legisla- tion; if they did not, Mr. Gladstone would know what to do.

Tim ATTEMPTED SUICIDE IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE. The young woman who attempted to commit suicide in a Brighton railway carriage was on Thursday committed for trial. She obstinately refused to give her name, but the police believe she has lived in Hastings, and is named Lucille Dudley. BANQUET TO LORD CARNARVON.—A telegram from Mon- treal states that a banquet was given to Lord Carnarvon on Wednesday night. Sir Francis Rincks presided, and a num- ber of distinguished men attended. Replying to the toast of his health, Lord Carnervon said he was glad confedera- tion bad been a greater success than at first anticipated, and that he had some share in bringing it about. AN EXTRAORDINARY RACE.—A novel race between a pigeon and a pony has just taken place at Bedworth, the former flying a mile and the latter galloping half a mile. A capital- start was made, the starter standing half-way between the pigeon and the pony, and after a most exciting race the bird won by eighty yards. The pony belonged to Mr. Mockford, and the bird to Mr. Darlison. A MEMBER ) F PARLIAMENT SHOT.—Great excitement was caused t Be ford, on Thursday morning, by a report that Mr. Whitbread, M.P., had been seriously wounded whilst shooting in Scotland. The hon. gentlemaa left London for grouse shooting before Parliament rose and has spent the whole of the season at or near his Scotch shoot- ing seat. It is stated that his son accidentally discharged a gun, the contents lodging in Mr. Whitbread's forehead. SHOWING "LIVERPOOL LIFIL"--11eDry Ayris, 15, of Manchester, was remanded at Liverpool on Thursdiy, on a charge of stealing 31s from Henry Smith. The prosecutor came to Liverpool from Rugby to go to America. He was accosted in the street by the prisoner, who offered to show him Liverpool life, and took him to several low resorts, con- cluding with visiting a disreputable house. Here the pro- secutor entrusted his money to the prisoner who decamped with it, but was,arrested shortly afterwards. CAUSING A PANIC IN A TRAIN.—At the Dublin Police I Court, on Thursday, a man named Newman was charged with wilfully causing a panic amongst the passengers in a train on the Midland Great Western Railway. The accused was travelling from Mullingar to Dublin, and suddenly cried out that the engine had burst and that another train was running into them. The passengers were frightened, and , some jumped through the windows. The prisoner was sen- tenced to 14 days' imprisonment. DEATH OF A VETERAN TRADE UNIONIST.—Mr. James Scotson, who for many years held the office of general secretary to the Steam Engine Makers' Society, died on Wednesday last at the ripe age of 83. The society was established in 1824, and in 1826 Mr. Scotson joined it at Liverpool. In 1851 he was appointed permaneut secretary, and held that office till 1874, when failing health compelled his retirement, and the present general secretary, Mr. James Swift, succeeded him. The members voted Mr. Scotson a [superannuation allowance of £2 per week, which he en- joyed. to the time of his death. He died at the residence of his daughter at Prestwich, where he had been for some time residing. Mr. Scotson was not known as a politician, and took little part in any public movement outside the sphere of his own society. EARLESTOWN GOOD TEMPLARS AT LEIGH.—AbOUt 26 members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Terri- piers paid a fraternal visit to the Leigh Alpha Lodge on, Wednesday evening. The party left Earlestown by train about seven o'clock, and on arriving at their destination were heartily welcomed by the Leigh brethren. A miscellaneoue , entertainment was given by the , Earlestown friends, 1 Bro. Geofge—Clarke, DIA. (of Earlestown), ,preeicling; A capital programme of songs, recitations, &c., was excel.: lently gone thraugh, and at the close a coffee* supper wee held, and it was much enjoyed. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the visitors, who arrived home about eleven o'clock.

IRELAND. The remeins ef the late Lord Chancellor of Irel knd were interred at Mount Jerome Cemetery, Dublin, on Suurday moraing. The Lord-Lieutenant was present. At the Dublin Police Court, ou Wednesday, William Par- tridge, the son of a colonel, pleaded guilty to stealing a clarionet, and was remanded. After committing the robbery he enlisted. ATTACK ON A 'SHOOTING PARTY IN IRELAND.—On Wed- nesday, Lord Richard Brown and his son, while elmet- ing at Doolough, ou the estate of the former's brother, the Marquis of Sligo, were attacked by the tenant and a party of men, who took away their guns. • CAREY'S ASSASSIN: O'DONNELL'S TRIAL —An effort is to be made to obtain the services of Mr. Charles Russell to lead the defence of O'Donnell at the Old Bailey, A Central Committee is immediately to be formed in Lon- don to collect necessary funds for the prisoner's defence. IRISH SPECIAL MAGISTRATES.— An important circular has been issued to resident magistrates by the Lord-Lieu- tenant, in which it is stated that the office of special resi- dent-magistrates will cease on the 30th inst.; the services of the secretaries and office staff attached to each special resident magistrate will also be dispensed with on the same date. SHOOTING CASE IN DUBLIN.—On Monday the deposi- tions were taken of a draughtsman named Jerome Mooney, who was accidentally shot on Sunday night by two iron- workers named WEvoy and Gilmore, while they were en- gaged in target firing. Mooney lies in a precarious state, and though he attributes no blame to any person, M‘Evoy and Gqmore have been arrested. A REBEL'S REMAINS,—WhiIe some . workmen were en- gaged in laying water pipes at Ballymorey they came upon a coffin containing the remaine of a man named Gamble, who was executed in 1798 for participation in the Irish rebellion. The remains were claimed by Gamble's three grandsons. A new coffin was procured, and the body re- interred in the parish graveyard. THE PHOSNIE PARK MURDERS: THREATENING ANOTHER WITNESS.—Nt Dublin Police Court, on Monday afternoon, Alexander O'Reilly, printer, was charged with threatening Alice Carroll, the young girl who, it will he remembered, gave important evidence against the Invincibles at the recent trials, she having witnessed the attack on Mr. Field, the juror, made by Joseph Brady and other Invincibies, since hung for the Phoenix Park murders. The prisoner was re- nianded without bail. THE NATIONAL LEAGI7E.—A political demonstration, under the auspices of the local branch of the National League, was held on Sunday, at Soulmount, Carrick-on- Shannon, when resolutions were adopted expressing disap- proval of Colonel Tottenham and Mr. O'Beirne as Parlia- mentary representatives, and confidence in Mr. Parnell and the Irish Parliamentary party. The Land Act was con- demned as entirely inadequate, and tenant farmers were re- commended to second the labourers in their efforts to avail themselves of recent legislation. MWERMOTT AND THE FENIANS: HIS REMOVAL DE- MANDED.—The American correspondent of the Times writes: —A telegram from Liverpool announcing the release of the Fenian prisoner APDermott has caused a sensation among Irish Amerieens. They recall that on September 6th O'Donovan Rosa sent the following telegram from New York to Mr. Gladstone in London ;—" Abandon the mock trial of your spy M`Dermott. When the British Empire plays such a farce as this you must be hard driven." The Fenians generally declared that M`Dermott has been for several months past a British spy, and that he ought to be followed ml "removed," as Carey was. MR. O'Branee, M.P.—Mr. O'Brien, M.P., addressed his constituents at Mallow, on Sunday. A large number of extra policemen were on duty in the town, but the proceed- ings did not call for their interference. A Government shorthand writer, who was guarded by a body of con- stables, took note of the speeches. Mr. O'Brien spoke of what a small party had been able to accomplish during the past troubled session, and expressed the hope that the Labourers and Tramways Act would be taken advantage of by the people. What they still wanted for Ireland was a new land act. He recommended them to continue the struggle, looking forward to the ultimate goal—the national independence of the country, which they would win, by peaceable means if possible, but which they meant to win. RESISTING AN ETICTION: Two PERSONS INJURED.—A large force of police and bailiffs proceeded for the third time to Fregat, seven miles from Kells, to evict a man named Farrell and his family for non-payment of rent. The door of the house was found to be barricaded with stones, the roof partly stripped, and a black flag displayed. A bailiff, in going up a ladder to effect an entrance through the win- dow, was struck with a large stone and injured. The rifle of a policeman, who was helping to push the bailiff through the window, struck one of Farrell's daughters on the fore- head, inflicting a very serious wound, necessitating her re- moval to the hospital. Her sister also sustained some in- juries in the course of the struggle. An entrance was at length effected, and Farrell, who was found to be armed with a scythe, was overpowered and arrested. He was taken be- fore a magistrate, and remanded for a week.

AGRARIAN LAW LESSNESS. Some time ago a farmer named Patrick O'Brien was evicted from his holding at Donohill, near Tipperary, for non-payment of rent, and the landlord took possession. On Saturday night all the fences on the farm were smashed, and the cattle were driven into the highway.—The house of a man named Murray, a labourer and dealer in asses, Graigue, Carlow, has been burned to the ground; and as his two daughters had been harvesting for the past few days on a boycotted farm in the immediate neighbourhourhood, the burning is believed to be malicious. A young lad has been arrested on suspicion.—At Limerick, Wm. Casey, a farmer, has been sent for trial at the assizes charged with being in company with a party of Moonlighters, and firing into the house of Patrick IWNarnara, a labourer, who bad been accused of taking care of a boycotted farm. Men were wounded on the occasion.—About midnight on Mon- day shots were fired into the dwelling-house of a farmer named Martin Tierney, of Turnquin, Ennis, but no personal injury was inflicted. The outrage is attributed to agrarian motives, and a man named Patrick Brvnes has been arrested on suspicion. On Tuesday Brynes was charged with the offence, but a complete alibi was proved and he was discharged.—At Lifford, near Ennis, on Tuesday, the residence of Mrs. Billon was set fire to. The incendiary used paraffin oil, which was poured over the thatched roof of the house. The fire was, however, extinguished before any serious damage was done. Mrs. Dillon has evicted some tenants from her property, and to this circumstance the outrage is attributed. THE WIDNES BLUE RIBBON ARMY. A meeting of tha Widnes branch of the Blue Ribbon Gospel Army was held in the Volunteer Hall, on Monday evening. There was a large attendance of the public, and the platform was crowded with men and wcmen, representa- tives of a number of the "stations" in the country, amongst them being the Rev. M. Baxter, the president of the Army, and Major Richardson. The chief event of the evening was the "presentation of colours" to Staff Captain limes, who has charge of the Whines detachment, but the Rev. M. Baxter previously delivered an address on "The Signs of the Times, and the speedy coming of Christ, He said he looked upon the Blue Ribbon Army as one of the signs of the times. It was originated in 1877 by Francis Murphy, a farm labourer and. publican, who, becoming converted to sobriety, wished to aid other drunkards in becoming so too. Millions of blue ribbons were now worn in the United States and England. The object of the Army was to change the bad clothes of children into good ones; and it was causing the publicans, distillers, and brewers to cry out, but was of great benefit to the bakers, bootn-aakers, and others. They bad reason to thank God for the movement, and a retrospec- tive view ot the temperance cause for the past 30 or 40 yeers would show that more progress had been made during the last six years than in the previous 60. He expressed a hope that the movement would spread to all parts of the inhabited globe, and went on to deal with the second part of his subject—" The speedy coming of Christ. Turkey, he said, was "drying up" to prepare a way for the Jews to return to Palestine, for so long as Turkey remained' this was impossible. He stated that the extraordinary occurrences which had taken place at Ischia, Java, and the choleraic outbreak in Egypt were all predicted in the bible, and affirmed that the world was to he" turned upside down" in a few years. They were told that after the Euphrates was dried up and the Jews had gone back to Palestine, the world would be visited by an earthquake such as was not known since man dwelt upon the earth. Nihilism, socialism, anarchy, and landleaguers were going through the land in every direction to prepare the way for this great earthquake, and these things were evidences that they were entering the milleniurn. The Church had almost ended its last troubles and trials.—Major Nelson having spoken of the work of the Army in Scotland, the President pre- sented a flag to Staff-Captain Elmes.—Major Itinnannsox followed with a few complimentary ohservations respecting Staff-Captain Elmes, whom, he said, would be true and loyal to the Blue Ribbon Army of Widnes.—Staff-Captain Elam replied that that WAS one of the proudest moments of his life. When he first came to Widnes it was hurled in his teeth that he came there "on his own hook," and other statements equally false were made, bet the " soldiers" had stood by him, and they had come off victorious. Station after station was going to be opened, and he believed that greater victories would be achieved in the future than in the past,—Captain Whitehead, of Widnes, then spoke, and then there was placed on the table an ordinary cradle, which the president presented to Major Richardson as an expression of the interest the Widnes corps took in his welfare.—Major RICH&RDSON returned thanks, adding that the Blue Ribbon Army had 104 stations, 144 field- officers in Engla;id and 13 in Scotland.—The evening's proceedings were diversified by the singing of hymns. Solos were given by Miss Bold, Mies Atkisson (Winsford), and Miss Robins, while Misses Bickerdyke !Ind Siddall sang a duet. The Widnes 'Temperance Brass Band pleyed selec- tions. At the conclusion of the meeting a "coffee supper " was provided.

Fhe prisoner, it seemed, had gone to the chemical works of Messrs. Lockwood and Leith, where her husband was engaged, and raised a disturbance there. It, however, ap- pe-red fi- • O't had br•rm driven tl this action by the neglect of her husband. He had recently been committed to gaol, fcirr,f9ur Montba,foryeglectiug hie:wife'and family, but thisi dad.not aesuf to -have worked .'4.n amendment, as he was -agatn neglecting them as much as-before. In view :of tlais' the Bench decided to dismiss the prisoner on her promising not to cause further annoyance to Messrs. Lockwood and Leith, and to call the attention of the relieving officer to the ease.

_ EE( INTELI,IGE _ The cab ant omnibus drivers of Marseilles have struck for higher wages. Dr. Thuillet, of the Pasteur Fcientitic Nliesien, has died in Alexandria from cholera. The French comm ander in Tonquin has suspended opera- tions pending the arrival of reinforcements. Princess Bismarck, wife of the German Chancellor, is re- ported to be alarmingly ill. It is reported from Alexandria that a son of .erabi Pasha is about to enter the British Army. Two Egyptian soldiers, convicted of participation in the massacres in Alexandria, were hanged in that city on Tues- day. The nnmber of Italians who emigrated to other countries daring last year was 161,562, as compared with 135,832 in 1881. Intelligence has been received from Coomassie of the de- feat of Koffee K death in his attempt to recover the Ashen- tee throne. Six peasant women have been killed by lightning while standing for shelter under a tree during a thunderstorm at Kolen, Bohemia. A sulphur cave has fallen in at Lercara, Fridda, in Sicily, killing several persons. Among the injured was Mr. John Rose, the proprietor. A. large public meeting was held at Buenos Ayres on Mon- day, at which resolutions were passed in favour of obligatory and secular education. The Sultan of Zanzibar has been presented by the British diplomatic agent with the Grand Cross of the Order of St. Michael and St. George. It is reported from St. Petersburg that new arrests have taken place there among the officers of the Navy and of the Guards, especially of the regiments Ismailovsky and Sealenovsky. Prince Alexander of Bulgaria has re-established the Tirnova Constitution, and the Conservative Ministry having I resigned, a Liberal Cabinet has been formed, with M. Zank- off as president. The Servian parliamentary elections, which closed on Wednesday, resulted in the return ef 40 supporters of the Government., 14 Liberals, and 59 Radicals. In 19 cases s]cond ballots will be necessary. The Hawaiian Minister of Fo,.eign Affairs has sent a formal protest to the English, French, and American Go- vernments against any annexation of Pacific islands by alien or colonial Powers. A silver crown, sent by the French colony of Rosario, Santa Fee has been deposited on M. Gambetta's tomb in the presence of M. Garnbetta's father and the Prefect of the Alpes Maritimes. It is reported from Rome that Mr. Errington is expected there in November. His object, it is said, is to continue the negotiations for establishing friendly relations between the British Government and the Vatican. Official statistics show that the number of suicides in Russia in 1882 anmunted to 1,811, and during the last five years to 7,713. Moscow furnished the largest contingent, then followed Kieff, Warsaw, and St. Petersburg. DIATEI or ran ELDER BOOTH—The death was ennounced on Tuesday, at an advanced age, of the veteran actor Junius Brutus Booth. He is best know •to this generation as the father of the distinguished tragedian, Mr. Edwin Booth. SALVATIONISTS IN SWITZERLAND —News comes from Geneva of the imprisonment, at Neufchatel, of Miss Booth, for contravening the order prohibiting Salvatimnist services within the canton. For a similar offence, the Geneva police authorities have ordered " Colonel " Clibborn, of the Salva- tion Army, to leave the canton. BLOWN TO PIECES —A young officer in the 4th French Engineers has committed suicide, at Paris, in a peculiarly horrible manner. Unstrung at the idea of having to face a court-martial for some trivial fault, he tied a belt tilled with dynamite round his waist, and applied a match. Be was literally blown to pieces. TSB ENTRY OF ITALIAN TROOPS INTO ROME.—A tele- gram from Rome announces that the commemoration on Thursday of the entry into that city of the Italian troops on the 20th September, 1810. passed off very successfully. The demonstration was attended by members of the munici- pality, representatives of the army ald of various societies, and an enormous crowd of people. MADAGASCAR.—A despatch from Tamatave reports that the state of siege proclaimed by the French commander continues, and the political situation remains unchanged. The Malagasy forces have remained strictly on the defensive for the past two months. The Hove ambassadors returned to Madagascar on the 30th ulthno. They landed at Mala- ' tave, but did not proceed to the capital. Tint DUTCH PARLIAMENT.—The Dutch Parliament was opened on Monday by the King, who, in his speech from the throne, said the relations of Holland with foreign states were friendly. As to the colonies, his Majesty said revolts had been suppressed in several parts of the Dutch Indies, but in Atcheen serious efforts were still required to complete the pacification of the country. Reverting to home affairs, he said the revision of the Constitution was still being dis- cussed by the Royal Commission appointed to examine it. The Socialists seized the opportunity of the opening of Parliament to make a demonstration in the Hague in favour of universal suffrage. STATE OF ZuttriAND.—A detachment of artillery and a squadron of dragoons, a Durban telegram states, have been ordered to proceed to the Natal frontier. Their distinction is believed to be the reserve territory, where preparations are going forward which will inevitably result in another aenfiict between Cetewayo's followers and the unfriendly tribes unless there is an intervention sufficiently influential to keep the peace. Dabulamanzi, Cetewayo's brother, who was recently arrested at Greytown while coming frem Isandula without a pass, has been reprimanded, and sent back to Zululand under escort. It was telegraphed from Durban, on Tuesday, that the Governor of Natal had sent an ultimatum to Cetewayo ordering him to surrender him- self and all his followers within ten days to the special Minister at Ekowe, but this statement was contradicted in a ,ter telegram.

_ RUNCORN RURM, SI-NITARY AUTHoRiTy. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhous-e on Tuesday, the Rev. Canon Barclay presiding. There were present Messrs. John Ashton, J. Weir, E. A. Walling- ton, J. Darbyshire, Rev. J. Lockwood, W. Jackson, P. Hall, J. Smith, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. The MEDICAL OFFICER (Mr. J. G. Bride) presented the following statement :—rhave to report the death of Frances Wittingion, at Astmoor, Halton, on the sth inst., alleged to be due to choleraic diarrheas. During my inspection of the cottage premises occupied by the widower, Henry George Wittington, I found no insanitary condition to account for the outbreak. Dr. Carruthers had caused disinfection of the premises to be practiced, and I instructed your inspector to disinfect the c)ttage and premises. I have verbal and written instructions as to the thorough disinfection of house linen, clothing, and drains, and the thorough cleansing of clothing, linen, sc., as well as the lime washing of all the walls and ceilings of the cottage. No other CASO has been reported. The woman (deceased) was very delicately constituted, therefore, I have little doubt that death resulted from exhaustion consequent on diarrhoea attacking so weakly a subject. This form of diarrhoea is very frequently met with in most parts of the kingdom during the autumn season, and I have no hesita- tion in stating that no anxiety need exist in the public mind as to the character of this case. I mention this because there is reason to fear that much uneasiness already prevails concerning the cause of death of Mrs. Wittintton. I have also to report a very extensive outbreak of measles at Helsby. During my visit, on Friday last, full directions as to disinfection and isolation were given to the parents of children infected. Instructions were also given to the master of the schools. With reference to the cottage pre- mises occupied by CoifTit.h Griffiths, next to Mr. Walling- ton's house, at Sutton, I have no difficulty in stating that the manure heap in its present position, as well as the privy, 1 ashpit, and pigstye, are a nuisance dangerous and injurious to health. The privy, ashpit, and pigstye were in a filthy condition, and require regular attention. This was all the business of public interest.

FARN WORTH TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. A successful demonstration took place on Saturday in con- nection with the Farnworth branch of the Church of Eng- land Temperance Society, the occasion being the inaugura- tion of a new banner purchased out of the funds raised by subscription among the members and friends of this pros- perous branch of temperance work. A procession left the girls' school, Farnworth, shortly after half-past two, and, to the enlivening music of tbe Widnes Star of Temperance brass band, marched through a portion of the village. In the procession was carried for the first time a new bannerette, the gift of Mrs. Hibnert, Charlesville, Farnworth. The procession was accompanied by the Rev. Geo. Bond, M.A. (vicar of Farnworth), Mrs. and the Misses Bond, Rev. J. Wright-Williams, M.A. (vicar of Widnes), Rev. J. Holden, Rev. C. E. Gaussen (St. Luke's, Liverpool), Miss Hibbert, Mr. J. W. Davies (hon. sec.), Sze. The venerable church was reached at twenty minutes past four, where service was held. The prayers were read by the Vicar, the first lesson by the Rev. C. E. Gaussen, and the second lesson by theßev. J. Holden. A sermon was preached by the Rev. C. E. Gaussen from the text "Lift ye up a banner." Miss Bond presided at the organ. A public tea party was afterwards held in the girls' schoolroom, to which upwards of 300 persons sat down. A miscellaneous entertainment followed, which was presided over by the Rev. George Bond. During the evening addresses on temperance work were delivered by the Chairman the Rev. C. E. Gaussen, and Mr. J. A. Enwright, of Litherland. The entertainment was very in- teresting and enjoyable, being taken pert in by Miss Bond, Miss Amy Bond, Miss Hibbert, the Misses Pilling, Messrs. Banks, A. Carter, A. G. Davies, J. T. Lowe, Prescott, the temperance glee party, and the handbell ringers.—On the motion of the Rev. J. llownx, seconded by Mr. PEATTIE, and supported by the Cifenalfax, a unanimous vote of thanks was accorded to the Rev. C. E. GallSSell and Mr. Enwright.—Mr. WILLIAM JOHNSON (Lunt's Heath) pro- posed a similar vote to the subscribers to the banner fund, also to Mrs. Hibbert for the bannerette, and to all who had assisted in the arrangements for the afternoon and evening. —The proposition was seconded by Mr. Halinixrr DEN- :TErr.—Iu responding. the Cnernsfare, rn.ade special reference to 'Mrs. Iliblaert'S. klndnAs'ilAre-cI also to .-.ll.er,*ood VFork;e4 complished bY-Mias HibberL. not only that ,day,,butlieyet; since the society WAS formed.—We should mention tat :.on. leaving the church the members of the juvenile section were each presented with a bun, it being Ufa intention of the committee to treat them to a tea in a week or two.

The prisoner was ap- prehended on the previous day whilst in the act of pledging some of the ariicle2,, of which he was unable to gives satisfac- tory account.— d e was remanded until Monday. ATTEMPTING TO DEFRAUD THE CHESHIRE LINES COMMIT- TEE. —John Shaw, springmaker, Swinton, was charged with riding in a third-class carriage on the Cheshire Lines Railway from Livereoel to Warrington without haying previously paid his fare, and with intent to defraud the company of the same. The defendant was found under the seat of the careisge on the , previous day, by the foreman porter at the Warrington I Central Station He had neither mosey nor ticket.—Defen- dant, who plesded he was very drunk at the time, was fined 2.s and costs; or. in default, 14 days' imprisonment. WILFUL DAMAGE TO A DOOL—Thomas Forbes, forgehand, Heath-side, was summoned for havieg on the 15th inst,damaged a door, belonging to Charles Longshaw, to the amount of 3 /s. A young man named Wa,d was in his house, and had just locked the door, when it fell in, followed by three bricks. The door was in good order before, and he heard the defendant's voice in this street, but did not see him do the damage. A gi-1, however, stited that she saw the defendant at the door.—De- callei several witnesses, who denied that he did the damage, I but the magistrates were of opinion the defendant had-done it, and fined him 2os and costs, total £2 9s, or in default of pay- ment, one month's imprisonment.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNEsDAY.—Before Mr, Edward Gieenall and Mr. James

Marson. DRUNK OR SOBER?—The only case for d:sposal was one of d unkenness. John Roach and Mictsael Walsh, Martinseroft, who were summoned at the last sesslons for being drunk on the Manchester-road, Woolston, on the 2nd September, and whose ease was adjourned in order to obtain additional evi- dence, were again charged with the offence.—The constable (McFarlane) who had the case in hand called a man to support his statement, and the defendants called two young women Their evidence showed that Walsh was slightly intoxicated, but that Roach was apparently sober.—The charge against Roach was dismissed, but Walsh was ordered to pay 5s and costs, 21s In all.

Moicni.r.—Before Mr. 3. Brundrit and Mr. W. Bankes. RIOTOUS OHARACTERS.—James Mulhearn, of Water-street, and John Fish, Ring-street, were charged with fighting in King-street on the Bth instant, and were each bound over in his own recognisances to keep the peace for twelve months.— For a similar offence, committed in Brook-street, on the 14th September, William Leeson, a L mdon and North-Western Railway Company's waterman, residing at the Ferry-hut, was also dealt with in a similar manner. VAGRANCY.—Joseph Variables and George Pa.rtington, both of whom stated they were only released fromigaol on Saturday, were charged with cnnrnitting a breach oftthe Vagrants' Act. —P.S. 161 c Ilichael said about a quarter to two on Sunday morn- ing, he found the prisoners sleeping in an unoccupied house In Cooper-street. They stated they could n it obtain lodgings.— Mr. Brundrit said this was a very lame excuse, and committed them to gaol for 14 days. \BREACHES OF THE HIGHWAY ker.—For not havir4 his name marked on his cart, Robert Price. of Weston, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE —Henry WatklD, of Halton, was sum- moned by the Runcorn Union School Attendance Committee, for neglecting to send his child regularly to school, an,l on the evidence of Mr. Wright he was fined ss. including costs.

Gasket'. jun. lIIINTENANCK OF A SON.—Thomas Molyneaux was sum- moned to show c :me why an ordor sh iuld not be made upon him to c3ntrlbule towards the support of his son, aged ten, who was committed to an industrial school, on the 29th August, until he was 16 years of age.—Supt. Barker said he could not ask for less than Is per week,—lnspe3tor P.-Arnett said the do. fendant's earnings averaged 14s 6d per week. He had at home a boy between 13. and 14 years of age, who, howevei, was not at work.—Defendant stated he was unable to pay anything at present, but Supt. Barker ob,erved that it would have cost him more than a Is to keep his boy at home, and the Bench i made an order for is per week.

ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Cook and Dr. Gask-Al. CHIMNEYS ON FIRE —Lewis Morgenrath of College-street, and Patr:ck Roach, of Parr, we-e each fin dls and costs, for having allowed their dwelling-house chimney to be on fire. UNLICENSED DOG —Samuel Coates. farmer, Parr, was fined 5s and costs for keeping a dog without a license. MONDAY.—Before Mr. T. Pilkington, Dr. Twyford, and Mr. A. Sinclair. BREACH 07 THE PEACH. Two young men named Lewis Marshall and ttichard McOormick were each bound over to keep the peace for three mouths, for having been fighting with each other in Liverpool-road, on Saturday night.

ST. HELENS couN ri PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. T. Pilkington. STRAY OATTLE.—Joseph Owen, farmer, Wiadle, was fined 2s 6d and casts for having allowed four horses to stray on the highway on the 31st ult. This was the secon.,l conviction of de- fendant far like offenses within a short time. BREACH ,HT THE PEACE —A charge of breach of the peace against a young man named Edwa-d Kelly, of Eccleston, was dismissed.

PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. Earle and W. Pilkington. BREACH OF THE PEACE —Thomas Aldred was bound over for one month for having caused a breach of the peace by fighting with a man unknown in Prescot, on the 25th tilt.—John Win- stanley was also bound over for one month for a like offence at Prescot, on the 15th Inst, VAtiIIANCY.—An old and decrepit tramp named Thommt Holme waS Sent to gaol for 14 days for having been begging in Frew3t, on NI ocday.—Jeremy McCarty, another of the itinerant fraternity. was charged with sleeping In a shippon on the pre- mises of William Longton, Whlston Pottery. An officer said that shortly after midnight on Tuesday morning he found the prisoner sleeping in a sack of straw in the shippon mentioned. Seven days' imprisonment. OARELF_SS DRITEES.—John Almond was fined 5s and costs for having driven a horse and cart without reins at Huyton Quarry; William Finningham was fined in tho same amount for having been drunk in charge of a horse and cart at Knows. ley. on the 11th lost; and William Hesketh was fined. Is ed and costa for a like offence at Knowsley, on the 6th Inst.

A PUBLICAN CoNvicrma Htalsimr.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Charles Whitfield, the landlord of a beerhouse in Ashfield-street, Parr, was charged with hav- ing sold drink during prohibited hours. This charge was based upon the evidence given in an alleged burglary case at Parr, an account of which was given in these columns last week. It appeared that two men natned Maurice Hanley and Edward Maley had been served with beer by Whitfield after eleven o'clock on the night of the 9th inst., and again about one o'clock the following morning. On the same night the landlord's gold watch and chain were stolen, and he suspecting these two men gave the above information to the police. The men were arrested and committed for trial, and as a further result the police brought forward the pre- sent charge, based on the landlord's own statement. .Mr. J. 0. Suift appeared for the defendant, and admitted the offence, but asked the Bench to take into account the former good character of the defendant, and the fact that he had been compelled to leave the beerhouse. A fine of 20e and costs was imposed. A DANGEROUS OPERATION BY MINERS.—TWO named Henry Ashcroft and John Williams, were charged kt the St. Helene Police Court, on Monday, with having com- mitted a breach of the Coal Mines Regulation Act. Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted on behalf of Messrs. Richard Evans and Company. It appeared that the defendants worked con- jointly in the Havana Mine, and that on the sth inst. they had a shot in their working place which had missed fire. The proper course to have taken was to have drilled another shot hole, and prepared another shot; but instead of this the old shot was withdrawn, apparently for the purpose of saving the pound of ponder. This, it was stated, might have caused an explosion which would probably have resulted in the Injury or death of the defendants. The de- fendant Ashcroft stated that be bad drawn the shot himself before Williams had come to work, and in consequence the charge against Williams was withdrawn. Ashcroft seas fined 105 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. 1 MUIMER OF A FARMER AT LOWTON. ARREST OF A RELATIVE. On Tiles lay night about ten o'clock Inspector Charnley, of Leigh, arrested John Gibbon, lain labourer, 27 years of age, on suspicion of having caused the death of his uncle, an old man reamed Joshua Rigby, farmer, Cheetham's Fold, Lowton. Rigby was found on Tuesday morning lying dead with his throat cut in his own bedroom. At the tinle it was thought he had committed suicide, and this was gene- rally accepted as the cause of death. 'Deceased, who was formerly a Cow doctor and pig killer, was a bachelor, and was regarded by his neighbours as an eccentric person. The prisoner was brought up at the farm by the deceased and his two sisters,andrecently got married. Mrs. Gibbon was ineincsi to go to live with her husband and the deceased last June, about which time an aged maiden sister of the deceased had gone to live elsewhere owimr, as is alleged, to tilS violence of her brother (Rigby). As an inducement for Mrs. Gibbon to join her husband at the farm, the deceased • made a certain disposition of his property, b it ii is aheted that he had since revoked this dispositiore A tuan, rietasee William Richardson, fist reported findine be:lv to • Police-Constable Naylor, who went to the farm and found the body lying between the bed -and the wall of the bed- room. The body was still warm. Near the deceased was raz e. and a pocketknife, the blade Ut the latter tieing covered with blood. There were also marks of blood upon the sacks, which had been used as a carpeting for tha floor, and there were blood marks in venous places on the floor and at the top of the stairs. The police reported the case to Mr. Barker, district coroner, as one of suicide, bet fro:n the circumstances Inspector' Cherniey took Gibbon in charge. The Coroner ordered a post-mortem examination of the body, and this was made by Dr. Perrin on Wednesday afternoon. Ad doubt as to the cause of death has been re- moved by this examination, and it now appeals that a foul and delibe!ate murder has been committed in the dead of night. but by whom there is not at preeeet ev:dence to show. John Gibbon, the man in custody, is spoken of by the villagers as a person who in his station of life has borne an excellent character: He was quiet, according to some rather taciture, and, generally believed to be in fear of his uncle's diepleasure. By common consent the de- ceased was held in small esteem. He was intensely selfish ; he was, in fact, a miser, passionate, and often brutal in his conduct towards his sisters and other relatives. Mrs. Martha Gibbon, mother of the prisoner and youngest sister of the deceased, became a widow 24 years ago. The prisoner, then a child three years old, was taken to the old homestead and there reared. The two maiden sisters of the deceased were older than he. Mary Rigby, the elder, died last October, owing, report seid at the time, to injuries inflicted by her brother, who, the mother of the prisoner says, refused to let anybody except herself assist in laying out the body, which was covered with marks of violence, caused by his ill-treatment. Something was said at the time about obtaining a warrant for his apprehension, but he threatened to cut off any of his relatives who took or sanctioned such a step, and the remains of the woman ' were allowed to be interred. The inquiry naturally suggests itself, how could such a case have been permitted to pass un- noticed by the authorities? The woman had reached a ripe old age (77), and, therefore, it is probable that the gentleman who granted the certificate which enabled the death to be registered in the usual way had no suspicion of the circum- stances. It is, however, affirmed by the relatives and friends of the deceased that she died from a blow on the bead inflicted by him. The inmates of the house appear to have lived in complete terror of, and in subjection to, the deceased. The other unmarried sister, Sarah Rigby, was likewise frequent- ly assaulted In a cowardly manner by her brother, and she finally left him through his brutality, and went to live with her sister, the widow Gibbon, mother of the prisoner, at Bradshawgate, Leigh. A prosecution was then threatened, for the woman is described as then having a hole in her leg, the result of a kick, but the fear that it might influence the ultimate disposition of the old man's property again prevailed in his favour. Being then deserted, and in a state of isolation, Rigby, who was a powerful broad-shouldered fellow, and possessed great muscular strength for his age (73), found it impossible, or at least undesirable, to live alone. It is said that Joshua Rigby, his other nephew, who lives near, declined to take his wife and family to the farm, and that then the deceased made a will in favour of the prisoner Gibbon, whose wife there left her own parents to join her husband at the farm. The last event in the family history occurred last June. There was many a scene of violence between June and the finding of the remains of the deceased last Tuesday morn- ing. Rigby maintained his authority in full sway. It is said that his nephew, the accused, took no action by word or deed, even when his wife was the subject of an abusive attack, so much was he under the spell of his uncle. Last Sunday the deceased gave rein to his passion in regard to the poultry coming into the kitchen, and on that occasion the younger Mrs.Ciibbon said he went towards her in a threatening attitude with an open razor in his hand, having previously sharpened it in her presence. She adds, "I was afraid he was about to do something, but be suddenly turned round and got hold of the water, which he ' slat ' all over the floor." It was mainly owing to the latter incident that the woman left the house to go 'sack to her parents. What transpired afterwards has not come fully to light. The prisoner's movements on Sunday night—whether he slept in his uncle's house or not—are surrounded with some little mystery. Strong and powerful as the deceased was, he must have been unequal to the attack made upon him, which was evidently effected from behind by a knife or some other sharp instrument during part of the struggle. The house being away from any other dwelling will account for the fact that nothing was heard of the struggle or of calls for assistance. 'lle Louse of the deceased is very old. His bedroom window was to the right hand of the top of the stairs, and there is no door to the room. Thus a person reaching the top could see where the deceased lay at a chance, because the left side of the bed where he was found is directly opposite. P.C. Naylor &WS deceased's right arm was on the bed, on which there were some blend marks. The razor and knife were on the bed about half a yard apart, the knife being bloodstained. Sacks were used to cover the floor, and on one or two of these, as well as other places, there were marks of blood. The sympathy of the inhabitants in the neighbourhood of the.murder is slrongly against the murdered man, and his own relations are not as yet taking any steps to bury him because only 3s. sa. was found in the house. The police are experiencing great difficulty in ebtaining trustworthy evidence. THE PRISOFER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. During Tuesday the prisoner was taken before Mr. F. W. Booth. Inspector Charnley described the condition of the body, there being two large contused wounds on the head and another behind the shoulder blade. There were similar wounds behind both arms, which led him to think the man could not have caused the injuries himself. There was an incised wound in the throat. Prisoner admitted be- fore being apprehended that deceased and he Were the only persons in the house on Monday night. He also stated that his uncle had been getting drink on Monday night,- and on getting home went straight to bed. Prisoner said he got up to his work about five o'clock next morning aud attended to his duties until breakfast time. Soon after eight, thinking something, was wrong, he called in a neighbour; he had before that seen the deceased lying by the side of the bed, but be did not go to him. Prisoner now said that he told the Inspec- tor that William Richardson and Thomas Bent were in the house when the deceased was found. They suggested to him (prisoner) that be should go upstairs to look, and having done so he sent Richardson for the policeman. The prisoner was remanded. THE INQUEsT. The inquest was opened by Mr. Barker, on Thursday, at Lowton. Mr. Richardson, of Bolton, appeared to watch the Case on behalf of Gibbon. The Coroner regretted that they were called upon to in- vestigate the cause of a death which he thought there was no doubt was the result of violence. The police, in John f exercise of their discretion, bad effected the arrest would Gibbon, the deceased's nephew, but he hoped they wond not be in the least prejudiced against the prisonerhd he did Ann Battersby, who laid out the body, said a not I wnomiticehiaonyncyastidine tahtethneigthimtcoa.p offierthospmo was that the deceased. The cap bruises w es on the body were self-inflicted. She cut the shirt and flannel singlet from the man, and did not notice any other cuts. Martha Gibbons, sister of the deceased, and mother to the young man in custody, said she examined the shirt (which is in the hands of the police), and found no ca's in it. At the close of her evidence she asked to be allowed to make a statement, and said deceased had a sister in the churchyard whose head he laid open. The Coroner said that had nothing to do with this in- quiry.' Mr. John Beswick Perrin, surgeon, Leigh, deposed that the throat of the deceased was cut. There were two wounds on the skull, which was fractured, and there were wounds on both arms, two on the outer aide of the arms being caused by a stab. Bet'weiiithe right eye and the right ear there were four small punctured wounds.. The injury to the scalp would cause instantaneous death.-He believed the gash in the throat was inflicted after death. Of itself it would not have caused death. awlonsth:neread until' , ont nextlea Tuesday. application of Superinten- dent T h Jackson, t d CAPTAIN WEBB'S SISTER 'DROWNED. Mr. W. R. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 22, 1883,

41131 r a large majority the Executive of the 411 chester Liberal Association have decided ticilAt to contest the seat rendered vacant by tc death of Arr. HUGH BIRLEY, who was pf Illinority member for the city. A variety vleasons must, of course, have weighed e"LI the Executive in determining their, I°,llrse of action, and it may be urged in. t4,lllless that they are 'Dater able than out- falcSB--necessarily unacqttainted with all the 11,1;:s,', to decide the important question voi:-‘ller it is politic at this juncture to pro- paZ! a contest between the two political Fari:be it from us to question the th,—‘loin. of the resolution at which the Execu- gi'e have arrived; we can only say their deci- 0, has been received with surprise through- the country, and we hope that the th'llerosity- which they have shown towards be Political opponents in this instance will reciprocated by them if a similar state of threuinstances should arise in the history of obe. Liberal party of Manchester. One .Jection urged against a contest is that if a i'lliberal were returned—and in a fair fight between the parties this would undoubtedly the case—he would of necessity have to &A`ve place at the general election to a Con- That may be quite true, but sup- it is, surely there is sufficient political of"llacrifice among the Liberal gentlemen tanchester to submit even to such an wil:rlgement as that especially at a period Qo'll it is essential that the hands of the tiyvernment should be strengthened. Lib refusing to contest the seat the tiiroerals of Manchester have deliberately the 41 away two votes on a division during thafrettainder of the present Parliament, and for‘ certainly cannot be a pleasant reflection Pea, anY Liberal constituency. There ap- k, also, to have been in ' the Liberal PAW:. a wholesome dread of the Radical Dr. this '''itißsT. It is now some time since- -404 distinguished Chancery barrister an triliced his intention of contesting the city 1144 e first opportunity, and he is proving ,therserlf as good as his word. It would, eeei;`°re) under other conditions, have so„, .11ecessary to reckon with the doctor b '44ehnie etter , and it would have been to do so nbw, we are in- 3iori. Aso think, than on a future occa- titan Ile is bound to poll more votes now well. " there were a Liberal in the field as ,„„With a good Liberal his poll might be futl-;;Iall as to give him his quietus for the toe The lefeat of both in such ba._ritest could be no loss to the Liberal arld the Conservatives would only bold

their own. A good poll in the present instance, however, will embolden the doctor foranother attack at the generalelection ; and such an attack may just throw two seats— instead of only the minority seat—into the hands of the donservatives, another very un- pLeasant reflection for the Manchester Liberals. Be that as it may, the circum- stances as they now present themselves must be dealt with. We have no hope that Dr. PANKHURST will be successful, we - do not suppose the doctor himself has any serious idea that he will be returned; but he is deserving of our 'sympathy if nothing more tangible for his pluck. He is opposing the ' strongest candidate which the Conservative party could possibly put forth, and there is arrayed against him a combination sufficient to frighten a person of harder mettle. For a long time the Conservatives have been pre- pared for an emergency such as this, and on their side the campaign commenced in earnest on Wednesday, and on Thursday it opened in the interests of Dr. PANKHURST, whose re- ception was most enthusiastic. A careful perusal of the two addresses issued by the candidates show that they have been framed in a conciliatory spirit from the two different standpoints. Both candidates are evidently angling for the votes of the moderate Liberals. For instance, Mr. HOULDSWORTH has recently made so much progress in his political educaticn that he is in favour of the assimilation of the county and borough fran- chise: and if he will study the speeches of Dr. PANKHURST he may, before the con- test closes, become a convert to equal electoral districts having equal electol al rights, irrespective of any representation of property. Though opposed to Local Option, it is something to find •Mr. HOULDSWORTH in favour of the liquor traffic being, if only to a limited extent, governed by representatives of •the ratepayers. Such an admission is an indi- cation that on this-question he is-on the right tack. He promises his support. to a Sunday Closing Bill for England, and on his attitude in regard to -this print we can congratulate ; him; but we are afraid he is immovable so ' far as giving any countenance to the senara-1 tion of the, Church from the',gtate. - When compared with .his ,utterances of ,1•886; Mr. HOULDSWORT,H'S present address is an ex- tremely mild production On the other hand, it is noticeable' that pr. PANKHURST has somewhat modified his political platform. He has expunged those planks which were likely to have estranged many voters from him, and so far as we can see his address is now such that any sound I Liberal ought to be able to acquiesce in. If there be any Liberal who objects—though we cannot understand why any Liberal should— to the abolition of the House of Lords as an; assembly of hereditary legislators, we would ' point out that Dr. PANKHURST makes no mention of that " consummation so devoutly to be wished" in his programme on the present occasion, we conclude he does not propose to advocate it just now, and there- fore weak-kneed Liberals need not be afraid to support him on that score. If it be objected that the doctor is an advocate for , the exclusion of religious teaching from our national schools, and many with us considerl it very desirable that the religious element I should be excluded from these schools. then those who are in favour of retaining the' religious teaching need not withhold their votes from the Radical doctor, because he seems to have expunged that point from his declaration of political belief. Then the doctor makes no mention of that dreaded "universal adult suffrage" of which some Liberals make so much, yet we fail to see why every man should not have a voice in the making of those laws which he is bound to observe and is punished for disobeying. If ob- jection be taken to Dr. PANKHURST'S advocacy for Ireland of a 'just measure of local self- government on federal lines," we may remind those who do so object that the Government are already practically pledged to some such measure. On the whole we can find nothing in the doctor which need cause the Man- chester Liberals alarm. He has long been a faithful worker in the cause of reform, and if he is more advanced than some Liberals, that is their loss and his gain; he pogsesses the ability to make the voice of Manchester heard and felt in Parliament if returned; while his intimate acquaintance with the requirements of that great cons tituency make him a most suitable representative. We trust the Liberals of Manchester will sink their prejudices, and for the sake of supporting the Gladstone Government by an addition of two votes during the present Parlia,7nent, return even that dreadful Radical Dr. PANKHURST.

MANoNEsTEN NAVIGATION —A correspondent writes to a contemporary :—" A movement is being made with the view of forming a syndicate, to be composed of leading members of the mercantile, manufacturing, and other com- munities of the city and adjoining districts, to consider and determine upon the propriety of making an application to Parliament for powers to carry out such plan of navigation as may be decided upon." SHOP ROBBERY IT WIDNES —At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. John Brock, Mary Mclnery, a woman with a child in her arms, was brought up in custody charged with haying, on Saturday night, stolen 51b3 4 ounces of fingering wool, value 10s. ed., from the shop of James Birchall, hosier, Waterloo-road. On Saturday night the wife of P.C. Boardman was walking down Waterloo-road, in company with Mrs. _Sandland, when she saw the prisoner stoop into the doorway of Mr. Birchall's shop, and then place something under her shawl. bhe followed the prisoner into Marsh-street, where the latter stopped to speak to a woman, and Mrs. Boardman returned and informed Mr. Sandland, Mr. Birchall's assistant, of what she had seen, and together they went after the prisoner. After chasing her down an entry into Wellington-street, they caught her, and subsequently handed' her over to P.C. Thompson. The wool was afterwards found in Wellington- street by John Concannon, beerhouse keeper.—The prisoner pleaded not guilty.—lnspector Barnett remarked that the prisoner had been previously convicted of drunkenness and theft, and the Bench sentenced her to a month's imprisen- ment with hard labour.

WESLEYAN DISTRICT MEETING. The September Or financial district meeting for South Lancashire and the Liverpool district was held on Wednesday in the Brunswick School, Liverpool, The Rey. T. M'Cullagh (President of the Conference) was welcomed to the chair of the meeting by Rev. Charles Garrett, ex-president. The President said it was singular that while no president of the Conference had presided over the Liverpool district meeting for the last 90 years, vet during the past year they had had two. Per- mission was granted for the erections of new chapels in die Tarporley, Preston (Wesley), and Southport (Trinity) cir- cuits. It was resolved that the May district meeting should be held at Runcorn. In connection with the visit of the Rev. H. P. Hughes to Liverpool (where he conducts a mission from Wednesday, September 20) it was resolved i to hold a convention on Friday, September 28th, n the morning, for ministers only, and in the afternoon open to all Christian workers. A scheme was read for a revival mis- sion to be conducted through most of the circuits in the district. It was announced that the following were the missionary deputations to the district, viz : Home Mission, Rev. T. H. Hopkins; Foreign Missions (autumn), Revs. J. R. Gleave and S. T. House: (spring, a general secretary, Revs. T. G. Clapham and S. Whitebead. Their work was arranged for. It was resolved that special efforts should he made in all the circuits to revivo the interest in the Foreigh Mission Fund. Attention was called to the serious difficulty arising from the circuits not fulfilling their pledge to provide an additional minister's house. tit present, in the Con- nexion, more than 100 ministers are married and nmble to obtain a house. This involved the Home Mission Fund In an annual expenditure of between £4.000 and £5 GOO, which might be more profitably expended in evangelical aggression.

MEM:SET MISSIONS TO SEAMEN AT RUNCORN.-011 Sun- day. at Runcorn Parish Church, the Rev. T. Patrick, M.A., chaplain to the Mersey Mission to Seamen, preached a ser- mon on the work and character of the Mission. The col- lection including a donation of £1 lOs , amounted to £lO 12s. 9d.

Tnn WIDNES Scßoor. BOARD BLECTIONL—A meeting, having reference to the forthcoming School Board election, was held in Lacey-street schoolroom on Saturday evening. The proceedings were conducted in private, but we have since learned from a trustworthy source that an eff.nt will be made to get a majority of Nonconformist candidates on the Board, but that the Nonconformists were not averse to effect- ing a coalition with the Church of England candidates if it could be brought about. PEOPESSOR ANDRE'S ALPINE Cnom.—This popular com- pany of young lady vocalists attired in picturesque Swiss costume are to give three of their popular concerts in the Drill dal, Widnes, commencing Monday, Octobert Ist. They come to us with the highest recommendations. The vicar and other prominent gentlemen are announced to pre- side, so that here, as in most other towns visited by them we may expect the hall to be crowded each evening. SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE REVISION COURTS.—The re- vision of the South-West Lancashire lists of voters com- menced at Bt. George's Hall, on Friday, when the Liver- pood district was taken. The other districts will he dealt with as follow :—Bootle, October Ist; Leigh, Bod ; St. Helens, 3rd; Widnes, 40; Waterloo, sth; Warrington 6th; Newton, Bth,; Wigan, 9th; Ormskirk, 10th; and Warrington, 11th, 12th, 13th, and 15th. The revising barrister is Mr. W. H. Butler.

LECTURE ON SINGING AT RITNCORN.—On Monday even- ing next Mr. J. Graham, G.T.S.C., will deliver a lecture on " How to learn to sing," in Ellesmere-street school-room, Runcorn. The lecture will be illustratd by large coloured diagrams, and during the evening the members of tho tonic sol fa class will sing several sacred and secular pieces. Au interesting event will be the singing of a sight test, com- posed for the occasion. Further particulars will be found lb oar advertisement columns.

ALLEGED OUTRAGE AT RUNCORN.—Mr. John Brundrit, magistrate, at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, heard in private a charge against William Cheiters, a labourer, living in Loch-street, who was accused of attempting to critninally assault his stepdaughter, Edith.Snencer, seven years of age. Mr. F. A. Lake appeared for the defendant. After hearing, , the evidence of the prisoner's wife, the girl, and Dr. Bagnall, his utorshiQ, without calling upon Mr. Lake, decided that thne was not a prima facie ease for the assizes, and dis- chargita the prisoner. ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES.—The wall round St. AmbrOse Church is now nearly ready for the railings, which will be ' fixed immediately. They 'are of an exceedingly handsome design, and when completed will greatly im- prove the appearance of the edifice. The wall is of subSlan- tial proportions, being built of red brick, crowned with terra cotta iirrtarneptal copings. The total 'cost is about £5OO. Some months ado a bazaar was held to raise this sum, but the fund is not yet complete,.aud. a few.subscriptions.evill. be rivisi acceptable. The church will be-consecrated when the work is finisliee ' RUNCORN HOARD OF GUARDTANS.—The Rev. Canon Bar-, clay presided over the meeting held on Tuesday last. Mier d were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, John LOCk"-. wood, Messrs. J. Ashton, T. Nurnian,.F. Faithuret,:J; DarloYshiia, G. Whitlryi, J. Weir, w: Whittaker, J. Smith, J. W. Hamilton, Wallington; P. Hall, H. Lin,tker (clerli);W: H. Linaker (deputy t!erk). The Wily business of iniporance trinsadted by the Board was the'passing .of the minutes of the Finance Committee, who recomtnenAled the payment of £1,408-11s on account, of comity rate, and the sum of ra9 to Mr: Thomason for sewage tanks in con- nection. with the Workhouse sewerage scheme. PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAEkAR, RUNCORN.—A grind bazaar, in cannection with the Greenway-road Primitive Methodist Chapel, will be held in the Public Hall, on Tuesday next, and two following days, with the object of defraying the cost of a new heating apparatus which has recently been fixed in the chapel, and also to assist the cir- cuit fund. Mr. John Simpson will perform the opening ceremony on the first day. The ladies of the congregation have been preparing for the bazaar for several months, and it is expected to be one of the most interesting and success- ful that has taken place in the town for a considerable period. Concerts will be given each evening, and the other amusements will be of a varied description, including wax- work, speaking bees, &c. • PRESENTATION TO A WIDNES MAN AT PORT ERIE.— Our Widnes readers will be glad to hear of the.success of Mr. Thomas Rhodes;son of the late Mr. William Rhodes, who formerly represented the firm of Messrs Richard Evans and CoAn Widnes. Mr. Rhodes served his apprenticeehip with Messrs W. H. Kershaw and Co., and in 1869 left Widnes for Canada, where he obtained a situation on the Grand Trunk Railway. In Jane last he paid a short visit to Widnes, and stayed with his brother at 5, Mersey-road, Widnes. On returning to Port Erie, he was met by the workmen who are under his charge, and they presented him with a set of silver ware, comprising ice pitchers, goblets, and bowls which had c )st the sum of 360 dollars. Mr. Rhodes is the foreman in the car department of the Grand Trunk Railway, in which position he has been very success- ful, and he is highly respected. A SELF-ACCUSING WIFE AT WlDNES.—Michael Carney was brought up under a warrant, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, charged with assaulting his wife, Rose Ann Carney. The woman, when placed in the witness-box, pro- tested that her husband had done nothing whatever to her. —Mr. Lewin: Do you think you'would have been granted this warrant if he had done nothing to you. What did you tell Mr. Brock ?—Witness replied that she was drunk and smashed two panes of glass, whereupon her husband, who had been teetotal for 12 months, ran her out of the house with the intention of striking her, but he did net do so. A policeman saw her drunk.—Mr. Lewin: Arn't you afraid of sending your husband to papal P—Witness : No —P.C. Snow- don was then called, and stated that he saw the woman one evening recently, but he could not remember the date. She was drunk. She complained to him that her husband had been assaulting her. She was bleeding about the face and ears. She asked him what she should do, and he told her to obtain a summons.—Prisoner said his wife and her sister were fighting. He denied assaulting his wife.—Mr. Gossage : If let off will you promise to be quiet and peace- able with her P—Prisoner : Yes, sir.—Mr. Ciossage : Very well; you are discharged. _

THE- LANCASHIRE IRON AND GOV', TRADES,—The meet- ing of the Iron and Steel Institute at Middlesborough had a tendency to diminish the attendance on 'Change at Man- chester, on Tuesday, but apirt from any outside influences there was again a very fiat market. In the pig iron trade the business offering continues very limited in extent. Lan- cashire makers of pig iron still quote 453 to 455 61 less 2i for forge and foundry, and qualities delivered equal te Man- chester, but they are being undersold by outside brands even where the local brands can be offered with favourable fates of delivery, Toe leading district makers of pig irone are still so fully sold that they are holdime r 44s 101 to 45s 10d, less 2i for forge ellel fz,undry Lincolnshire delivered here, but there are eellters who, if orders were offered, would be open to book at lower rates. There is a centinued demand for finished iron for prompt delivery chiefly in connection with orders for shipment, which is keeping makers in most cases busily employed, and for imenediate specifica- tions nrices are firm at the full rates' ordinary bars averag- ing £6 25 6d to £6 ss, hoops £6 12s 61, and good qualities of sheets £8 5s to £8 7s 61 per ton, but there is not much forward buying on the basis of these figures.— A fairly good business continues to be done in the coal trade of this district. The pits are kept running five days a week, which is practically full time, and the output is going away. Hou3e-fire coals move off pretty freely, and at the pits in the Manchester district there has been a little filling up out of stock to meet teguirements. Common classes of reund coal are also in fairly good demand for steam and forge purposes. Engine classes of fuel, how- ever, still meet with only a very elow sale; btergy is in but quiet dein:and, and slack is more or less of a drag generally. with heavy stocks accumulating at some of the collieries: At the pit mouth prices average about as under :—Best coal, Os 61 to 103; seconds, 7s 61 to 8s; common round coal, 6s to 6s 61; burgy, 4s 61 to ss; best slack, 4se good ordinary qualities, 3s .l;6 with common sorts to be bought from 2s 9,1 per ton. The demand for shiprneat has scarcely beea so brisk as of late, and anything more than an ad- vance of 61 per ton on last month's rates has been difficult to obtain Ss per ton representing the full average price for good qualities of steam coal delivered at Gareton or Liver- pool. RUNCORN Fame: LIBRARY COMMITTEE. - The annual meeting of the Runcorn Free Library Committee was held on Thursday. fhere were present the Rey. J. Barclay, Dr. Steele, and Messrs. W. Handley, F. A. Lake, J. Simpson, P. Briscoe, T. Riley, J. Meadowcroft, W. Brookes (secre- tary), and J. D. Jones (librarian). The Rev. J. Barclay was chosen as cligirman for the ensuing year, on the motion of Mr. Simpson. seconded by Dr. Steele; and the letter gentle- man was chosen as vice-chairman. Messrs. Lake, Handley, Meadowcroft, and Simpson were appointed a committee for the purpose of recommending the purchase of books, and in exceptional cases, for purchasing books. Mr. Handley, Mr. Briscoe, and Mr. Lake were appointed a committee to con- fer with the Waterloo House Committee. The fir3t Thurs- day after the first Wednesday in each month was adopted as the committee's day of meeting. The librarian's report showed that during the month there had been issued 1,042 books theology, 16; philosophy, ; history, travel, aEc., 111 ; science and art, 31 ; poetry and drama. 10 ; prose fiction, 822; and miscellaneous, 45. Mr. Isaac Pitman had presented 104 volumes, including the Bth edition, "Encyclopedia Brit- tenica ; ' Mr. T. Riley had presented Sullivan's " New Ireland ;" and Mr. W. Handley, "Goldsmith's &UM'S." The total receipts on the month were £l. 7s. 81—Mr. Meadowcroft remarked that the number of books issued during the past month as compared with that: of the corres- ponding month of last year was much less' but the librarian explained that the library was opened in the cor- responding month of last year, and that there was, of course, a rush.—Mr. Handley said he had looked through the libraries' statistics of the kingdom, and he found that Aneust was the slackest month in all the year for book reading. August was the holiday month. He referred to an institution whose books were not allowed to be out more that seven days, but said he had known some of their own books to be kept out six or eirht weeks, and the finest() be paid.
