OUR LONDON LETTER.
FIRE INQUESTS-MASHER NOVELTIES-OFFEN- BACH'S NEW OPERA AT BRIGHTON-HANG- MEN - SUICIDES - THE STRAWBERRY HILL LIBRARY-BAD THREEPENCES.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

The number of fires in London this past or rather passing year has been quite exceptional. What attracts public attention is, of course, only the great fires, such as the Alhambra at the end of last year and the[city warehouses about the same time; but though these are calamities the total loss. to the fire offices is not so great as arises from the aggre- gate of insignificant fires, the account of which scarcely occupies a paragraph in the evening papers. It is a very significant fact that the shares of the principal fire insurance offices have gone down considerably, and the dividends in two .of them have been rmkterially reduced. This is the best teat of the general prevalence of fire losses during the year. When a theatre is burned down, or a country man- sion destroyed, the loss falls practically on one or two of the leading offices, but when there is a general reduction it must be attributed to a very disastrous year. These offices work on a principle of average; and where the average is greatly disturbed one looks for the cause. There is a very general idea at present entertained that the cause is not so much accident as arson. In very many instances it is found that houses just falling out of lease and requiring repairs by the lesst2e hitfoA surrender to the lessor are most effectively destroyed by flames. The company has to rebuild or re- decorate, and both lessee and lessor are satisfied. This has happened so frequently that the offices are beginning a little to clamour. There is, however, such competition in this business that many losses are paid, where it is shrewdly suspected that the insured have been the authors of their own good fortune. A company does not like to appear as defendant in an action unless the verdict is perfectly safe. So the money is paid, and the householder's success leads to similar losses by the company. If the fire is attended with loss of life, then 'there is an enquiry, and awkward facts would come out. But in cases of arson there rarely is less of life. The subject has become so serious that the dif- ferent insurance companies are now clamouring for a remedy, and they are very definite in what they demand. it .is that in every case of fire with foss, of property amounting to a certain sum, there should be an inquest held by the Government authorities. The inquest would not neceisarily assume: misfeasance on the part of the householder, a bit more thafl a coroner's in- quest Mulder where there hes been .sudden death. That-it would check the pregress of arson as Li pro- fitable crime: Companies larwt and small seem wanimous in their determination to agit ite Pie this change.

Not only have the Mashers reappeared at the Gaiety, but they have used their holiday to good effect. They have worked—w 4 it was generally supposed they did not possess—their brains; and the result is taSiv evident. They have invented a new variety in evening dress. The. jam- pot collar aud the spier trousers are of coarse adhered to. The novelty has been the rejection of the waistcoat. Trousers are made very high, a band of about threeinches width surmounting the tops of them, so that they come on the shirt front to where the open of the vest used to. begin. Thus the hips are accentuated and an almost feminine figure secured triumphantly. The Masher himself is still brilli- antly illuminated with-a single diamond stud, and his coat completes his costume. This "arrangement:" worn by one or two of the Gaiety troop, produced an awful admiration amongst the rest; but it has within the week become almost general, and is regarded as a triumph by the whole fraternity. Oscar Wilde has been credited with the glory of this new idea, but the praise was not deserved.

Tnere is a very good fashion inaugurated, I think, by Carl Rosa, of bringing out rwveltie3 in the provinces and transferring them afterwards to the capital, if they pass their first ordeal. Provincial theatres are found to supply unusually good audiences for first night performances. I mean they are both very friendly and at the same time very critical. Mr. Locker says in one of his London lyrics that
The Cockney met iii Middlesex or Surrey,

Is often cold, and always in a hurry. Now this is never so in the large provincial towns. They are more appreciative, more friendly to failure, and in less starish admiration of a star—unless, of course, be happens to belong to the town. Carl Rosa has brought out most of his nevelties while he has been in circuit, and transferred them to London after adequate re- hearsals. Mr. Henderson, who manages nearly all the comic opera theatres which Mr. Hollingshead does not con- trol, is practising the same rule. I was down at Brighton this week, and saw the production'at the pretty little theatre there of the new opera that is to be on the boards of the Avenue eirly next month. The music is by Offenbach, the libretto by Ferule. I doubt very much whether it will suc- ceed, but it must have cost a great deal. Worth supplied some of the dresses, and the stage was thronged with pretty girls in every kind of masculine get ups. Tee truth is that we have no longer a taste for the kind of opera which Offenbach and Schneider made so popular 20 years ago. No kind of piece succeeds now-a- days like Comic opera. Bat two conditioles are necessary. The music must be good, and the plot muet be interesting. Mere buffoonery, however clever, is not enoagh. fl Madam Angot," " Medane Pevart," "Lee Cleches de CeilleVille," and "Olivette" were all interesting as well as amusing. The performance could have gone on almost without the music. Now "La Vie" is both improbable and tedious. Lionel Brough is so clever that he pulls the piece through, but when he is off the stage the action drags. An old German beron with a pretty daughter arrives at Charing-Cross &adopt, wilefd an hotel tout is to meet them and take them to the hotel. The hero, who has saved the life of the girl under dramatically romantic conditions, changes clothes with the tout and brings the party to his own chambers, as if it were the hotel. He has to dress all the servants as guests for his supposed table d'hete and to get up a diplomatic ball with the same meteriels. The tout in the meantime takes the hero's name, and the heroine falls in love with him. Ultimately there is an ecaivcisseincnt, and all goes right. But this thread of a plot is worked wearily, and the adoption into this caste of a music hall actor, very clever in his own way, is rather a degradation even to burlesque. We have plenty of good music halls in London, and the production of "talent" on treating is not to be encouraged. The music is pretty, but it is feeble. It sounds like Offenbach—and water. The play wiil remain for the rest of the month at Brighton, and evi- dently has been produced at great cost. The tremendous competition for the office of hangmen is certainly not to the credit of English humanity. The pay is scercely muck :of a temptation; a fixed salary of, I believe, £5O a year, and then £5 for every jab, travelling expenses ef course included in the Treasury disbursements. The next man who is hanged—and there certainly is one prisoner who is in very great jeopardy of that fate—will settle the appointment of English executioner. In the meantime it would be interesting to see what kind of tes- timonials are those which are at present under the notice of the sheriffs of London and Westminster. Mere good conduct and exemplary character would scarcely guide these judges in the exercise of their singular patron- age. It ought at least to be stipulated that whoever is appointed should have an understudier, who would under- stand his methods and be ready to take his place. Under no conditions can it be a pleasant thing to be hanged, but it must be peculiarly distasteful to feel that you are providing the necessary material for an important professional debut. It is curious that in an age of philanthropy and of publicity candidates ehould be so numerous. In Germany in the middle ages so difficult was it to get an executioner and so important was the office that the hangman was ennobied,and at the end of the 17th century there were several noble families who claimed their rank from an ancestral Jack Ketch. /n Spain exclusiveness was carried still further. The hangman lived cutside the city. His house was painted red. He wore the COSturne prescribed by law—the arms of the province figuring in ornament of his coat, and he was only allowed to inter- marry with the families of other hangmen. His son suc- ceeded to the cace ore his death. Perhaps this fact !night assist the sheriffs out of their present difficulty in making a choice. The preference should certainly be given to respectable married man with a lerke family of sons. The appointment is to be made in the course of the next few days. It is no exaggeration to sty that the public take greater interest in it than in the succession to the Woolsack in Ireland.

The object was to dater criminals, 1 but the working of it was strauzety :t.situoith t, encourage them*: Thef:e was something so horrible in ttie.;ittai of bury- ing a person at erOas'_roads that ifriea inesii.4;:ii!Wilt out of the difficUlty by 'finding. , 'yerdiCts . 'of crime committed under : the -:', induenc: of 4.-temporary insanity. ' 'Now that the -barbarity • b.a,i ti.ien re- moved from the course of the•law a verdict 0 r..7i' 'a ,?e se i,, possible whoze the facts warrant it, and certainly the coroners should in future assist in seeing that a true decision is arrived at. false sentiment did not stop suicide. It only served to convert jurors into perjurers. Jest at present there . seems an epidemic of suicidal mania. There were three cases of it in a single day this week in London. The verdict returned by the Durham jury is likely to act as a salutary check.

A large collection of books and MSS., that have enjoyed for nearlya century undisturbed repose, has just been brought into daylight and notice. Strawberry Hill has changed owners, and the new tenant takes the house, but not its libraries. So skilled workmen have been busy ran- sacking the treasure-house of literature that Horace Walpole collected after his own singular fashion. I am told that the value of the books turns out to be very much greater than was at first believed. Curious old MSS, tall folios with valuable or at least in- teresting notes and comments in their margin, parchments, engravings, and charters have all been. brought into the daylight. Lord Macauley described Strawberry Hill as a museum of oddities, but the bookshelves and even the cellars have nvealed treasures which the essayist would have delighted to turn over. The hooks are not to be sold. They are merely being removed to Dudbrook Hall in Essex, which is one of the seats that 1),1 .1 to the late owner of Strawberry Hill. •

I see that a stat,?ment made by me last week has this week received the contradiction of facts. There are false threepences in circulation. I believe the case is very rare. One of the counsel for the Treasury in Mint prosecutions told me that in all his experience he had never met with a case. It shows that the coiner has fought new pistures where he hoped to be less disturbed. ' No one hitherto ever doubt.ed the genuineness of a threepenny piece. The cost of production was so great that it scarcely paid to produce and circulate. At the present rate ?.,e shall soon have, bad pennies in circul ttion.

On entering the su:h doer, ,the'faot ars.: a4r-icted attention by the effectivenem of its drcord,ions, which consisted of the green leaves of various plant, hewed with bunches .of bright red berries, of the inuuotain ash, while depending from the carved cover were sprays of leaves. Fixed in prominent positions on the pillars and av*lls of the church wss a large number of shie:ds, quartered according to the rules of heraldry, and most artistically de- signed: Some were formed of wheaten straw, and others of beautiful flowers, while all were pretty, and bore the im- press of bright brains and lissom finger's. The appropri- ativeness of one shield deserves special mention. Over the pulpit, whence the BisfiOp preached, was a blue shield, with the " mitres" formed in veheaten straw, while the pulpit itself was almost hidden beneath its decorations of oars, wheat, and flowers. Grouped round the foot of the lectern was a number of plants from the Grange conservatories, whence 'plants in other parts of the sacred edifice had also been obtained. Wreathed round the lectern was a garland of green leaves, charmingly intermixed with choice flowers. The altar and reredos had again been most elaborately decorated. On the altar was a beautiful cross skilfully made by Miss Barclay. It was composed of crysanthums and lilies, the gift of Mrs. C. Hazlehurst. On each side was a Gothic arcade constructed of oats, the designs of the panels being formed of wheat and fi mars. Above the reredos were the texts, "I am the living bread," "I am the true vine.' Over the west entrance WAS a scroll containing the words, "The earth is filled with the fruit of Thy work ;" over the south entrance was the text. div.head: WIDNES GROCERS AND THEIR SCALES.
div.p: WIDNES GROCERS AND THEIR SCALES.
HEAVY PENALTIES.

At Widnes Patty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. F. H. Gessage (chairman) and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Samuel Sadler, grocer, Anne-street West, was summened to answer a charge of haying in his possession three pairs of scales which were unjust. Tne defendant, who pleaded not guilty, was represented by Mr. J. W. Knowles.—Superin- tendent Barker said he visited the defendant's shop on the 11th inst. and found three pairs of scales which had on loose adjusting balls. It was a very easy thing for a elis- honest shopman to cheat his customers to the extent of half a pound hy removing the ball.—Mr. Knowles cross-examined the superintendent to show that it;was as easy to remove the , the loose plate and substitute a heavier one, and yet that was not an offence against the law.—The Superintendent ' admitted that all the eceles balanced, and the balls were on when ha visited the shop; but it was contrary to law to have a loose ball.—Mr. Knowles s Lid his client instructed him that this was a test Case. He (Mr. Knowles) had been in the 11Abit ef aktending magistrates courts. for the last eight years, and he ad pever heard a case like this. l' He did not think their ' woins' learned clerk had either. He contend A that the Bench had no power whatever to fine in this case, because the ball were part of the scale as oeiginally mane. If anythitg had been useZ: to adjust the scales Vaicil WAS- not part of their construction 1, then the detenhui would. have been liable ; but he respect- full V Btihmitted that under the circumetarices he was not. Mr. Sadler was a man in a good position and would not wish to defraud his customers, and he had no intentien of G. frauding in using the loose adjusting weig!lts. His client told him that it was almost inieeiSitile to comply with the various Weights and Measures Acts, and he had every morn- ing to adjust his scales—Before deciding this case the Bench wished to hear the complaint against Edward Johnsott. of St. Helens, who was summoned for having in his possession a pair of unjust scales.—Superintendent Barker stid there was a loose adjusting ball on this scele.---By Mr. J. O. Swift (who appeared for defendant) When he entered the shop the ball wes,on and the scei.es weighed cerrectly. ['he ball weighed nearly half at otlnd.—Mr. Swift, for the the defence, fol lowed tile same lines as Mr. Knowles, • and asked for the defendant's dismiee al. He called Thomas ;ism:, the manager of the' shop in Anne-street West, where the faulty Ctl was COUnd. This witness said he had been in ch i.rge of the shop for two anontha, and during that time the ball had never been removed. The scales were used for weighing hurter, which was sold in quantities varying from 21bs. to 2ers Mr. Johnson was then charged with having unjust weights at his shop in Anne-street West.—Supt. Barker said that on the 11th instant he visited the defendant's shop, and foun a 21b. weight 5i drachms light and a 41b. weight 1 drachm light. The 211). weight had evidently been used instead of a hammer for breaking open boxes, ate., and a piece was snipped off.—Mr. Swift said lie dicleaot know what to say in this case.. Mr. Johnson had given implicit directions to his managers that the weights were to be regularly adjusted. The 30 weights in the shop were examined in June, :and their worships would see that the defiziency was a small one. Mr. Johnson hid a very large business, and. was to some extent at the mercy of his managers. He had three shops in Widnes, two in St. Helens, two in Runcern, one in Warrington, and one in Earleetown.—The magistrees retired to consider their decieion. On returning into court, Mr. Goseage said the Bench were of opinion that to have a loose ball on the scales was an offence. As it was Mr. &idler's first convic- tion lie would be fined 20s. and costs. Mr. Johnson had been repeatedly fitted, ad he was ordered to pay penalty of £5 and costs for the faulty scale, and -a similar' sum for the unjust weights.—Mr. Johnson said he thought the magistrates ought to look at his position —Mr. Gossage replied that if a man chose to heve 20 shops he must be pre- pared to take the rises. FARN WO RTII AGRICULTURAL SOOIET Y.

ANNUAL SHOW. The annual show of the Farnwortle Agricultural Society was held on Thursday, in the show field, Farnworth-in- Widnes. To have a successful exhibition of the anitnils of the farm yard, and the stable, and the various parapherna- lia which enter into the arcadian calling of husbandry, tine weather is an indispensible attendant, and fortune has in former years smiled with constancy on the Farnwcirth So- ciety's anneal event. The 18th show was a miserable ex- ception. Thursday morning opened most inauspiciously. Dark clouds, where they could be seen through a rift in,the foggy atmosphere, were an unpleasant augury for the day's proceedinge, and about half an hour before the judges com- menced their skilled labours rain descended in a steady drizzle. Widnes was enveloped in the exhalations of its own chimneys, the roads were quickly made like puddles, and the conveyances that were plying between the town and the show field had very few fares, though a number of the hardier sort were to be observed tramping along the muddy thoroughfares to the show. Notwithstanding these unpropitious appearances the field was the scene of the usual life and bustle, but the spectators of the judging were far from as numerous as in former years. At noon the weather had become considerably worse and whilst the luncheon was proceeding rain descended in torrents, and in places 'penetrated through the canvas roof into the interior. The determination to support the society was evidently very keen in the inhabitants of the neigh- bourhood, and at two o'clock, in spite of the storm hun- dreds of people passed through the gate. Clothed with overalls and armed with umbrellas they bravely went the round of sight-seeing, and not only gentlemen, but ladies were gathered round the rine where the horse jumping was proceeding. Before closing time arrived the field was one vast puddle hole, and locomotion' was not less difficult than unpleasant. Considering all. these adverse circum- stances, the show must be granted to have been a success. Theexhibits,4lthough not so numeteue asi,it year, were of good quality, and the money taken at the entrance amounted to upwards of £lOO. ) Ilhe,FttnwortfteAgekultu- ral Society has braved the " slinpandlarrows ". of fortune

for 19 years. and it may be with justice and safety stated is still in a healthy arid vigorous condition. it possesses three influential patrons in the Right lion. the Earl of Derby, Sir Richard Brooke, *Bart ;and the Hon. E. A. Le3pnld, while Mr.'Edward Whitley, M.P. for 'Liverpool, occupies the' pre-. sidential chair: Mr. Gongton is chairman of management committee. Mr. Robert Whiteeide is an energetic and: Obliging secretary, and labours for the society's iticceis in a manner which reflects great credit upon him, and must hire a beneficial effect on the society. The prizes offered for competition included 14 silver cups, and £5OO in money, being about £lOO blow the amount offered last year. The entries were not so numerous as last year.; in fact,, the total entries show a decrease of over 100, hat' the aPpended comparative statement will show this difference more clearly :

- 1879. 1.c:80. . 1881. 1882. 1883. ' ' eattle 34 • 48 39 ,35 33 dorses and Den'ieys llB , 1.57 153 133 123 Pigs _l6 20 17 Batter it:wts Potatoes Bi-ed,.00:14, &C • 3 23 14 '27 7 Piiultry,'ite 216 . 24 163 184 107 Pigeons 1)9g1 implements Extra Stock ::t 0 4 5 19

It will be seen that the greatest falling off was in the entries for poultry and dogs, while in the cattle there is an increase of one, which fact must be considered very satisfactory. The society cannot hope to make a largo exhibition of cattle in a neighbourhood where dairy farming is so little in vogue, aril the arevalence of foot and mouth disease in all parts of the country would effectually prevent any exhibits from a distance. The cattle on the field, however, were a very good .stock, Mr. Robert Whalley showing some particularly fine animals, and he succeeded in carrying oil a good number of prizes. The pigs were a credit to the local breeders, whose animals were mostly shown, the boars being splendid animals. The horses in each class included some excellent specimens. The draught horses, with few exceptions, pos- sessed capitarproportions, with free action, and the lighter animals were a fine lot. What the poultry lacked in quan- tity was compensated for by quality. The purity of the birds was very apparent, and in the cochins, dorkings, and game classes the judges had a rather difficult task in giving their decision Dogs are always a special feature at this show, and the present occasion was no exception. The pointer class, though small in number, contained some very crack specimens, and there were some splendid setters. 1 The retrievers were a very strong class, Chickory, a cele- brated winner, having to be content with a v.b.c. Collies were a very good class. The butter and vegetables attracted some attention, and much interest was manifested in the immense specimens of potatoes shown. Takinginto account the state of the gronotl, the horses which competed in the jumping class made a creditable show, and no mishap of any consequence occurred. There were several interesting exhibits in the implements and extra stock departments. Mr. Henry Cmaar, of Knutsford, had on the ground several rustic houses of artistic design, which combined a roomy and comfortable interior with a most picturesque exterior, and he, in addition, showed garden furniture of useful con- struction and pretty pattern. The condensed milk company of Ireland, Lansdowne Limerick, had on view a quantity of condensed milk, which, as a new product of the-sister isle, met with seine attention. The rich grass lands of Limerick are celebrated for the excellency of the milk they produce, and in the condensed form the milk is said to be superior to that exported from Switzerland. The product was awarded a silver medal. Mr. Spann, wheelwright, of Warrington, exhibited a capital lot of his prize waggons, and Messrs. J. S. Warburton and Co., agricultural engineers, Orchard-street, Prest.n, showed their patent chain pomp for steam power, and the patent potato digger, both of which have been awarded prize medals at various shows. There were other interesting hte- Mements to be seen. The judges of the various classes were :—Horned cattle and pigs, Mr. C. W. Brierloy, Rose- dale, Tenbury, and Mr. James Parr. Hatton, Warrington; heavy horses, Mr. P. Blundell, Weeton, near Kirkham, Fyldf, and Mr. Williath Dale. Somerville, Seacombe ; light horses, Mr. C. W. Keltock; Gateacre, and Mr. F. W. Earle, Ruby; buttor, roots, seed corn, and implements, Mr. R. Webster Litherland, Mr. James Hulme, Melling, and Mr. 1 George Whitlow, Hatton, near Warrington; poultry, Mr. R. Teebay, Fulwood, Preston, and Mr. George Fall, War- riniton ; pigeons, Mr. W. GArnon, Chester ; greyhounds, variety class litter of puppies, Mr. James Taylor, Roch- dale; sheep dogs. Mr. J. J. Steward, Frodsham ; fox ter- riers. Mr. E. M. Sohthwell, Bridgnorth ; other sprting dogs. Mr. Frank Adcock, Birmingham, and Mr. J. S. Skidmore, .N intwich ; oth.r non-sporting dogs, Mr. James Taylor, Read-ate, and Mr. J. S. Skidmore, N,antwich.

div.p: THE LUNCHEON

At one o'clock luncheon was provided in the tent, the caterer being Mr. smith, of the Giffin Ina, 'F.irntvorth. E. Whitley, M.P., the president of the society, occupied the chair, and the following gentlemen were seated -ivith him at the cross tale :—Lord- Lionel- Cecil, Rev. George (vicar of yarnwertli), Rev. J. Cssells Brown (vicar of Dittos), Co!onel Blackhnrne, M.P ;' Colonel Wyatt (agent to the Earl of ftora), Messrs. G. C. Hale- (agent to ti.lc Eirl of Derby), Robert Davies (Warrington), Jhn Waite. J.P. (Warrington), Fredrick Earle (Roby). The PnEstnENtaffbr proposing "The health of the Queen, and the Prince and Princess of Wales, -and the rest of the Royal family," gave with' much gratificatiun a toast, which, he was thankful to believe, would receive a ready accep- tance—" The bishop and clergy of the diocese,*and ministers of every denomination." These rev, gentlemen would be founefaithful in discharging their spiritual duties; but to hi mind there was another aspect of the question, and one in which the clergy could play and ought to play a 'very im- portant part. When we looked at other countries we found that the great danger of the ,days in which We lived was the separation of the different Classes of society (Hear, hear.) To his mind the clergy going from high to low, from rich to poor, were the men to whom We naturally looked to keep together the different elements of society, and their influence in this direction was the source of Hie happiness of our own country. It was, therefore, with great gratification that at a meeting of the agriculturalists of that district he proposed the health of the bishop and clergy, coupled with the name of the Rev. George 131nd and the Rev. Father Finegan. The toast was honoured, and the Rev. GUORCIS BOtlp ireplied. They might depend, he said, epee the clergy dm ng all they could to promote union between class and class, and the prosperity of those among whom they lived. They were only too glad to do it. They wished to be all things to all men, rejoice with those that rejoiced, hut he wished they could rejoice a little more with the 'fine weather. (Laughter.) They had at times to be present with thode that wept, but they were met that day to rejoice over-a better harvest than they generally had had to do. As re- garded the weather, they must try to make the best of it, and if they did not happen to get enough money for the funds that day some kind friend in the background worild perhaps try to make it up. (Applause.)

The PratSIDENT, in proposing success to the society, sa`d his earnest endeavour would be to do everything in ha power to promote the cause of the agriculturists in th t ! neighbourhood. He was thankful it was his privilegelo address them at a time when certainly their prospects iS agriculturists were better than they bad been for the Mit four or five years. He had confidence in the pluck, lucid!). try, and indefatigable perseverance of the English farmers, and it was to their credit that for the past five years, In spite of bad harvests and low prices, they had conducOd themselves in that loyal and orderly way nhich had alWate endeared them to him. (Applause.) It was true that tke had only recently become an:agriculturist, but in his earliest life he was deeply identified with agriculture. He dare say that he had loaded many a cart of hay and many a cart of wheat, probably before most of the farmers present. His earliest years were spent in Dalamere Forest a,p.mgst the farmers of Cheshire. (Hear, hear.) There waz geat deal of talk by so-called farmer's friends with regard to the nationalisation of the land, but did not their natural 'shrew+ ness tell them that such's' scheme would be destruction 'of the prosperity of the farmer? Depend upon it, any schenie by which a revolution in the land was caused in this cottn. try, would be fraught with serious consequences to the farmer and labourer. The truest interests oC this county were bound up in the tinitm, the auction, and the confi- dance which must exist between the landlords and the it o tenant farmers. e The toast was enthusiastically honoured. Mr. LoNerox, in 'responding, thanked those present sr the kind way in which they had received.4:at toast. - society was a very small one, and a great many , appeared to be a usel— T.T society.. ,uict like to it Pm; gentlemen tint the societV simply enprivi f.nant farmers, people trying to compete on: with tho other, nd if they eneceeded in winning a prize, they were encouraged to enter one of the larger societies and compate for larger prizes. (Applause.) =Of. rarnivorth Society .hart dontl a great deal of good 111 this way, and the comtnitfre was coat- posed of small, practical agricultural farmers. There was:no class of men that deserved more encouragement than tios tenant farmers of this day. They had had a few years, of , depression, but this yflar there had been , an, excellent surri?ner, alai although thucrops were sound the prices were low, and what they had to sell ws,S good. They' hoped the quantity would makeup the, deficiency of low 'pr:ces. lie thanked those .present for the kind way in ;Thiel they Te- ceiyed the loast, and,proposed the health of theikpresidelat, Mr. Whitley. " '

The toasi.was drunk with three cheers; and 'rho PltEstAirfrrt 'observid that -be had etily nUt-dit his agricultural armour that day, but he hoped in years to come to halls the , grati6e4ion of knowink those present personally. • ! , Mr. WARBURTOM 0141 gave "The Ind ords. of • the ; neighbourhood." Ile said thy had occasion Oa be.pronctof , their landlords, and they had one good sppcitwen •prsesit. He all aded to Colonel Blackburne. (Applause.) The toast was heartily drunk, and Colonel BLACEDITENE, NIX., replied. He skid the land- lords of Lancashire were anxious and willing to do every- thing they could to forward the interests of their tenant farmers. Nobody could dispute that, and he was quite sure that no legislation was required for South-West Lancashire. Complaints were constantly made that tenant farmers and others were suffering from the effect of local rates and other .taxation, and he believed that the occupiers. (.1 the nil needed to a larger extent to be relieved of the chars of the maintenance of the poor, lunatic asylums, and other matters. The whole system of the out-door and in-door relief of the poor would have soon to be revised, not so much because the existing laws were bad as unsuited to the ircreased pop.hhu adt isoani d iAles:btoonteisietlyAbgealicieuvietngeHteonldanintgefarAmcetr,swofhsi loet,itahs. West Lancashire did not require any legislation in this direction, the Act would be beneficial to agriculturists, tending as it did to encourage higher cultivation, and pro- tect the iaterests of those who invested capital in the land. He fervently hoped the powers in the Act with reference to county court judges would not be put in operation to settle matters in dispute, for he was one of those who believed that landlords and tenants should vie with each other in for- warding their common interests. The PRESIDENT then proposed the Press in (dinars. -terms, and Dr. MACKIE responded.

A DISOREDIEINT APPEENTICE.—At the Prescot Petty 6es-- Bloos on Tuesday, Mr. Berry, watchmaker, asked the Bench to order an apprentice of his to pay 6s Sid as damages for having left his work without reasonable cause, and also to order bim to complete the term of his indenture. Tne ff,ndant. it seemed, had above a year yet to serve under his indentures, but recently bad absented himself on several Oe. isions from work, whereby Mr. Berry bad sustained the loss named.—Both orders were made.

A VALOROUS COMBAT BETWEEN FEMALES. A young woman named Jolla Kaye was on Tuesday charg:d at the st. Helens Police Court with having unlawfully wounded Mary Pander. It appeared that on Monday evening there had bOn A stand-up battle between the two parties in dila case, which was foaglit out after the manner of women. Mrs. Pender clutched hold of her antagonist's hnir, and the ratter retaliated by striking Mrs. Pender on the head wi:h a bottle and making LBO blood flow freely. it tuck ~s.ccr to discntarigle the two combatants.—The prisoner was reman- ded till Friday.

OUR NATIONAL CHUCH. "The Church of England has not only been a part of the history of this country, but a part so vital, entering so pro- foundly into the entire life and action of the country, that the sveiing of the two would lta, e nolhing behind but a bleeding and lacerated mass. Take the Church of England out of the History of England, and the EUstory of England becomes a eha is without order, without the, and without ineaning."—

Gladstone. Sir,—Seeing that "Clifford Dix" had not supported the assertions made by him in his first letter, and that I had already tr nagressed and followed him on points which had in reality no bearing on the " principle " of an Established Ohurch, I had deemed it better to pursue the subject no farther. But his lengthy letter in your issue of the Bth brings out fresh points, which I will endeavour to reply to, and at the same time sum up my defence in support of an Established Church by quoting most weighty authori- ties on its bearing. I may as well say here that he has stated no " real " objection to an Established Church. What seems to grieve him most is its abuses ; also, I may say (although giving no addtional satisfaction to myself— being already cognisant of the fact), for the information of "Visitor," that I have "drawn," "fair copied," and "engrossed " the communications which bear my name— though I fail to see that the arguments I give would be weakened if it were not a fact that they were mine. Now let us take the objections in order, as well as I have been able to arrange them : Objection.-1. The Romish Church asserts that the Re- formation robbed it of all that the Protestant Church now calls her own. Reply: There never was a. Church of Rome in England. The Pope never exercised supremacy in England before the Reformation. It was only lawful for him to exercise spiritual jurisdiction with the consent of the Crown. No new Church was founded at the Reformation. There was, therefore, no transfer of Church property from the Roman Catholic Church to the Church of England. But there was a great transfer of Church property to secular hands, in which it has ever since remained. Objection —2. The ground taken now is, that the wealth of the Church was given for the benefit of the nation, and must revert to the nation—that is the people. Reply : The nation—that is the people—do receiva the benefit from it—at any rate it is their own fault if they don't. I cannot agree that if this property, according to "Clifford Dix," is held "in trust "for the nation, that it

must "revert" to the nation. Objection.-3. Mr. Westbrook seems to agree with me about the loaves and fishes, and, as a palliative to the doings of the Church, tells us that he knows "a few little episodes connected with the circuit dinners of a certain dissenting body." August the 13th he says, "Well, it appears that the only conclusion that could be arrived at was that Church people de hunger after loaves and fishes, but then Dissenters do the same." Reply : I most certainly do not agree with "Clifford Dix' about the loaves and fishes. But when he states that one of the main arguments relied upon by Dissenters for Diaestablishrnent is "that the clergy look too ranch after loaves and fishes," I am certainly justified in reminding that "moral body" that "those who live in glass houses should not throw stones." But it is, perhaps, better to give the opinion of a Nonconformist on this point. Listen to the Rev. H. S. Brown, of .Liverpool. "The Church of England sets us Nonconformists an example which we should do well to follow. The official stipends in multitudes of parishes are totally unequal to the fair support of the ministry; but in many, very many cases, gentlemen of learning and of property are content and glad, for the Church's sake, to live and labour in such places, and as far as money is concerned to do far more than their Churches do for them." " How large a share, too, of the endowments of our "bloated parsons" find their way to the homes where poor men dwell in alms and charities that prepare the hearts of the grateful recipients to listen all the more willingly to the "good news" from the lips of the giver. And if we are told that this is bribing the poor to hear the gospel, we can only say that it is such bribery as He practised, who, wherever He went preaching the word of His Kingdom, went also "doing good, and healing all manner of diseases, insomuch that great multitudes were gathered to Him out of every city."—The Voluntary System. Objection.-4. The memoirs of the late Bishop Wilber- force clearly shew to the people the large amount of anxiety displayed by the clergy when a chance of prefer- ment opens out to the view of those servants of Him who had not where to lay His head. Reply: Why "C. D." quotes this in favour of Disestahlishment is not quite clear to me. Does he mean to say that if we had not a national Church such a state of things would not exist? Does "C. D." know how the ears of the ministers of the " Free Churches" are pricked when "a chance of preferment opens out to their view?" The Rev. William Braden lays :—Numbers of churches are constantly in want of pesters, and vice versa. NA hat happens when a church is announced " vacant " everyone knows—our deacons most painfully. From all quarters come letters of recommenda- tion to the authorities ; some from brethren of popular re,)utation, and these usually produce the deepest impres- ario/. Yet it is possible from the peculiar circumstances of the writers, from their accumulated engagements, &c., their words "may be" the least trustworthy. Ministers have been known to send vivid pen-and-ink sketches of their own estimable virtues, accompanied by elegant photographs of their appearance, and a printed sermon,or scraps of eulogy, from local newspapers. Time compels me to cut this letter shorter than I had in- tended. " Clifford Dix" will, it seems, accept some authori- ties; whose will he accept? Will he accept the authority of Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Forster, Lord Sel borne, Lord Broug- her; Dr. Dollinger, Dr. Warren, laymen? If he likes I can give him the opinions of all these gentlemen, with scores of others quite as weighty, all proving the ad- vantage of an Established Church. In conclusion, let rue add that if anyone who has seen this discussion would like to pursue this subject for himself, let him read " The Dead Hand in the Free Churches," also Lord Breugham's "Political Philosophy," or tl e speeches and twiaings of any of the above, and ha will then have evidence sufficient to form a judgment on the advantages of an Es- tablished Church.—Yours, ecc., H. J. WESTBROOK. {This correspondence must here cease as between " Clifford Dix" and Mr. Westbrook.—ED. W.

div.head: OUR NATIONAL CHURCH.
div.p: OUR NATIONAL CHURCH.

Sir,—l am sure our young friend, Mr. Westbrook, must feel rather annoyed at the tome introduced into this discus- sion by "A Churchman." lam also sure that we none of Ili lost sight of the subject under notice. For a Church to exist in a national sense it must have a popular feature in it that will enable it to permeate the people's social and domestic life in an acceptable and welcome sense. If it does not cotne up to this standard it cannot be national. Can a Churchman prove that the Church, as established by law, fulfils these requirements? If not, why commence whining and moaning after the fashion of some street mendicant? "It is incumbent upon the State to uphold the religious character of this great country, and this alone can be done by maintaining its connection with the Established Church." "Once the State is divorced from religion, woe be to England!" Surely such nonsense was never before penned for reasonable men's acceptance. The conceit and egotism displayed is truly nauseous. No other sect in the country is looking after the people's spiritual welfare! Nay, the Church itulf, once divested of that glorious halo that surrounds its lovely countenance, and known as State Pdtronage, will at once close its portals and leave the people eblft for themselves. How self-denying,what a wonderful indifference to the loaves and fishes is here displayed! The suggested catastrophe is too good to be true. Depend upon it, Mr. Churchman, that so long as England's trade is looked After and attended to by men of brain and muscle, W 3 need not fear your dismal wail of "Woe to England." The greatness is in her natural-resources. These once exhausted, her secret is at once exploded. "An official spiritual counsellor is provided in every parish for cases of spiritual distress." Possibly herein lies the whole secret; and a 5 England, Wales, and Scotland are referred to as possessing tlie "inestimable blessings of a State Church," let us see the result. Mr. Cox, giving judgment in a case at Llandiloes, says: "The infamous perjury made all over Wales made one's blood boil. The perjury he met with was simply e:ckening. The piece was scattered with churches and chapels, and the people thought themselves religious, but at the same time unblushingly told lies." I think Freethought has not, as vet, entered the Princ;pality ; this accounts for the above sickening statement. It also poincs to the evil resulting from a spiritual counsellor being allowed to exist in an " official " sense. A senior clergyman, writing to the Times September 8, states that he is one of 4,000 out of work and anxious for regular empleyineut. I suppose these 'Spiritual cone?ellois" -e been tempted by the bait of spiritual peelerrnen in Church, and now their wasted and disappointed lives compels them to fall back upon the nation and supplicate for help, instead cf at once turning to a bit of real work., Referring to Dissenters, a Churchman asks, "Pare they prtiach as they would like?" and proceeding, makes reference to "that venerable friend of Warrington, Sir O. Oreenall, and the endo sweet of Walton Church.' There is an impression held I mustsity by a

great majority in this town, that in4ead of Sir Gilbert be'mg a friend to Warrington the town has been like a gold mine to him, and by its docility has allowed him, to quote Canon Wilberforce, "to do more harm to society in a month than a whole bench of bishops will do good in a year." Friend of Warrington! Ask the superintendentsof Sunday schools hew often since last election he has welcomed their scholars into any of his fields on Walking Days; ask those who like a day's fishing whose influence it is that bars any pleasure of the kind at Hill Cliffs, and you will soon know all about this "venerable friend." Speaking of Walton Church, what a miserable spectacle is here seen ; what a splendid moral is coaveyed to the villagers ! A Low Church patron and a High Church recipient of this patronage falling out with each other; the "venerable friend" driving past the insigni- ficant school-room on a Sunday to the church at Daresbury, there to murmur, " Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive them that trespass against us." Sir, this little episode proves the whole of my argument. Sir Gilbert owns the church, at present; he refuses to allow the builders to finish it, hence the requirements of a State Church cannot be completed, and the rev, gentleman is obliged to conduct service in the school-room. The only difficulty in the way is who shall be posture master, Sir Gilbert or Mr. Jones ? The congregation have no voice in the matter. If the parson will only knuckle under to the venerable squire, all will then be right, and the two between them will settle what kind of theology is suitable for these spiritually distressed villagers. A. nice sample this of freedom ! True, the parson receives the endowment sum £l5O, and I am told another £1.50 from the Queen Anne's bounty. On that score he is in an immensely superior condition to his Dissenting brother; but at what a sacrifice ! The Church of England is slowly approaching its dissolution.. It is torn within by senseless dessensions as to the character of the drapery to be worn by the high priest, the manner in which he shall adjust it, the correct arrangement of the altar frippery, the acceptable position to he assumed by the congregation, and with all this discord it lifts up its voice and cries out " Behold how eying we are; see what liberty we enjoy !" Warrington, Sept., 1883. CLIFFORD DIX.

Sir,—A glance at your correspondence column brings vividly to my remembrance some of the grand old days of over forty years ago—an auld tang syne ever memorable for its endearing associations, days of my youth, scenes of my youth, friends of my youth ye are gone, ye are gone. I refer, sir, to the time when the controversy between Church- men and Dissenters in Scotland was at the hottest. The former contending for Church extensions, the latter agitat- ing for the disestablishment and disendowroent of the National Church; and that, too, upon the grounds that all national establishments of religion were unscriptural in their nature, unjust in principle, and injurious in operation. I well remember being present at one of those Anti-State Church meetings, when the chief speaker of the evening did net fail to point out some of the most objectionable features in the character of the parish minister. He said they were bitter opponents to every political movement calculated to ameliorate the condition of the working classes. He par- ticularized the Corn Laws, making bread scarce and conse- quently clear by Act of Parliament, the Church clergy almost to a man being opposed to the repeal of those obnox- ious laws, as if they wished to drill the poor into Godliness by an increase of poverty. If such was their motive, he observed, it was a great mistake, for extreme poverty was not at all favourable to a state of devotion; and by way ot illustration he related a little anecdote descrip- tive of the predicament of two English tourists who were present on sacramental occasions in Scotland. The tourists were perfectly horrified by such protracted services, and were only saved from an untimely grave by the timely reflection that it was never ordained that souls were to be fed by starving bodies, and they would have their baps (buns) and beer at any rate. Now, sir, I dare say you are aware that the controversy referred to had its origin in a pamphlet published by Dr. Marshall, of Kirkenlolloch. It set are to the public mind throughout the length and breadth of Scotland, the flame soon extending to England and Ireland, and it has been burning with increasing inten- sity ever since, and I believe will continue to burn until all the churches are freed from the trammels of the State. The first visible fruits of the controversy was the disruption of the kirk of Scotland ; another of its fruits was the disestab- lishment of the Irish Church. The next in turn is to be the disestablishment of the kirk of Scotland; the disestab- ment of the Anglican Church will follow as a matter of course. Hence the Church and the State will stand each on its own basis, as far aeunder as God has put them—giving to everyone a fair field and no favour. This will bring about surely and speedily the wished-for calm—" Awake, awake! put on thy strength, 0 Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, 0 Jerusalem, the holy city; for henceforth there shall no more come into thee, the uncircumcised and the unclean !" No doubt, sir, all this will sound harsh in the ear of your correspondent "Churchman," who has already got the woe horn to his mouth ; but he is only dressing up a bugbear of his own, and frightening himself with his own creation. He evidently cannot endorse the opinion of the rector of Gusby (I forget his name) who over 40 years ago said that but for the leaven of Godliness from the Dissenters and Methodist, vital Christianity had been all but extinct in the National Church. If so, the life and activity manifest in the Church of England in recent years is in a measure attributable to the reactionary in- fluence ot Nonconformity, and I ant persuaded if she were set free from the influence of the carnal politics of the world she would be a more efficient instrument for good than she is at present. Now, sir, I think Mr. " Churchman " makes an unwarrantable use of the names of three most res- pectable ministers in the town. I believe them to be Godfear- ing men, faithful ambassadors of Christ, declaring what they believe to be the whole counsel of God. "Churchman's " insinuations reflect also upon their congregations respec- tively, as if it were necessary that they must have smooth things preached to them. Perhaps he is looking at both ministers and their congregations through the painted win- dow of the clay tabernacle which he himself inhabits. It so, he would have made a magnificent vicar of Bray. "Churchman," and others of your correspondents, as it seems to me, talk wildly about freedom and liberty. They seem to ignore the freedom of the laity. We are injoined by the spirits, whether they be of God, to search the scriptures daily to see if these things be so, in order to do which we must he free to think and to judge. Mr. Yonge, Mr. Warnock, and Mr. Moore are the chosen of their congregations respectively ; and they were not so chosen before knowing something about the nature of the teaching to be expected from them. Hence both teacher and taught are in the enjoyment of legitimate freedom and are in harmony with each other, being equally guided by what they believe to be the will of God. But the freedom that obtains in the Anglican Church is all on the side of the clergy and their patrons, therefore the clergy enjoy a larger amount of freedom of a sort than is enjoyed by Nonconformist ministers; but as a rule they have all the freedom they require or desire. They don't desire to luxuriate in a licentious latitudinarianism. Judge Hall in his day told the Anglicans that they bad a Popish liturgy, a Calvanistic Creed, and an Arminian clergy, and In our own day we have got High Church, Low Church and Broad Church. If it he a matter of indifference to Churchman " who ho has for his sAiritual adviser, others of his brethren have got consciences, as witness what has occurred at St. James's in our own town. I dare not say mere at present, lest I should be encroaching too far upon your valuable space.—Yours truly, LOOKER-ON.

div.head: "OUR GRAND OLD CHURCH."
div.p: "OUR GRAND OLD CHURCH."

. - - "A religion that has exhausted its moral force hss the feeble- ness of religion divided from morality, of Paganism itself." "U is too grand a Church—it is mot a Church for neighbours and equals." Sir,—A. "Churchman," I see, has now entered the lists on the specious plea of the attacks which have been made " upon Mr. Westbrook. He must be a very feeble duckling indeed for " Churchman " to "feel so much sympathy" for his friend, who was honestly, I believe, championing the *tune. The imputation implied, however, or the charge ntade indeed, is as gratuitous and unfounded as are con- scious failure and weakness thus made manifest. Bat under cover of this whining plea, exeunt Mr. Westbrook. This is a controversy that requires some backbone at least to sustain it, and none should enter upon it who have to cry peccavi as soon as they are confronted with stubborn facts and preg- nant evidence. Witheut intending any disrespect, I assume from the whole tenor of " Churchman's " letter, that he is another young duckling; for he rehearses in dashing and grandiloquent style the stale old prattle about "our grand old Church," which comes naturally and innocently from one in his adolescence, but which his seniors are cautious of resorting to except before an unenquiring and pre-committed audience. " Churehmtn " must have had this dull and un- informed clam in his eye, or he could hardly have dared to dish up such mouldy wails as this " Once the State is divorced from religion, woe he to England." Please substitute "the Church" for " relion"—which is his real eneaning—and the argument will run all the smoother. Now, I say that this woe which he so solemnly predicts has long since overtaken England. Are you sur- prised? Read the indictment against the Church drawn up by no less a luminary of the Church than Canon Gregory, which appeared as his contribution to the first number of The Natirmal Review. He there quite unintentionally shows how the Church practically divorced itself from the State and people by indolently abandoning them, by culpably be- traying the trust confided to it, and by guilty indifference to the moral progress, the educational wants, and the spiritual welfare of the nation. Canon Gregory undisghisedly admits that the Church had its opportunity for generations; to it was coufided a high and solemn inset; to its exclusive and even arrogant claims to be the sole, right- ful, spiritual guardian and teacher almost universal defer- ence was paid—it had the ball at its feet; yet what is now tba verdict when this paramount and momentous steward- ship is called upon for its audit ? Why we are landed, in !ins Year of our Lord 1883, in this alarming quagmire— lasses sank in darkness and vice, of impenetrable regions handed over to all the powers of evil, where nature herself fails to assert her ancient laws, and where- the lower eh- inn the higher in continual subjection." So ira- preesstr hold ywrites the Times. I wish your apace would per- mit of my supplying further incontrovertible evidence of like character, but let me add from the same authority these lines—" The Church of England has failed, and still fails, to reach more than the (range of the masses for whom it was founded. It has been driven t? follow tardily in the track of movements originated outside its own commanion. It has recognised at last teat all the arrangements of the Church are such as might be expected from a dominant hierarchy and aristocracy, while the people have been left to shift for themselves, as, iredeed, they have done." The courageous rector of Merthyr Tydvil has Just told us, It is too grand a Chnrch—it is not a Church for neighbours and equals. It is a rich man's Church. The poor man has turned his back upon it a hundred yews ago. It Is a sin for any eovernment to allow such

things to continue." In the face of damning evidence such as this—and much more like it—your correspondent "Churchman" bravely proclaims that the " religious character of this great country can alone be maintained by the connection ci the State with the Estab- lished Church." Prodigious! Let him tell, and not con- ceal, the true tale of the perversion, misappropriation, and even concealment in some instances, of the splendid educa- tional endowments which were the inheritance of the whole people, including all classes, tbe guilt cf which lies upon the Church. Let him tell all this to the workingmen—men of the whole realm, whose h:gbest interests he professes to love es, much at heart, and I predict the result weald be a storm of tesentment and indignation that would make him and his confreres quail. Repentance io the true ataitude of the Church towards the poor and ignorant, who have been suckled on sacerdotal mid aodden pabulum, or abandoned to the ignorance in which they were born; and thus we wit- ness a prevalent witless e,nd belated people, which is the opprobrium f the nation. Am I expected to treat seriously this delicious passage :--" If Dissenters think that they are deprived of privileges which Churchmen enjoy, it is their own fault; they elected to leave the fold, they were not driven from it, and they have no right now to grumble." There is here either genuine innocence or a designed stroke of shy humour. My brief reply Is to hark b.iele to the quoted passage above—" The people have been left to shift for themselves!" That ietru&—Canon faregory and a host of witnesses testify to that crashing fact. Ring it out—" It is not a church for neighbones and equals!" But you claimed, all through the centuries, sole right to spiritually nourish the peeple—you fie:cely reseated all collateral aid— and the result, was indole-ace and apathy; aye, and worse, arrogance an corruption. 'Nemesia is consequently en the track of the Establishment, visibly and undeniably, under whose chaeening retribettion we shall see a real and spiritual Church emerge, to refresh and elevate the nation, and nourish it with truth and righteousness. I have noticed but half the "grand " asseverations f " Churchman ; " I am, however, prepared to meet the remainder next week by your permission. He. has a "grand" scream about robbery and confiscation." But soft, young man; you are on dangerous. ground. B. A.

LIBERALISM 1N RUNCORN. Sir,—l was surprised to find that no one had taken up the question of political life in Runcorn, as put forward in a let- ter which appeared in The Examiner a few weeks ago from a Rochdale correspondent. This gentleman, it appears, has visited Runcorn and found no signs of political life whatever. I am afraid his very grave charges are to a large extent true, which accounts for the ominous reticence of the heads of the Liberal party in the town. Unless thole is the excitement consequent upon a contested election in the division political feeling in the district seems as dead as the proverbial "door nail." It were better to be left on the barren waste of poli- tical death than to be dragged out at every election to exhibit our cause as a galvanised corpse. Away with such hollow mockery ! Let us as a party—if the few voices crying in the wilderness may be designated a party—be content to work quietly, but earnestly, at laying the foundation of a strong public sentiment, in favour of free institutions, in the minds of the people, without which no true political good can be accomplished. It is all very well to put in and keep in a Liberal Government so-called— that is, for place-hunters, but surely Government has higher functions than finding comfortable places for its supporters. No Government will move in the direction of reform or in other ways for the special benefit of the people without there is a healthy public opinion continually pressing it. If the electors are not edu- cated in politics that public opinion cannot be created. An election carried by ignorant voters means nothing, which- ever side wins. But let the electorate be an enlightened and educated one, politically it will soon make an impression at the ballot box. Votes gained, by intimidation or cajolery are equally worthless. Let the voter be- come acquainted with the great facts of political economy and he will record his vote with an intelligence and inde- pendence which is seldom met with in these days of the caucus—Liberal and Tory. How is this desirable state of things to be brought about? Noobv "got up demonstra- tions" in public halls at which platitudes are hurled at the heads of a gaping multitude by an ignoramus with more ' lungs than logic, or a buffoon who can only tickle the ears of the groundlings, while he makes the "judicious grieve;" but by patient and careful teaching of the first principles of politics among the people. The sad neglect of educa- tion on this subject is at the root ef the great political failures of late years. For it cannot be denied by the strongest supporter of Liberalism that the present govern- ment, which is also the strongest government of - modern times, has done practically nothing. The cause is not Parnell, Bradlaugh, Egypt, or anything eise that has been put forward as an excuse, but the political darkness of the voters and their utter carelessness About public affairs. If the votes cast into the ballot box of 1880 had been the out- come of true political education they would have been fol- lowed up by a ceaseless urging on the part of the voters of the claims of the various reforms which are needed, and 1 their importunity would not have been unheeded. Instead of the old cry of Register! Register ! Register ! I would substitute Educate ! Educate! Educate I—Yours, Ltc., Runcorn, September 17, 1883. LIRE ti.A.L.

EARLESTOWN V. LIVERPOOL BTANLEY.—A. large number of spectators assembled at Wargrave Moss. Earlestown, on Satur- day afternoon last, when the Earlestown and Liverpool Stanley teams met to play their first match. The day was beautifully fine, and as a c nisequence a capital and exeiting contest was witnessed. The Branley team was a very strong one while F. Emmett and J. Duxbury were unable to play for Earlestown. The home team won the toss, and choose to play against the breeze and sun. Cuicin kicked off for Stanley about four o'clock, and a visit was at once paid to the Earlestown quarters Tbe ball quickly travelled to the opposite end, and the visitors for a shirt time were pressed. Even play succeeded during the first half—the visitors, if anything, having a sight advantage. Several good attempts to score were made by both teams, but up to half time neither secured a point. Ends were changed, and immediately afterwards the visitors had a corner kick Culcin landed the leather in front of the Earlestown uprights, and Holme rushing up headed it through amid applause For the next five minutes they seemed likely for adding to their store. but the good back play of the home team prevented them. One goal to the bad the Earlestown team strove hard ti get on a level witiptheir opponents, whom they afterwards pressed considerably. They met with bard lines on one or two occa- sion', but five minutes before the call of time Cameron headed the leather through tbe goal, and thus equalised the score. No additional point was registered, and the match—a very pleasant and enjoyable one throughout—resulted in a draw of one goal e• ch The players were :—Earlestown: J. Appleton, goal; R. Green (captain) and W. Rich, backs; J. Whalley and J. Green, half-backs; W. Cameron and H. Holeroft, right wing; A. Dag- nail and J. Mather, centre; It. Bowker and J. Simm, left wing. Liverpool Stanley: J. Lanighan, goal; A. McOallum and G. J. D:ivey (captain), backs; J. Davies ansl R. McCallum, halt- backs; G. Anderson and E. Ecjieston, right wing; J Holme and J. Culcin, centre; T. Daniels and W. Wilton, left wing. The umpires were J. Duxbury (Earlestown) and J. Keen (Stanley); Mr. P. Hestia officiating as referee.

MEETING AT THE WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB. SPEECH BY MR._McMINNIES, M.P.

An important meeting of the General. Council of the L:beral Association was held at the Liberal Club, on Monday evening, for the purpose of receiving a deputation from Manchester in connection with the Society for Promoting Women's Suffrage; and also appointing delegates to the Leeds Conference. J. G. McNlinnles, Esq., the membar for the borough, presided, and he was supported on the platform by His Worship the Mayor (John Crozfield), Dr. Gornall, Mr. F. A. Roberts, and other gentlemen. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said the first business of the evening was to receive a deputation from Manchester in connectim with the Society for Promoting Women's Suffrage. He then, in company with Mr. H. Roberts, the secretary to the Liberal Association, left the room for a few rnotnentcy and the gentlemen shortly after- wards returned and introduced to the meeting Miss Becker, of Manchester, and Miss Backhouse.

Miss BECKER. who was received with applause, referred to the fact that the agitation for giving votes to women on the same conditions as men had been carried on continuously since the passing of the Reform Bill of 1867. After the passing of that Act many of the revising barristers put women upon the list of voters in the following year. This action was upset by a decision of the judges, and now the only course which those who favoured women's suffrage could adopt was to appeal to the Legislature. It was estimated that about one-sixth of the householders in the country were women, and if the franchise were extended to these about 500,000 would be added to the voters in the three kingdoms. In conclusion, the lady remarked that ever since the measure relating to women's suffrage had been brought before the House it had had the support of the member for Warrington on whichever side be had sat. The friends of the movement therefore hoped that Warrington would continue its valuable support, and appoint delegates to the ensuing Liberal Conference at Leeds who would sup- port the passing of a measure which should give women their just political rights. (Applause.) After the withdrawal of the deputation

The CHAIRMAN' said the first business for the meeting to consider was the request which had been made to them. He had always voted or paired in favour of women's suffrage. He remembered that in 18613 the name of a lady was put upon the list of voters by mistake. He, therefore, took her to the polling booth and polled her name in favour of Mr. Rylands. (Applause.) 113, however, did not think the vote was counted, although it was recorded. In fact, they knew that there were one or two mistakes in counting votes upon that occasioe. (Hear, hear.) He felt some difficulty in re- ference to this matter, because he was a supporter of women's suffrage, and, as such, he voted for it, but he voted for it as an individual. He did not know that it would be agree- able to every gentleman when they might appoint upon the deputation toLeeds that his opinion should be controlled and his action impaired by an express intimation from the Liberal Committee that he must take a particular course on any given question. In addition to this, there was this difficulty. Women's suffrage had not be- come a plank in the platform of the Liberal party, awl some of their leaders were strongtv opposed to it—Mr. Bright for instance. A good deal had been said in favour of women having the franchise. Some people said that women would' act in voting under the irifluence of sentiments, and not from knowledge of polities. The question of war was a matter more or less of sentiment, and they would expect that, if a question of war or peace arose, women would vote against war or a war policy. He must confess that the matter to him appeared to assume the aspect of what it was politic for them to do under the circumstances, rather than to be a time for con- sidering the merits of the _question itself. (Applause.)

The MAYOR was strongly of opinion that whoever went to Leeds as a deputation from th,, Liberal party in Warrington should be perfectly free to judge for themselves upon this question. (Hear, hear.> He did not agree with their worthy chairman a bit upon this question. (Hear, hear, anil laughter.) If Mr. M'Minnies would excuse him, he would remark that it was just the onS point upon which he was weak. (Laughter.) In fact, he believed their borough member was a little bit afraid of Miss Becker, when she was in the room. If worc.en were given the suffrage, they would pros, e a very troublesome lot to deal with. (Laughter.) He did not think the experience which they had lud in municipal matters would lead them to favour women's suffrage. In conclusion, he moved a resolution to the effect that their delegates to Leeds should be let free to act as they might consider best as to the question of women's suffrage. Mr. F. A. ROBERTS seconded the motion.

Mr. H. WHITHAM said be could not sit there and I listen to a resolution such as that being made without showing that at leaat there was one dissentient, and he therefore moved that the deputation to the Leeds conference be instructed to support At Becker' :n the motion brought forward at the conference. He had ' t very strong feeling that the women of England had proved -hemselvesnapable of mastering every subject to which hey had directed their attention, whether these subjects, were ee..Entific, literary, or political. KILLING A PHEASANT Cnoxrcm—i man named I}ichard Wright was on Tuesday charged, at t1.,3 Preecot ettY Sessions, with having trespassed on land in pursuit of Eatne at Cronton, and also with killing a pheasant.— Mr. '4ackenzie prosecuted on behalf of Colonel Parkes, the owner tlf the land in question. The prisoner, it appeared, hail been !eon on the 29th ult. to leave the highway and go on to the 'ind in question, and there throw a stone at a phc!sant, which fell to the ground, and was picked up by him and put Uder his coat. He was then accosted by the man who had 14.9, la him, and he gave ap the pheasant.—A fine of Ll and "SW was imposed.

SALE oF THE DITTON BROOK Inoswosas.—These works, ,Ithich occupy about 80 acres of land on the Mersey, at Dit- `,.°°, have been sold by auction. The works comprise six rst furnace.s, with foundry and appliances for producing -POO tons of pig iron and 100 tons of casings weekly. here are excellent rail facilities, and a wharf capable of ...kcesremodatitilk vessels of 150 tons barthen. As the sale was announced to take place without reserve, a fairly large e2imPany assembled to watch the proceedings. Mr. Gamble, St. Helers, has bought the property for £20,000. DEPARTURE OF THE REV. A. M. DE HAZA RADLITZ ROaI DlTlON.—Father do Haza Radlita, S.J., the principal Ditton College', has left Ditton to join the province of t'imburg, Holland, where he has been assigned a large and 4°Dortant station by his church. His removal has caut;,•,', tgeauine feeling of regret throughout the district. The Father was appointed to the mission at Dittou in 1879, llnce which time he has laboured &truestly and devotedly VI behalf of the parishioners. Ameng the poor his kind har'd has often been displayed, and in tiAe to9tclell of the sick his voice was ever beard, in ties of sympathy and affection. His zeal °t the church has been untiring, aul the .en behalf success of the c4oltege due in a great measure to his alous n efforts. liaza Radlitz addressed his fewell speech n.ts. Father le to a deeply ',ll.tuected congregation the other day, many persons bursting 1,, to tears. The rev, father preached at Portico on Sunday. was followed there by at I.east 150 members of St. ftchael's Church, who desired again to utter words of fare- ,to) their old pastor. F ather Frederick Predeck, S. J., , ° has spent several rears in BombAy, succeeds the Rey. M. de Haze, Radlitz, and he has commenced his laboure the parish.

AGRicuLTIIRAL SIIONV.—The second annual exhibition of the Main Agricultural and Horticultural Society, which embraces the districts of Irlam, Cadishead, and Barton 1408 a, was held on Saturday in a marquee erected in a field Bear to Islam Church. There were 230 entries and £4O was given in prizes. The show of vegetables, especially pota- toes and celery, was very fine. Messrs. Dobie and Mason, ceedsmen, Daansgate, Manchester, who exhibited a fine col- lection of cu. flowers, fruit, and vegetables (not for compe- tition), offered a silver cup, value £2 25., for ten distinct !liaises of vegetables (potatoes excluded), which was won 7,1 James Upton, Islam Special prizes were given by uleeara. Webb and Sons, Worlsley. Stourbridge, for the best .Six dishes of vegetables (two of the varieties to be grown 'rum seed supplied by them). The successful competitors Were :-1. A special prize (a barometer) for the best Potatoes exhibited in the show was taken by George Ash- -IE 7, and one given for the best six dishes of vegetables (a PPar kettle) was taken by William Barber. There was a utile attendance of visitors. Harrington and he were ou the look-out for the defendant, and they saw him pass down Booth's Hill to the station, and back again, driving at a %re furious rate. He stopped the defendant's horse and took charge et it, but the defendant would not let go the reins and he had to unbuckle them. P.S. THE ALLEGED ATTEMPTED SUICIDit- AT Sr. HELENS.- The youth, named John Henderson, who was brought before the St. Helens magistrates about a fortnight ago on a charge of having attempted suicide, and who was then•re- mended, was again placed in the dock at the same court en Friday last. The prisoner, who has no relatives living, -it will be remembered, lodged with a man named Sylvester Eden, in Twyford-street, Parr. On the sth instant, he war found in the house unsanscious, and with a small bottle containing some laudanum by his side. It appeared that be had suffered much from toothache and other pains, and had been in the habit of taking laudanum in order to obtain sleep. He had also been subject to fits, and, it was said, on one occasion he had risen in his sleep and walked to Liverpool, not returning home till late in the day.—ln answer to the Bench, he said when taking the laudanum .he had no intention whatever of poisoning himself. He had been employed at Pilkington's top glass works.—After a few warning words from the Bench he was discharged. A MALICIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A POGICEMAN.—An elderly female, named Catherine Houghton, who was on Friday charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having been drunk and disorderly, took a not unusual ,but in her case a somewhat unfortunate line of defence.—Evidence was given by P.C. Chrystal which clearly went to show that there had been drunkenness on the part of somebody, and-the defendant, recognising this fact, said it was the officer who was drunk, and not herself. He had, she added. .beencotonly drunk at the time of the alleged offence„ but also when he served the summons, cn which occasion, she said, he was so intoxicated as not to he able to see either her or a lodger she had in the house. Shedid not explain hcw he managed to servo the summons at all under these cir- cumstances, and as evidence was given which entirely cleared the officer from the grave charge made against him, the Bench, having in a few severe remarks characterised the accusation put forward by the defendant as a malicious one, fined her 15s. and costs, 225. in all, or 14 days' impri- sonment.
