I•eaid that since last petty sessions he bad opened up the asource of the spout, and found that it was a small spring in a bed of quicksand about 12 yards from where it was de- livered at the spout. In close proximity to the spout weal a drain composed merely of rubble, which ran past a clocet, and from what he could see that would be a source of pollution to the spout. Another source of pol- lution was a manure wharf near at had.—Dr. Foz, medical officer to the Board, repeated his evidence given at the last hearing, that the water was greatly polluted with crganic matter, and utterly unfit for drinking purposes.— The defendant said he had no oh.fection to the spout being closed, but he would want to use it for slopping purpoees.— Mr. Bidway said that what the Board desired was that the spout should be so closed that people would be prevented from using the water for drinking purposes.—The defen- dant, in answer to the Bench, said that if an order was issued for the closing of the spout he intended to close it and carry the water a distance of about 15 yards further on, so that he could use it for a steam engine, but he did not think it was fair that he should bear the expense of that, because he had not compelled people to drink the water.—The Bench said that the matter of expeuse was beyond their jurisdiction.—An order was granted for the closing of the well. ANOTEXIL SWINDLER AT LYMM —Joseph Boyer, a young man, said to be from Bowdon, was charged at Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, with obtaining sundry boots and shoes, the property of Mr. John Thomason, Lymm, by false pre- tences.—Gre Saturday last the prisoner came to the shop of Mr. Thomason about half-past 10 and wanted to be mea- sured for a pair of new boots. Miss Thomason said her father was not in, and he said he would come again on Monday afternoon. He came again iu the afternoon, and eaid he was valet for Mr. Stuares,uncle, and he was stay- ing a fortnight at Mr. Stuart's, The Firs, and that he was to have some boots and Mr. Stuart would pay for them. She produced a pair of boots. and he took those produced. He returned about half-past two and brought them back, taking others in exchange. She made out a bill to Mr. Stuart, and booked them to that gentleman. Sergeant Harrington saiddhe went to Mr. Thomason's shop, and while there he heard a shout of "Sergeant," and on going to the place found Miss Thomason with her hand on the prisoner's throat. He went to prisoner's lodgings and got the boots and shoes produced, which had been identified as his property. The prisomer's landlord was wearing one pair, as he was making them easier for prisoner's feet, he being troubled with corns. (Laughter.) He charged him, but he made no reply. He added there was another charge of obtaining board and lodging by false pretences at Lymro, aid he had also reason to think he was wanted in Liver- pool.—Mr. David Stuart, residing at The Firs, Lymm, de- posed that there was no such a person as his uncle staying with him. The prisoner was in his employment about four years ago, and he had to discharge him for misconduct. He never gave him authority to go to the shop for hoots at anything else.—Prisoner said he was not discharged as stated. Mr. Btuart said his uncle was in Philadelphia, and could not be with him.- -The prisoner was then further charged with obtaining board and lodgings by false pretences from Ann Hamilton, an aged person residing at Booth's Hill. The prisoner came to her house on Thursday, the 15th inst., and asked for lodgings for ten days, saying that he had conic to Lymm to audit Mr. Stuart's books, and that he would not trouble her only for breakfast and tea. He agreed to give her 58. a week for the lodgings: She supplied him with food, and should have received 108. on the Saturday, but be was arrested and she had received nothing. On Saturday morn- ing she lent him is. 9d.—at first 3d., then 6d., and after- wards is. She would not have let her lodgings or lent him money if he had not made the representation about Mr. tqc;ext, because she had been duped with lodgers so often.— Mr' Stuart said that the representations the prisoner had made regarding him 'ere false.—The prisoner was committed Ito take his trial at the Run ford Sessions. PRESTON BROOK. PRESTON BROOK WESLEYAN CHAPEL. •—• The Preston Brook Wesleyan Chapel, which has been closed for some time for the purpose of beautifying, was re-opened on Thursday last, when it presented a pleating and tasteful appearance. The Rev. John Bateman preached in the After- noon, and, after a tea meeting at hail-past four o'clock, a public meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. Thos. Iterman. The chairman narrated some interesting reminis- cences of the chapel in the old days, pointing out that men occupying high positions bad been trained there. Perhaps • , in the near iuture rrestan Brook would send Out SOMe emi- nent men, for he observed with great gratification that there were many young men connected with the chapel who had promising careers before them. Addresses were also delivered by Revs. (leo. Hack, Jebn Bateman, Messrs. Willett, R. Norman, Ravenscroft, and Ck,veniq. dal statement was read by Mr. Jones, showing the cost of the decorations to be about £6O, which it was expected would be cleared off after next Sunday's services.

SOUTHWORTH- WITH -CROFT. I SOIITHWORTH-WITH-CROFT 'CHOOL BOARD—The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board School, on Tuesday evening. Present: The Rev. T. P. Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and Messrs. Richard Turner, Lewis, Birchall, and Alfred Dixon (school attendance officer).— The attendance officer submitted his report, which stated that he bad visited the schools in the district during the past month, when he found that several of the eldest boys bad been away from school, in consequence of haying been employed during the harvest; and that 21 children had been absent sick daring the month. He also stated that he had warned 16 parents that unless their children attended school more regularly they evotiid be summoned to appear before the Board snote a rea3onable excuse for such absence, and that he had warned one person for illegal employment of a child, he stated. He therefore summoned three parents to appear before the Board for neglecting to send their children to sch.ni in conformity with the bye-laws of the Board, all . of whom appeared and were cautioned.—The ieport having been unanimously adopted, sumnionges were orthred to be issued in three cases against parents for neglecting to com- ply with the bye-laws.—The attenJance officer presented the accounts of the children's tre it, which stated that the receipts (inclts.llng a balance-in bend of £1 19s 8d from last year's treat) amounted to £l9 183 4d, and the expenditure ; to £l5 23 2d, leaving a balance in hand of £4 16s 2d. The • accounts having been passed, the proceedings terminated.

WINSFORD. SUBSIDBNCE.—WhiIe everywhere in the valley of the Weaver and in the vicinity of the salt works may be seen some trace of subsidence, yet the appearances are strong° at in tho parts of the salt towns near the river. Certain parts of Windford, as Market Place, Lower High-street, Church - street, &c., abound with evidences. Not a day passes but some appearance, or other confirms the observation. Here a water main gives way and out comes the water in torrents, till turned off for repairs ; there a house, built as most new ones are now, of timber and brick, after the old fashion in Cheshire, level a week ago now many inches out of the hori- zontal, so that the plate glass window is seen to crack, or the doors and windows refuse to move in the normal man- ner till the jacks have been under. A town market-hall even has to come down first to provide safe room or more commo- dious standings, where the same in other towns would have done for generations yet unborn. The question may be asked could not this be prevented without stopping the works which arc socially and financially the very existence of the place. Some may be spared by filling in certain shafts as soon as the pumping is finished in tuat loc OUT. Yet it has not so acted in the Market Place near the Royal Oak to wit, though a shaft there was tilled up, or partially filled up, years ago when it ceased working. We cannot, however, say what the result would have been had it not been filled up. Many think, however, that so lon4 as the space whence the .brine was pumped is left unfilled up that the water will accumulate there, dissolve the rock, form brine, and so cause the subsidence. Whatever the remedy may be short of stop- ping the works, which would be suicidal to the towns con- cerned, the cracking, unlevelling, and falling process goes on tmabatingly, and private and public owners are alike called on to repairing the damage achieved. SALVATION ARMY.—The 212 corps is the one at Winsford, and it is quite alive yet. No sign of decadence seems to be matsifested. Ever and anon some change is projected in the plans by which the public is kept alive to the fact there is such a body in existence. A grand tea bath!, fire and blood attack, or some such high sounding phrase, as minis- ters to or borders on the sensational. Alter long watching of the movement, and giving the most charitable construc- tion imaginable to the work, it does seem that much of the latest phase of religious excitement consists of big words, high and loud seunds, and a ritualism that abounds with gesture and outward show, larer,ely differing from the meek, unostentious introducer of the Christian religion. " Who did not strive nor cry, neither did any man bear his voice in the streets," whose example other bodies of Christian workers have followed mostly up to the days of the Puritans and Wesleyans, who departed from that practice because often they had nowhere to worship in but the open air, being shut out of the usual churches by those whose hearts were less on fire for the good of their fellows.—Coninitini- cated.

ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. SHOCKING RAILWAY FATALITY AT CHESTER.—OH Tues- day, as Peter Griffiths, a shunter, aged 24, in the employ of the joint railway companies at Chester General Station, was engaged in his occupation at the end of the goods yard, a train came upon him unperceived, knocked him down, and the wheels passing over his body he was killed instantane- ously. SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR CHESTER.—A re- markable accident happened to a gamekeeper named Jeilicoe, at Ledsham Station, near Chester, on l'hursslay evening. Jellicoe, who was employed by Mr. Corbett, of Aston Halt, was a little late for the Chester tram, and came down the steps leading to the platform in such a hurry that he was unable to stop himself at the bottom, and bounding across the platform fell on the rails in front of an advancing train, and was cut to pieces. SHOCKING SUICIDE IN A CHESTER HOTEL.— A young farmer, named Pennington, of Sack., Lodge, near Chester, committed suicide on Monday r.iot under extraordinary circumstances at Chester, by driiiking an immense dose of carbolic acid in his beer. Dec-a-,:d proceeded to poison himself in the coolest possible rnion,e. It appears that he bought the carbolic acid from Mr. ilirk's shot,. Red. having signed the book, proceeded straight to the old Queen's Head Inn. Here he called for a glass ,f 1).,,,r and draek half of it. He then took the bottle cont,iiing the carbolic acid out of his pocket and filled the glass up to the brim and drank itloff. The landlady did not notice the occurrence, but, smelling the fumes of acid, exc'aimed, "Dear me, what is it that smells," and the deceased, in a most casual manner replied, "0, I have just ooisoned myself." Fie stumbled to a table, and ;Alen on to the fluor, where L he expired.

The annual sermons in aid of the funds of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Simm's Cross, Widnes, took place on Sunday, when the Rev. J. Butcher, of Barrow-in-Furness, I preached two sermons to large congregations. The choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Drought, rendered special music suitable to the occasion. On Monday evening a suc- cessful tea party was held. About 160 persons partook of ties teems% the following ladies presiding at the tables:— Miss Pinchers, Mrs. Crossley, Mrs. Drought, Miss Wiles, Miss Fannie Wiles, Miss Barker, Miss Shaw, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. Hughes, Mrs. Schofield, and Mrs. J. Heath. Subse- quently a public meeting was held in the school chapel, Mr. J. W. Coxoa presiding. He was supported by the Revs. J. Butcher, L. Miles (Frodsham), and T. Rollason. The Rev. L. Miles having offered up prayerethe choir sang, the anthem will praise Thee." The Chairman offered a few prelinate nary observations, and called upon Mr. E. Rollason, the treasurer, to give his annual report. He remarked that he did not view the financial position of the society with the sad- ness that treasurers were apt to do. The ground and the school chapel were obtained at a cost of £1,300. The ground was of considerable extent, and upon it could be built a class- room on each side of the school, and behind there was sufficient room to erect a chapel. When • the building was opened, something like £4OO had been raised towards the cost, leaving a debt of about £B5O still unpaid. The interest on this sum amounted to £4O per annum, so that so far they had paid £l2O in intere3l, and besides pay- ing all current expenses they had reduced the debt to £BOO. The treasurer had a balance of £9 in hand, which would be increased by the profits on that eyeeing's tea party to over £2O. They had also purchased a quantity of crockery, itc., with money which the ladies of the congregation had suc- ceedect in obtaining. The question was how were they to raise rneney to wipe off the debt. The best way he thought was to get a revival of God's work—(hear, hear,)—for he never yet knew the pockets of a man to be closhd who had an in'erest in the gospel and the salvation of souls. The prcser.t sphiteal and financial position of Primitive Metho- diee' ia Widnes was a credit to the denomination, and the eee:re prospects of the Sirnm's Cross Primitives were bright wttn hope. Last year they held a sale of work, by means or which they were able to pay £2O off the debt, against £4O in the previous year, but considering 'the state of tride he thought that was very good. The sale of work which should have been held this year Would take place later, probably ext March, so that the ladies had no need to become anxious about the sewing meeting. They considered that is a Church they had ~.done well. The school was becoming overcrowded, and the div was not far distant when they would have to ask the congrezation to put • up the class-rp6ms' ,he had mentioned, and the building altogether enlarged to give the Sunday school workers .full scope for their exertions. It was a great credit to those workers that parents con- tinued to send their children to school, and on behalf of the trustees he thanked them for their .labours. It was gratify- ing to think that they had the sympathies of the neighbour- hood, and it was his earnest wish, and the earnest wish of all connected with the church and school that these sym- pathies might be enlarged. (Applause.)—The Rev. L. MILES delivered an address, in which he touched upon the scepticism of the age; and the Rev. J. BUTCHER followed by giving an interesting narration of his experience as a street missionary, counselling the Widnes brethren to be constant in their efforts to extend Grid's kingdom.—During the evening the choir sang a number of antherne in capital style, 'Mr. Drought weildink the baton. •

RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRIS- TIAN ASSOCIATION. With the object of discussing and devising means to in- crease the usefulness and extend the influence of the insti- tution whose name heads this paragraph, a conference be- tween. the committee and delegates from .various Sunday schools in the town was held in the association's rooms, High-street, on Monday evening. The Rev. J. D. Thomas presided, and delivered a short address. Letters of apology were read from the Rev. Canon Barclay and Dr. Steele, the president of the association. The schools represented were —Parish Church, Holy Trinity, Holy Trinity Young Men's Christian Association; Wesleyan: Brunswick.; Millbrow, Nelson—street, and Camden; Bethesda Congrega- tional, Primitive Methodist, St. John's Presby-. terian, and the Ragged School. Mr. R. Evans, the hon. secretary, gate an interesting account of the work of the Association and stated that it was contemplated to form, during the winter session, classes of an educational, moral, and social character. Among others it was intended to establish an historical society, a bible class, a shortkand class, a shorthand writers' association, debating sticiety, and to organise winter lectures on scientific subjects. Mr. .T. Humphreys followed with an address on the importance of Young Men's Christian Associations, and the following gentlemen also made a few observations :—Messrs. C. Gar- nett (Manchester), W. Shaw (Mersey Missions), Craig, Capt. Le' Contier, Ashler, Harrison, Cunningham, Leathwood, S. C. Beckett, W. H. Rogerson, J. A. Smith, and S. Coven- try. The gathering was regarded as a success, and it is ex- pected that the work of the coming session will be of a very extensive character. The meeting comprised about 20 4ele4ates and 20 members of the committee, and members the Association. They were supplied with light refresh- ments during the evening.
FORTILOMING VISIT OF THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION TO WIDNES.

'Et,o omelet programme ot the British Association con- tains the following list of arrangements in connectioa with the visit to Widnes on Thursday, the 27th September:— Number limited to 100. Walking half-a- mile. Conductors: Messrs. Gossage, Gaskell, Mathieson, and others. The ex- cursionists will leave Chapel-street station by a special train at 10 a.m., reaching Widnes about 11 a.m. The pirty will depart frcm Widnes at 4 p.m., and is timed to arrive at Southport about 5 p.m. The works will be visited in the following order :-1, Messrs. William Gosssge and Sons' soap works, wood-cutting and box-making machinery. Luncheon (given by the proprietors of the works visited) 1' p.m. 2, Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s works, 2 p.m. —The Le Blanc soda process:—
FIRST OPERATION.

SULPHURIC AClD.—Salphurous acid (from pyrites) and nitric acid (from nitrate of soda)—steam and air are con- ducted into lead chambers furnished with " Glover" and "Gay-Lussac "towers, liquid sulphuric acid (brown vitriol) is produced.

SECOND OPERATION. SULPHATE OF SODA (SALT CAKE) AND HYDROCHLORIC AClD—Sulphuric acid and salt are heated together in cast- icon pots, the resulting sulphate of soda is dried in "close " or " muffle " furnaces, and the hydrochloric acid condensed or used in the gaseous state for the prodaction of chlorine for the manufacture of bleaching powder. THIRD OPERATION.—(A.) CARBONATE OF SODA—Sulphate of soda, limestone' and tine coal are heated in a revolving furnace. The black ash thus produced is lixisliated with warm water in iron vats. An impure solution of soda and alkali waste is the result. OLD PROCESS —The impure solution of soda is evapor- ated to partial dryness by the waste heat from the revolving furnace, the resulting salts are finished in reverberatory furnaces, and commercial carbonate of soda or soda ash is produced, the remaing solution is used for the production of caustic seda. The soda ash is subs quently used for the i production of refined alkali, soda crystals, and bicarbonate I of soda. NEW PROCESS.—The impure solution of soda is treated with carbonic acid and air in blowing vessels, and exposed to an elevated tempefature in coil furnaces, by which treat- ment silica, alumina, and the iron of ferrocyanogen are pre- cipitated. From this purified solution after filtration, various forms of pure carbonate of soda, such as refined alkali.and crystal carbonate !hay be obtained. THIRD OPERATION.—(R) BLEACHING POWDER —When liquid hydrochloric acid is required the gaseous acid is passed through condensers. The liquid acid is used ter the production of chlorine by heating it in stone sills with peroxide of manganese. Chlorine and chloride of manganese are produced. Peroxide of man- ganese is recovered from the chlorida of manganese by the ".Weldon process." In the " D,acon process" for the manu- facture of chlorine the gaseous hydrochloric acid is taken direct from the sulphate of soda furnace into an apparatus where it is heated in contact with air and a salt of copper, the result being chlorine and water. The chlorine when made by the old or manganese method is conducted into lead cham- bers on the floor Of which slacked lime is spread, the lime absorbs the chlorine and chloride of lime or bleaching pow- der is produce4l. The Chlorine made by the " Deacon process " being' diluted with nitrogen and surplus air, is conducted into special chambers made of slate, in which a very large surface of lime is exposed to the gas, and cblotde of lime or bleaching powder is produced. 3. Messrs. N. Mathieson and Co. The Le Blanc soda process. Caustic soda. Extraction of copper from burnt pyrites by the "wet method."

THE WALKING} FEizr AT,E.trer.EsTowti. Tne greatest interest seems to have 134er: excited in Earlestown by the attempted walk of 2. 020 miles in 1,000 hours by Bob who has previously obtained soprm3 notoriety through his pedestrian performances. He states that he is engaged 00 bis present task simply to gratify hts ambition to accoin• plish a hitherto rinp ecodenfed feat. An impression hall been spread about that he is doing for wager, and be h i as been promised certain sums of money fhe i! successful. - But such is not the case, the fict being that he is dependent upon the public for support. Since be came to Earlestown his splendid walking abilities have been much demonstrated, and his public performances have been of a most remarkable character. On Saturday last he commenced walking along a measured track en the Earlestown market ground —3;xteen times round being counted as three niiles, although it is a little over that distanne. Since be began his walk on the 17th August he travelled up to Saturday night last 1,404 miles—And on Monday—in the presence of a large number of vectators throughout the day, he fairly and honestly tramped round the market i.irounil about 290 times,—walking no less than 55 miles.—On Tuesday be accomplished 51-i miles, on Wcdnes,liv 54, and on Thurs- day 52 miles, making a total of 1,614 On the last-named day rain fell pretty heavily, but the pedestrian gamely kept to his work. The 1,000 hours expire oil Thursday f night next, and the walker is confident that he will accorn- plisb the' self-imposed task.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF . GUARDIANS. The hirtnightly meeting of the Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday. There were pre- sent :—Mr. Greening (chairman). Mr. Cooper (vice-chair- man), Major Cartwright, Dr. Mackie, and Messrs. Caldwell, Yoolfall, Brown, Derbyshire. Owen, Appleton, J. Hougai- ton, Worthington, Bonnet!, Walmaley,Sicideley, Humphries, Greenall, Hunt, Gibeen, Kilshaw, and W. Houghton ; and Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk). THE WORKHOIISE MASTER'S REPORT. The Meterrnia reported that the number of inmates in the House during the past week was 276, against 4416 in the corresponding week of last year. The number of vagrants relieved was 51, of whom 31 were men, 9 women, and 29 children. The number of inmates in the House was 36. Thelnumber of children in attendance at the Union school was—boys 25, girls 29; total 54. There were receiving in- dustrial training—boys 12. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE, The School Attendance Committee reported that they had dealt with 13 new and 15 old cases—total 28. THE HOUSE COMMITTEE. At aaneeting of the House Committee, held on the 14th instant, it was recommended "That the adults get 12oz. of fish in lieu of meat for dinner, and children Boz., once a week." It was reported that the present number of adult inmates in the Houze was 213; children, 66; total 279, a decrease of 9 on the' coiresponding week of last year.— After some conversation about the fish dinners, which are still giving satisfaction, 'the minutes were adopted on the motion of Major CARTWRIGHT, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY. THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the Schools Committee, on the 18th I instant, it was rrportsd that there were in the schools-101 children under class I.; 63, class II.; 17, class III.; total; 71. The tender of Messrs. Johnson Brothers was accepted for furnishing and decorating the committee-rooms according to the de- tailed tender and description of -work tq _be executed, the sum amounting in the whole to £57 83. The tender of Mr. Joseph Mounfield was also accepted for the carpeting of six roams for the sum' of £lO, as described in the tender. An additional tender from Messrs. Garnett and Sons amounting to £43 163 for other gocels was submitted to the Board, and. this was also accepted—use confirmation of these minutes were moved by Mr. DARRYSHIRE, seconded by Mr. Hoerr. —Dr.-BLecieti oblected to so mach decoration at I:tailgate , Schools; which, he'eald, was to be greater than the Board nerlao eat in that room enieved ; and said he could not help Ithinking that the tendency to decorate was by no means worthy of the Board. .Referring to the estimates for furni- tore the doctor hed that £l2 for a bookcase for a person at the schools to hold his private books was far too inuch. He thought tenders ought to have been I properly sent in for the furniture and for the decorating so that they would know exactly what they were doing, and , be therefore moved an amendment to the effect that the I minutes of the committee be approved, with the exception of that portion relatiep; to the furnishing of the offices and committee roonts.-Mr. JOLLEY seconded the amendment, ob- serving that the estimates had not come before them in a proper business manner. He did not like the furnishing, the architectural alterations, the mouldings, and such like,, and he thought they ought te be very careful. He thought the whole thing ought to be rec insidered by the commitee. —Major CARTWRIGHT said the course adopted That morning, was very amusing. What, he asked, was the difference be- tween Mr. Garnett's tender and the tender first obtained and which was accepted by the committee but not adopted by the Board ?—The CLERK explained the course pursued in I regard to this furniture—which he said had been on for six months, and four or five times before the Board—was that after the Committee made a selection and submitted it to the Board it was rejected on the ground that it was too high, on the motion he believed of Major Cartwright. A committee was formed of the opponents of the expense combined with those who supported it, to whom the Board delegated the duty of going and inspecting the furniture as they thought best. They went to Messrs. Garnet and were two hours there, but the Major was absent, though he was a member of the com- mittee. (Laughter.)—Major CARTWRIGHT : Now, Mr. Clerk, don't put it in that way; you know I could not attend.—The CLERK continuing said the committee did not want to put all in the hands of one individual, but they selected what they found ,suitable at Messrs. Garnet's, Messrs. Johnson's, and Mr. Mounfielde. The articlee were of a mixed character, and the committee told thee(' gentlemen to send them in at the price they had given. Major CARTWRIGHT again asked the difference in amount between the tender first recommended by the committee and upset by the Board, and the tender that the Chairman recommended that morn- ing in favour of Messrs. Garnett P—Mr.DARBYSEIIIIIC said he did not remember the total, but -he might say it was £25. -Major CARTWRIGHT : Isn't it a little over? He reminded the Board that sum bad been saved in consequence of his action. When the Clerk said he (the Major) did not go to the com- mittee meeting Mr. Sutton ought te have stated that the meeting was fixed for three o'clock at his own office, and he (the Major,' had a meeting at the Workhouse at half-past two. It struck him the committee did not want him, and he did not himself want to go particularly. (Laughter.) He had stood up against reckless expenditure for years, in every way he had tried to cartail the expense, and now they had the result—Mr. CALDWELL said the committee were fully satisfied they had got the worth of their money, and they bad • done more for that Board than they wcu:d have done for themselves in the matter of selecting furniture.—The CHAIRMAN said he also should certainly support the committee.—Mr. DARBYSIIIRE, in re- plying, said that the ornamentation proposed at the schools was scarcely worth the name, and it could not possibly be much, seeing that the cost was to be only £14.-0n the amendinent being put to the meeting only the mover and seconder voted for it, whilst all the others recorded their votes for the original motion, which was accordingly car- ried.

WESLEYAN METHODISM AT . WARRINGTON. Over 200 persons assembled in Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, on Monday evening, to take part in what is termed a "recognition meeting," the formal introduction of a new minister to the congregation. • The minister who was introduced to the assembly was the Rev. James McTurk, last from Brixton Hill, London, who has succeeded the Rev. J.-Agar Beet, the latter gentleman having removed to Wrexham. The recognition was preceded by an excellent tea which was served in the vestry, and was presided over by the following ladies :—Mesdames Biddle, Horton, Gornall, Smith, Eglinton, Hensball, Guest, John Bennett, Collins, Shaw Green. and Miss Dutton. The subsequent proceedings were presided over by the superintendent minister (the Rev. J. Eglinton), who was supported by the Rev. J. McTurk, the Rev. T. Rippon; Messrs. M. Bowden Robert Cook, J. Henshall, E. J. Guest, J. Shaw Green; I. J. Biddle, John Bennett, I. Haywood, E. Ford, and J. Sum- mersgill. After the singing of the hymn" Crown Him Lord of all," prayer was offeied by the Rev. T. Rippon, who, feelingly alluded to the death of Mr. .hubb, a member of the congregation, and who had long b Len connected with the Wesleyan cause in Warrington. The rev. CHAIRMXN said he rejoiced to be present en that very auspicious occasion. It was not so long since they met together to speed the party guest, and they would 1 bog remember, he thought, the impressive and touching service in connection with the removal of their beloved 1 brother Beet, to which reference had already been made iii I the pathetic and impressive prayer in which they had all joined. Remarking thca an unexpected shadow had fallen upon them' he touchingly alluded to the death of Mr. Chubb, and said, as he would not like that shadow to rest e throughout commencement. thew hol e of Theythe service,we re me he et that td nightm e n - tenisnopneenecditahil tleymat t o encourage t ey w e eachwere given, other and w a in theyth e e met twolrekot! t 1 Lord to whichhth wel- come their dear, brother Mr. _ McTurk—(hear, hear)— who had happily come amongst them, mill whose entering in amongst them he thought they had already had evidence had been blessed and good. (Hear, hear.) Ehey could only. assure Mr. McTurk, in the presence of those :before him, of all proper sympathy, affectionate regard, reverence, and help, in every way which he could possibly help, for his own personal comfort, his family enjoyment, and his ministerial success; and he was quite sure that the brethren there. that night would spa* successively in that strain, that Mr. Mc Turk's heart might be Cheered by the expectation of good things to coins. It was now his duty , to ask their senior circuit steward on behalf to some ment of the whole circuit to offer wo..ds of welcome te- their ' beloved brother. (Applause.) . ' Mr. M. BOWDEN then referred to the removal of Mr. Beet, and observed that he had felt ex- ceedingly anxious about his successor. He knew that Mr. Beet had served them well, and he knew that he had been appreciated in the circuit. As a teacher there were 'very few to equal him; and he (the speaker) felt sere that many had had similar misgivings as to who should succeed Mr. Beet. Ile felt no anxiety now. {Applause.) He had never seen their friend Mr. kcTurk, be had never seen his photograph or anything of that kind, but almost as, soon as he sew him get out of the train he felt sure they had got the right man. (Applause.) Speaking in reference to the circuit, he said he felt bound to confess that for the , past two or three years they had been gradually increasing in strength. Their congregations had been increasing and their collections had been increasing, so that it made those officially connected with the circuit doubly anxious that the progreei that had been 'going on should not be arrested. They would excuse him if he told them his con- viction that they had been making progress for the last two or three years, and that so far as the spiritual power of the circuit was concerned—he spoke now in reference to War- rington in particular—it wasa great deal better and higher than it was before that time. Re had felt in his own mind since Mr. McTurk had come amongst them that they had now arrived at the flood tide, and it would be for them to consider whether the progress that had been made during the past few years should still go on, or whether it should be arrested. His own conviction was that now they had arrived at the flood tide, they should put their hands to the work much more diligently and secure the blessing, for the possibilities were that if advantage was net taken of the wave of blessing that was now passing, it would recede. He appealed to those present to render them much more assist- ance than they had done in the past, and remarked that he I had long wished the churches would see with greater I force the great mission work that could be done I outside. That was a grand and good work, and he wished the friends engaged in it every success. The Sundly schools also required at the present t!r.s.t ?. i."..rgef• amount of help than they had hitherto had. He felt that practically his work in be Sunday school was finished, and pointed out that it was time they sent better educated men to teach the children who were now-a-days being so highly educated. He did not think any of them were aware of the weak state of their teaching power, and observed that whatever they did they ought to support the Sunday schools as it was from them that the churches were fed. After dwelling upon the necessity of placing an offertory box at the chapel door to provide funds for contingencies, he believed they would find the words uttered by Mr. Beet in reference to his suc- cessor to be true. Mr. Beet said that Mr. McTurk would serve them and serve Christ, and he believed Mr. McTurk would. (Hear, hear.) He therefore asked their support for Mr. McTurk. (Applanse.) Mr. E. .J. GUEST, B.A. (junior steward) said they rejoiced, to see Mr. McTurk present that night. His praise preceded him, and all that they had heard of him had been greatly in his favour. He had not had the pleasure of hearing him, but all the reports ha had heard were eminently in Mr. lqcTurk's favour. He trusted they would find—indeed, he believed with Mr. Bowden' they would find—they had been divinely guided in taking Mr. McTurk in Mr. Beet's place. He rejoiced to believe that Mr. McTurk came to them as an united, peaceful, prosperous people. There were amongst them no breaches to make up, no disagreable strifes to quell, there were no half-empty chapels to be filled, no structures loaded with debt. They were united. They were united, he trusted, in the great cause of Christ, and desired above all things to see His glory in the midst of them. They were not satisfied, and their watchword was not rest but rather agression. There were needs amongst them, and those needs must be supplied. A greatly-felt need for many years bad beEn the erection of suitable school premises in ri.iTioVon. (Hear, hear.) Under the able guidance of their superintendent and those who were working with him, he believed that these schools would soon become erected—(applause)—and that would be a very great occasion in very many ways to the town, to Methodism there, and to their circuit generally. He must thank the chairman on this occasion that they had gained the services of Mr. McTurk to join with him and others in promoting Silver-street day school. Ever since its birth that school had been regarded too much as an orphan for whom few had cared. He -hoped the school would be made one of the family, and that they would find it an auxiliary to and helpful in church work. He rejoiced , to think Mr. McTurk would join with him in the work in connection with the Foreign Missionary Society. I The cause in Warrington was not as healthy as it might be. For the past few years it had been gradually creeping up to something better, but it was not now what it was when Mr. Berry was amongst them. He I' looked forward to Mr. McTurk achieving in the circuit great good, and he hoped the work in Warrington would prosper, and that the Foreign Missionary Society would be more effective than it had been in the past. When the ! schools in connection with Bold-street Chapel were erected I he hoped it would be the happiness of Mr. McTurk to in- augurate a new chapel at Sankey Bridges. They had there la very hopeful cause, and a cause which bad been produc- tive of much fruit already. It was part of their circuit, it was rapidly increasing, and the sooner they took this matter up the better. Let the school scheme 'be completed, and then take up Sankey Bridgework, If it was not done others would step in before them, and they might lose something of i yearth e h wo lidt ht bgerye aht a id-i 0 tpl el ef ruein e sHs . e l To Hod hadfo r w in nr dt ht oe ethhaei rcnoi ma ni n ag good business man and an eloquent preacher; they had in. Let them all heartily I join with their ministers in the work of the Church. (Ap- plause.) Mr. J. HENSRALL observed that the congregation at Bold- street were all very favourably impressed with Mr. McTurk, I and he might venture on a little prophecy and say the more 1 they saw of him, the more they would liked him. (Ap- plause.) THE REV. G. S. REANEY AND STATE- DIRECTED EMIGRATION. A public meeting, which was practically a sequel to that held some ti ne ago at the Mansion House by the State. Directed Emigration Society, took place on Monday even- ing by the invitation of the Rev. G. S. Reaney in Stepney Hall. The ball, which is a large one, was crowded with workingmen and those generally interested in the subject to b 3 discussed. The Rev. G. S. Reaney occupied the chair, and, in opening the proceedings, explained the object of the tneetlng, which was to discuss whether State-directed emigration was the best way of meeting the distress existing among the poor, or whether there was another scheme which was better. He also begged those who took part in the meeting to abstain from Politics, and not to attempt to make the matter a party question.—Mr. G. F. Boyd then moved "That Stete-directd emigration and colonization is for the United Kingdom a necessity of the time ; and that the scheme of the association for promoting it is a practical method of aiding the unemployed poor, diminishing pauperism, reduc- ing local rates, and developing our colonial resources— deserves the most careful consideration of Her Majesty's Government." The speaker pointed out that the scheme proposed was to remove in the first instance 10.000 labour- ing men from London and other places to give them a free passage to Canada, find them work for six months or a year at remunerative wages, and ultimately to place them on a farm of 80 acres in exchange for an agreement to pay a moderate rent for it or to purchase it by instalments.—Mr. H. Hall seconded the motion.—Mr. J. Williams, of the Democratic Federation, moved the following amendment, of which notice had been given :—" That this meeting, in view of the industrial depression now prevail- ing in the United States, in Canada, in Australia, and New Zealand, declares against State-aided or State-directed emigration as any remedy for the present distress amongst the unemployed at the East-end of London; that this meeting therefore calls for a reasonable scheme of home colonization at d State em- ployment of labour at home to be set on foot at once, so that the unemployed who are ready and willing to work may not see their wives and children as well as themselves left destitute, or forced into pauperism during the coming winter."—Mr. McDonald, also a member of the Democra:ic Federation, seconded the amendment.—On the chairman calling on any one favourable to the resolution to continue the discuseion no response was made. Speeches then fol- luwed in support of the amendment, the speakers all being strongly against the system of emigration, dwelling espe- cially upon the unwi;:lom of sending able-bodied workmen out of this country to enrich another. The amendment was ultimately carried by a large majority.—A hearty vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the businese.

SCHOOL A TTE24'D.INCE.—Several cases of irregularity of ot attendance were brought before the magistrates at the Petty essions held at Prescot on Tuesday last. The full penalty was inflicted in seven of th,, cases. If. parents only knew the anxieties of teachers, and ho much is dependent on regular attendance, they might—if only out of sympathy for the teacher—contrive to send their children regularly to school. i

spoken by one and another that night with a ' great sense of responsibility resting upon him. He felt a little as if he had been on the dissecting table—not a very pleasant feeling—and that they had been testing him, prov- ing him and regarding him with a great deal of hope. He was willing they should prove what he was. He was not afraid of some little work for the Master whom he tried to serve, and he was not afraid to have poiated out to him how he might serve them in Methodism. He hoped to be able to do some little; but while they expected something of him' don't forget that his power came from above, and that they could help him to receive it. He had noticed many things that had pleased him much. He liked the chapels in which he had to preach. He liked Bold-street-- a fine specimen and grand type of Methodist chapel, such as old Methodist orators would like to find themselves in. (Ap- plause.) 'There they had a specimen of the more modern style. Some toldthemthat there ought to be no Gothic chapels. That, at any rate, was so built that they found it undoubt- edly'pleasant to worship in, and he did not doubt they had seen in years past Soula" led to Christ in it. He had seen the country chapels—Moore, Lymai, Padgate, Penketh, and perhaps one or two others—and he was pleased to have seen them. He had had the privilege also of preaching in Sankey Bridge Chapel. He did not admire very much the chapel there—(laughter)—and he hoped the friends at Sankey Bridges would have a more pleasant place to wor- ship in before long. He thought it necessary there should be such gatherings as that now and again, and that the officers should meet and approve themselves upon the plans for the future, and about what had been achieved in the past. He thought the review they had heard that night' would be the means of inspiring them to serve more faithfully and zealously their God. He was pleased to find they had a scheme in hand for the extension of their circuit •work, and that they had mapped outs scheme for building better Sunday schools. He roticed too on the first Lord's Day he spent here that they had mission work in the town. He was pleased to find that. He thought it was a sign that there waft" some 'vigour in the Christianity they had—that there was sill life in the soul if it went out to seek those who ne:cled it mast. There were many in the town who needed work of that kind. He had been strack as a new corner wit) the drunkenness th it abeunds, with :the foul language that he heard issue from the lios of men and women. These were loud calls to them as Christian people to be up and doing, if by any means they could win souls for Christ; While they had been looking at him and wondering what he should be able to do, he had been thinking of them and wondering what they would do during the coming winter months for the glory of their God and the advancement of their church. , In conclusion, he pointed out that they could make the Methodist Church greater even than it had been. and he expressed a hope that God would grant unto them rich blessinefe, and that His namft might run and be glorified. BOILER EXPLOSION IN. AMERICA : FIVE PERSONS KILLED AND MANY INJURED.—A despatch from Pittsburg announces that a boiler explosion has occurred at the Slig.) Ironworks there, by which .five persons were killed aid many injured. FATAL Has 7LT OF I STABBING AFFRAY.—A young man warned John Anderson, belonging to Port Glasgow, who was stabbed during a quarrel at Greenock ten days ago, died in Greenock Infirmary yesterday morning. Two young men are in custedy. The Central News is enabled to state that the Home Secretary is about to cause a medical enquiry into thtl mental condition of William Gouldstone, who was sentenced to death for the murder of his five children at Walthamstow on the Bth August. • I MYSTERIOUS DEATH FROM VIOLENCE.—Swan Hansen, a Swede and second mate on the steamer Houre, was found on Thursday night in a trimmer's cabin at the South Dock, Sunderland, with a severe stab in the breast. He refused to say bow he was wounded, and being removed to the infirm. ary died in abon.f.: two hours. Isto arrests have been made. HORRIBLE DEATH.—An inquest was held at Coventry, on Thursday night, on the body of Charles Pathwell, a painter, aged 32. Deceased was engaged painting a skylight on the roof of Messrs. Caspe's factory, when he slipped and fell Bead downwards, a distance of 50 feet. His injuries were of a horrible nature, and death ensued shortly afterwards. Verdict," Accidental death." SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A BUTCHER.—liobert Horrocks, a butcher, at Bolton committed suicide by cutting his throat with a large butcher's knife. When discovered he was in a cellar lyingt a pool of blood, which we, issuing from a frightful gash in his throat. He had been suffering from acute melancholia, and recent- suic!des in Bolton appeared to prey on his mind. He was removed to the Infirmary, but died in a few hours.

MILITARY FUNERAL AT WAR- RINGTON, Eleven months ago the permanent staff of the 3rd Bat- talion of the South Lancashire Regiment met in the regi- mental orderly room to do honour to their Sergeant-Major, Jacob Chubo, in his retirement from the service, by pre- senting him with a handsome timepiece, which they did with many fervent expressions of their desire for the pro- longation of his life and for his future welfare. The hope!! then expressed have not, however, met with fulfilment, as the recipient of the gratifying testimonial died on Sunday last, after a brief illness, at his residence hi Hoyle-street; and OD Tuesday afternoon the same members of the per- manent staff, together with many of their former and pre- sent comrades-ia-arms, and, large numbers of townspeople, did honour to the memory of the deceased by following his remains to the grave. The demonstration was an un- mistakeable proof of the respect which the late Mr. Chubb heel gained amongst the townspeople during his long resi- dence in Warrington, and must have afforded much conso- lation to the sorrowing relatives. The funeral cortege, con- slating of a hearse and three coaches left Hoyle-street at two o'clock and proceeded as far as coaches, Wesleyan Chapel, where the mournful procession was met by the per- ,l manent staff and men from Orford Barracks. Here the coffin was removed from the hearse and covered with a flag, I was carried by Sergt.-Major Holmes, Quartermaster-Sergt. Roberts P Sergeant-Instructor Lee, and Colour-Sergeant Grundy into the chapel, where a short service was held. • Crewels or sympathising friends and spectators had gathered opposite the chapel, and before the melancholy eervice corg- i menced the gallery was filled with a congregation, nioet of ; whom were attired in mourning. The body of the edifice ! was reserved for the mourners, who occupied the centre seats, and a number of intimate friends were admitted to the side pews. As they entered the chapel the "Dead March" was played upon the organ by Mr. James Muir. The service, which was taken part in by the three , resident ministers, the Revs. J. Eglinton, J. McTurk, and T. Rippoo, cemrnenced with the reading of an appropriate psalm, after which the hymn, " Hark! a voice divides the shy, Happy are the faithful dead! " was sung. The super- intendent minister (the Rev. J. Eglinton) then gave a short address in which he sketched the career of the deceased. He said:—My dear friends,—l hope you will all allow me thus to address you, for as it is said "a touch of nature , makes the whole world akin," so we meet together to-day sharing a common sorrow, and one feeling throbs in every heart. We meet to do honour to the memory of a faithful and godly elan, and to offer if we can a few words of sym- ! pathy and condolence with those who so deeply mourn his loss. As in reference to one spoken of in old time the , memory of the departed one is fragrant, and the circumstances ;of those who survive not only demand but receive popular i sympathy. In the case of this widow as in the case of that , other widow much people of the city or town ardwith her, the , memory of our late lamented and excellent friend, being SCINOL STATISTICS. fragrant, and as I believe embalmed and enshrined , in many, many hearts. Many of you have in all We take frorii tU recently published report of the Corn- , probability known him long and have learned to mittee of Council on Education the following statistiss re- estimate his worth both as a man and a Christian. My lating to this district : ' knowledge of him, as many of you know, extends only over I WARRINGTON. It was his, as we know, after many toils, many modation attendance. Then, as St. Ann's, Oh *426 II many of you know, he was engaged—as perhaps some of St. Benedict, R 256 my friends here to-day were engeged—in what is popu- St.Mary,Oh. lady known as the war of the Punjab. He joined in taking St. Peters, John-st., 218 Ch. * the fort of Lahore, and with the rest of his comrades St. Peters, Infant triumphantly marched in. I find there is an)thcr reward silver-street aTnr:nitib W, Ba'n-k '' :7-8 given in reference to his conduct in the nerth-western frontier of India in 1351, that he fought under Sir Celia Wycliffe: B Campbell—the late Lord Clive—a name endeared to many RUNCORN. thousands of Englishmen as well as Scotchmen, a name *631 that is a household word in the home of many, as you 121 know, as the hero of Lucknow. After 21 years's service there was was another reward given to him for faithful service 110 and good conduct, and then in 1862 he joined the 3rd bat- 173 *BO6 talion of the South Lancashire Regiment, under Colonel WIDNES. Ireland Blackburne, and became sergeant-major of that regiment five yeere ago. Just about 12 months since he re- National tired from all active service, as you mly remember, faithful St. Marie's 12 and appreciated to the end. You gentlemen now before et. Patr'ek's me, I suppose, many of you, joined in presenting to him i Simms Cross a testimonial of your own regard in the form of a very , Iltieeary ratnof -road .... handsome timepiece, and the commissioned officers of the Wes art at the same time, with the same feeling, pre- i see- sented him with a beautiful slyer tea service, supplemented by a cheque for money; so that all through his career, while he has been faithful, that faithfulness has been mani- festly appreciated, and, as it was seen in co many in- stances, rewarded. I commend to you, dear friends, the course of our beloved and departed brother, in his conduct and character. You know he bad firm principles—princi- ples of the godly life within, which were manifested by his ;course and deportment without. He was a mate of truth, of integrity, of great fidelity. He served his Queen with ' faithfulness, he served his God most lovingly and earnestly, land then having served thus his generation he fell asleep. Now you know, there is a sense in which smitten friends are angels sent on errands full of love to us; it is "for us they sicken, and for us they die," that we may catch their mantle. And you know there is no heritage that a father can leave to his children, that a citizen or a soldier can leave to his country or posterity like that of a godly char- acter and a spotless reputation; and we rejeice to know as we look upon his loved remains that it was said of him that he was a good man, and faithful above many. He had been unconscious for days, when his mind wake up just before he died. Responding to the call of his Commander, be said, "Yes, Lord, I am here ; I am coming," and thus doffing his helmet, and sheathing his sword, and furling his banner, he said in effect, as said the illustrious apostle of the Gentiles, "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith ; henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day; and not to me only, but unto all them also that love His appearing." My great wish and earnest prayer for you, my dear friends, is that you may so live as to love His appearing, and thus, by following Him as He followed Christ, secure through faith and patience the inheritance of the promise. At the conclusion of the address the hymn, "Brief life is here our portion," was rendered, and a prayer having been delivered by the Rev. J. McTurk, the service terminated. The body was then conveyed to the hearse, and the cortege continued its journey to the cemetery. LORD TOLLEMACRE'S EXPERIMENTS WITS ENSILAGE.— Lord Tollemache has opened one of the large silos which he had constructed at Pickforton for the storage of ensilage, and has ascertained that the experiment has been quite suc- cessful. The ensilage was stored when very damp, after rain, but it comes out sound and sweet. Both horses and cattle have been tested with the food. They will leave dry !Oder, and take to ensilage with avidity. Seven of the Strome Ferry Sabbatarian rioters who were liberated from Edinborough gaol, yesterday, after under- their sentence of four months' going only fifty-six ...,:e;s7 9f imprisonment, started for home immediately. They Werc provided by the prison officials with a railway pass and Ss. each. The other three, Roderick Fintayson, Finlay MacKenzie, and Alex. Mac Kay, remain in Edinborough. They were entertained last evening at a tea party, presieed over by the Rev. Dr. Begg, and were presented with a considerable sum which had been collected on their behalf. TEA VERSUS BEER.—The Lancet understands that Mr. Edward Payson Weston has announced his intention of un- dertaking a pedestrian tour through England and Wales with a view to demonstrate the saperiority of tea‘over beer and alcoholic dricks in general during periods of prolonged muscular exertion. He proposes to walk 50 miles a day for 100 days, aod at the close of each day's wa!k deliver in the town to which his day's walk may have brought him an address on temperance, having for its title " Tea versus Beer." It is proposed to commence the tour on November 5, and the task, if successfully accomplished, will be com- pleted on February 28. As Sunday will be tiken as a day of rest, the actual distance traversed each week will bo 303 miles.

ACCIDENT.—On Friday afternoon, the 16th inst., a. coach- man named Caine Ratcliffe, in the service of A. M. Smith, Esq., of Bolton-hey, Roby, met with a serious accident, whilst exercising a horse in a partly ploughed field. The horse stumbled, and thus threw its rider, breaking his collar bone in two places, and fracturing the splinter hone and causing other injuries. Dr. Henry Gorst attended thq injured man immediately. THE MAINTENANCE OF A LUNATIC WIFE.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, George Moore was summoned for not complying with an order of the Bench to contribute towards the support of his wife, an inmate in the Rainhill Asylum.—Mr. S. H. Hartley prosecuted on behalf of the Prescot Guardians.—lt appeared that on the 24th July an order had been made upon the defendant to pay ss. per week towards the support of his wile, whose maintenance cost the Guardians 9e. per week, hut he had since then allowed arrears to the extent of LI 10s. to accu- mulate, together with 19e. costs. He was employed at the London and Manchester Plate Glass Co.'s works, and earned £1 17s. Bd. per week.—Defendant said he aould net possibly contribute anything to the support of his wife, as he had a woman to ply to keep his house and a large family to keep --The Bench, however, made an order for the pay- ment of the arrears by weekly instalments of 2s. Eld., and also ordered defendant to natinue his weekly contribution of ss.

GOOD TEMPLARY AT PRESCOT.—On Wednesday, a meet- ing was held in Ackary's Rooms, Atherton-street, for the object of forming a branch lodge of Good Templars for the Prescot district. The meeting ass well attended; and severai members of the Order attended from St. Helens. After dis- cussing the desirableness of the object, ,the ,opinion of the meeting was taken, when it was4vident•Hiat all present were in favour of the movement, and at once enrolled-them- selves as members of the new lodge. From the list of mem- bers the following brethren were elected to the respective offices appended to each name, viz :—T. Wedgewood, D.G.W.0.T.; J. Case, W.C.T.; H. Quick, W.V.T.; J. Fegan, W.S ; T. Waine, W.C. •, E. Lloyd, W.M. The above were installed by Brother Whitehead, of Liverpool. District C.T., who attended the meetini, and took-much in- terest in the proceedings.

ASSAULTING OFFICERS FROM A HOUSE -Top.—A young man named Thomas Ford, whose powerful and athletic figure was very inadequately covered with clothing, was on Monday charged at the St. Helens Police Court with the following offences, viz.:—with having been drunk and dis- orderly; with assaulting P.C. Walsh; with assaulting PQ. Stalker; and with damaging the helmet of the first-named ofiicer. According to the evidence of the constables, Ford had been behaving in a disorderly manner in Copperasi street, late on Saturday night. Walsh requested him to go ' into the house, and he ac once went up an entry which led to the back entrance of his lodgings, but quickly reap- peared on the top of the house, from the safe eminence of , which he commenced an attack on the officers with bricks , and slates. The policemen found themselves under the ne- cessity of taking shelter in a passage, and here they re- mained till Ford, thinking they had gone, catne down from the house top and was captured by them. He, however, at once commence 4 to kick tutt strike in the most violent manner, in the course of which he knocked Walsh to the g-ound and damaged his helmet. Ford, it seemed, bad been several times convicted of like offences, and on the present occasion he was fined and costs, or 28 days' imprison- nent, for each of the assaults, and 10s, and costs, or 14 days, for damaging the helmet, and a similar fine for the drunkenness.

Lawton, John Bennett, W. Collier, Rosenller, and E. Ford ;1 tnd then followed the men and the permanent staff from the Barracks. After them walked members of the Wesleyan body (with which Mr. Chubb was identified ror many years), amongst whom were Messrs. M. Bowden, E. J. Guest, I. J. Biddle, I. Hayward, J. iummeregill, Joseph Dobson, J. Taft, J. Sanderson, Prince, J. E. Hall, Johnson, S. Moss Jos. Mercer, W.Horton, G. Rawling, Sm. To them succeeded the choir and :ongregation of Bewsey-road Chapel, and members of the Good lemplar Order, with which the deceased was also connected, and a number of other friends, including Mr. mthur Potter and Mr. J. Bloomfield. The residents along the route showed their respect for the deceased by drawing the blinds of their house-lan t p irthtlly dozing their business establishments. On arrival at the cemetery the body was carried through the Nonconformist mortuary chapel to the grave, around which a large concourse of spectators had issembled. The burial service was read by the Rev. J. Eg- linton, during which the coffin, which bore the simple in- scription, "Jacob Chubb, died September ldtb, 1883, aged 59 years," was lowered to its last resting-place amid many evidences of regret. At the conclusion of the service the choir sang the hymn, A few more years shall roll," and the firing party paid the mark of respect usually shown to a deceased comrade by firing over the grave the customary volleys.
